News.title: Evil son fractured mum’s ribs while she bravely battled cancer in vicious attack
News.content:
Evil son fractured mum’s ribs while she bravely battled cancer in vicious attack

Benjamin Joyner, has been jailed for attacking his seriously unwell mother so severely she was 'almost unrecognisable' to her neighbours, Exeter Crown Court was told

View 2 Images Benjamin Joyner (Image: Devon Live)

A mum suffering with cancer was left 'almost unrecognisable' by a vicious attack by her son which left her with a fractured rib, cuts and bruises.

‌



Benjamin Joyner, 38, went on a drunken rampage to leave his mother with significant bruising, cuts and a fractured rib, Exeter Crown Court heard. She was forced to escape the violence by running to a neighbour who said she was 'almost unrecognisable' due to the ferocity of the beating.

‌



Joyner said he blacked out after downing vodka and Vimto cocktails and couldn't remember anything during the incident in November 2025. He admitted one count of assault causing actual bodily harm and pleaded guilty to an unrelated offence of GBH against a man.

‌



View 2 Images The couple were hauled before Exeter County Court (Image: BPM MEDIA)

Joyner of Hoyles Road, Paignton, has a number of previous convictions for violence, reports Devon Live.

‌



He was jailed for three years both offences. The court was told Joyner had been watching TV at home with his brother before the pair argued and his brother left.

When his mum asked him what had happened he flipped and attacked her. She was left with bruising to her cheek, her neck, arm and hand, as well as the fractured rib. She fled to a neighbour and called 999.

She told the neighbour she 'could not believe' her son had attacked her, said prosecutor Laura D'Alessandro. Police arrested Joyner after subduing him with spray.

‌



The court heard his 56-year-old mum had cancer at the time. Bathsheba Cassel, defending, said the victim's skin may have tore more easily due to her condition.

Joyner has PTSD and thinks he has ADHD. His mum said she wants him to get help for his mental health so he can get his life back on track.

The offence was committed while Joyner was bail for the GBH. In the early hours of April 14, 2025, Joyner brutally beat a man at a house in Paignton.

Article continues below

The court was told four people had been drinking and smoking cannabis. Joyner repeatedly punched and kicked the man.

Two other defendants, Elise Stevens, 37, of Foxhole Road and Carl Barton, 34, of Hoyles Road, were convicted for their lesser part in the assault on the man. Stevens admitted battery and was given a 12-month conditional discharge. Barton admitted GBH and was given a community order for 18 months.

News.title: Anthropic founder says ‘AI kill switch’ may be needed as Trump declares 'hoax'
News.content:
Anthropic founder says ‘AI kill switch’ may be needed as Trump declares 'hoax'

Jack Clark was speaking after the ‘Godfather of AI’ Nobel prize winner Geoffrey Hinton said there is a ‘10 percent chance’ AI could ‘kill all humans’ in the next decade

View 2 Images Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic

AI may need a ‘kill switch’ to stop it going haywire, a co-founder of Anthropic, the firm behind the Claude chatbot, has said.

‌



Jack Clark, one of the seven co-founders of Anthropic had his say on artificial intelligence safety on Monday. Debate on the technology's development is raging after multiple warnings, including from the ‘Godfather of AI’ Nobel prize winner Geoffrey Hinton who said there is a ‘10 percent chance’ AI could ‘kill all humans’ in the next decade.

‌



Hinton's comments came after Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic employee over his fears the technology could end civilisation as we know it by 2036.

‌



That led to the bosses of the three major American AI firms — OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, and Grok’s Elon Musk — to agree external ‘reviewers’ should be installed at ‘frontier’ AI firms.

Now, another leading light has told the BBC a ‘kill switch’ might be necessary.

‌



"Should you mandate for companies to definitely have a kill switch? Is that kill switch verifiable by a third party?" Jack Clark asked. He continued: "I think that's the kind of thing society is going to want to know and might want to eventually pass rules around."

View 2 Images Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said on Monday he would welcome third-party auditors (Image: Bloomberg, Bloomberg via Getty Images)

But when pressed on if he thought artificial intelligence had a chance of killing humanity, he said he didn’t ‘think these statistics are that useful’, although he added allowing AI to continue ‘totally unregulated’ was a bad idea.

Article continues below

Politicians in the US have proposed the Kill Switch Act which would require companies to have a way to shut down problematic AI tools. However, President Donald Trump has said he believes claims AI could take over the world are a ‘hoax’, potentially stopping the Kill Switch Act in its tracks.

In the UK, the government rejected the idea of introducing a kill switch for British-developed AI models only three days ago.

News.title: Megan Stalter unrecognisable as she dresses as an Emmy for 2026 ceremony
News.content:
Megan Stalter unrecognisable as she dresses as an Emmy for 2026 ceremony

Celebrities are out in force for the 78th edition of the Emmy awards - but Megan Stalter is perhaps the star who has put the most effort in to her look, dressed head to toe in gold

View 3 Images Megan Stalter at the 78th Emmy Awards (Image: Deadline via Getty Images)

Megan Stalter has made quite the entrance at the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards red carpet, turning up painted head-to-toe in gold, which rendered her virtually unrecognisable.

‌



The 36-year-old star, who is nominated for an Emmy for her role as Kayla Schaeffer in the HBO Max comedy Hacks, is known for her bold red carpet stylings. So it was no surprise when, on Monday night, she arrived to walk the Emmys red carpet dressed as, well, an Emmy.

‌



Her skin was painted gold. Her hair was painted gold. She wore giant gold wings. Gold jewellery. Gold heels. Gold, gold, gold.

‌



As she posed on the carpet with Hacks co-creator Paul W. Downs, Stalter even took the chance to re-create the Emmy statuette’s iconic pose, with a little help from Downs.

View 3 Images Arms aloft, just like the real deal (Image: Variety via Getty Images)

Whilst it remains unclear who designed the gown or did her makeup, she gets full points for creativity. During the NBC preshow, she was asked if she was “wearing Versace,” and later “who designed it,” but the Emmy-nominated star did not divulge any details.

‌



Instead, she simply replied, “This is a remake because, well, let’s say I’m not a size three.”

Previously, she has arrived to walk the red carpet dressed as a pageant queen with a sash bearing the words “BEST GAY ACTOR” for the Critics Choice Association Celebration of LGBTQ+ Cinema & Television; a Diet Coke can at the Las Culturistas Culture Awards; and a coffee cup at the MTV Video Music Awards.

View 3 Images Megan Stalter attends the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards at Peacock Theater on September 14, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Image: Getty Images)

‌



At the Critics' Choice Awards earlier this year, she and Downs wore matching bright orange outfits that appeared to be a subtle throwback to a couples' outfit previously worn by Timothée Chalamet and Kylie Jenner.

Mariska Hargitay is hosting the Emmys at the Peacock Theatre in Los Angeles.

The night kicks off at 1 am BST on Tuesday, September 15, 2026 (with the red carpet pre-show starting around midnight BST). Live and free coverage is available exclusively on LG 1 via LG Smart TVs starting from 11.55 pm on Monday.

News.title: Met Police officer sacked after calling colleagues 'wastemen' on award-shortlisted podcast
News.content:
Met Police officer sacked after calling colleagues 'wastemen' on award-shortlisted podcast

PC Idominik Efeotor was sacked after labelling his colleagues "wastemen" and "batty holes" on his podcast that has been shortlisted for an award for its contribution to increasing diversity in the force

View 3 Images PC Idominik Efeotor has been sacked for calling police ‘wastemen’ and other slurs on his own podcast (Image: X/MetPoliceFed)

A Metropolitan Police office has been sacked for posting describing the force as corrupt on social media, labelling his colleagues "wastemen" and "batty holes".

PC Idominik Efeotor hosted his podcast 'The Good, the Bad and the Ugly', which reveals details about his life as a black police officer and has been shortlisted for two awards.

In one of the videos shared online he published material that could have identified an officer under a anonymity direction.

View 3 Images (Image: BBC)

The clips often feature Efeotor being critical of the Met and its directorate of professional standards (DPS).

It was found in an accelerated gross misconduct hearing that Efeotor breached the standards of professional behaviour when posting these clips. He was dismissed without notice.

The court heard that in one video the officer referred the the DPS as "absolute wastemen and that cesspit", whilst referring to a DPS officer as a "batty hole liar" in another video.

He also says "Bun the DPS" in most videos, meaning to reject them.

Nasreen Shah, representing the Met said at the hearing that Efeotor "publicly encouraged others not to trust certain officers" and "expressed contempt towards the DPS".

Shah added that he "used derogatory language towards officers and police staff and published content which was capable of undermining confidence in the police service on multiple occasions."

In May 2025, he posted a TikTok video discussing another misconduct case as he displayed a photo of an officer who had been anonymised within those proceedings, Shah told the hearing.

She said: "You sarcastically stated words to the effect of 'This is not the officer I'm talking about'."

Lawrence Davies, director of Equal Justice Solicitors, defending Efeotor said the video was taken down as his client was not aware the anonymity order would apply to him, reports the BBC.

View 3 Images Efeotor will be appealing the decision (Image: West Lothian Courier)

Davies added that the comments had been taken out of context and the majority of his podcast was a "fantastic and innovative way to improve recruitment and retention of black officers".

The podcast was shortlisted in the Multicultural Business and Community Champion (MBCC) and the The National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) Awards for its contribution to increasing diversity in the force this year.

Davies said: "In this country, we have something called the freedom of speech, which means you are allowed to say things outside of work which cause offence or upset to other people.

"And we don't even have a single statement from anyone, who has complained about the content of this. In fact, you have 22 character references of people who listen to the podcast who say it's great."

The defendant also explained that the force has been found by numerous reports to be institutionally racist, with the Casey Review highlighting that black officers were 81% more likely to be in the misconduct system than white colleagues.

Commander Colin Wingrove, chairing the hearing, said Efeotor had "chosen to use a platform to criticise and insult serving colleagues, which is likely to undermine the confidence that the public have in the police service."

It was concluded his behaviour did not meet the professional standards expected of a serving police officer.

‌



Following the hearing Davies said: "This is, unfortunately, a travesty of justice. It's yet another example of a black officer being retaliated against for speaking up.

"We will be appealing. This will end up at the employment tribunal, and at the end of all of that process, hopefully justice will be done."

Efeotor added: "I'm not surprised. This is what happens when you stand up for yourself and stand up for people that can't speak for themselves.

"There are people who have done things far worse than what I've done, who are still employed by the Met. They just happen to have lighter skin."

Commander Adam Slonecki, head of Specialist Operations, released a statement after the hearing that said: "Our officers can be in no doubt as to how they are expected to act on social media, and it is clear that PC Efeotor breached these standards on many occasions and despite repeated warnings.

"Not only does behaviour like this undermine public confidence in the Met, but it had a harmful and lasting impact on those he openly criticised, as well as the rest of his colleagues."

News.title: NATO fighter jets scramble over Lithuania as drone from Belarus shot down
News.content:
NATO fighter jets scramble over Lithuania as drone from Belarus shot down

An emergency alert was sent to mobile phones shortly after midnight warning residents of a potential aerial threat - a drone was destroyed 30 minutes later

View 2 Images A NATO fighter jet [file image] (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

NATO fighter jets have downed a drone over Lithuania with the country's leader stating the country will 'defend its airspace'.

‌



Lithuania's president Gitanas Nausėda wrote on X: "A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets. I thank Allied personnel for their swift response.

‌



"With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."

‌



Lithuania officially joined the NATO in 2004.

NATO, a 32-member alliance, was formed in 1949 to counter the risk of Soviet attack. It now focusses protecting ally counties by promising that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

View 2 Images Russian President Vladimir Putin (Image: Getty)

‌



Officials said the drone entered the Lithuania's airspace from neighbouring Belarus, reports LBC News - Belarus is a Russian ally.

An emergency alert was sent to mobile phones in Vilnius, Trakai and Elektrėnai shortly after midnight and residents were warned of a potential aerial threat. They were also urged to seek shelter.

The drone was destroyed around 30 minutes later, the country's National Crisis Management Centre said.

Article continues below

This is first time a drone has been shot down inside Lithuanian territory.

Just one day earlier, Vilnius Airport was briefly shut over a suspected drone threat that was later found to have been caused by a flock of birds.

Radar signatures from birds and drones can initially appear similar, authorities said.

News.title: Rush in prostate cancer checks thanks to 'Sir Chris Hoy effect'
News.content:
Rush in prostate cancer checks thanks to 'Sir Chris Hoy effect'

Six-times gold medallist Sir Chris Hoy is among the stars hailed for encouraging more men to check their risk of prostate cancer after going public with their own diagnoses

View 4 Images Sir Chris Hoy has been praised for encouraging more men to check their prostate cancer risk (Image: Getty Images)

The 'Sir Chris Hoy effect' is being hailed as the reason more men are checking their risk of prostate cancer.

‌



Prostate Cancer UK said there has been a rush of men using their 30-second online risk checker after a slew of high-profile public figures shared their personal experiences with the illness.

‌



In late 2024, six-times gold medallist Team GB cyclist Sir Chris Hoy revealed his prostate cancer was stage 4 and terminal - and has since been among the leading voices calling for more screening of men in at-risk groups.

‌



Jeremy Clarkson, John Barnes and Sir Tony Robinson have also shared prostate cancer diagnoses - while Chris Kamara told last month of his health scare after blood tests showed a slightly raised PSA level.

Chris Kamara's son breaks down in tears as Sky Sports icon opens up on health battle READ MORE :

View 4 Images Chris Kamara revealed a prostate cancer scare last month (Image: Getty Images)

New figures from the charity highlighted that 280,000 men checked their risk in the two months after Sir Chris Hoy's diagnosis. Prostate Cancer UK said that nearly 50,880 men completed its online risk checker in the week after Jeremy Clarkson revealed his diagnosis in June, up from 8,425 men the previous week.

‌



Mr Clarkson said: "I feel incredibly lucky that my cancer was caught early. It's why I'm still here today, feeling fine and looking forward to seeing my grandchildren grow up. "I've always said that if my story gets even one bloke to stop ignoring the issue and do something about it, then it's been worthwhile. To hear that actually tens of thousands of men have already taken the risk checker is something to be hugely proud of. "But there's still plenty more to do. So, I'll keep saying it: if you're a man, check your risk. It only takes a couple of minutes and it could save your life."

View 4 Images Jeremy Clarkson revealed his prostate cancer diagnosis in June (Image: Getty)

Meanwhile, 22,562 men took the risk checker the day after former PM Lord David Cameron announced he had been treated for prostate cancer in November 2025, up from 2,175 the previous Monday. Prostate Cancer UK said that since its online risk checker was launched in 2020, it had been completed by more than five million men.

‌



Amy Rylance, director of health services, equity and improvement at Prostate Cancer UK, said: "Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in the UK, but too many men are still being diagnosed by chance and, sadly, often too late for a cure. "Our risk checker helps men navigate this complex disease, empowering men with a clear way to understand their risk and their choices. We hear from so many men who say a celebrity diagnosis, like Jeremy Clarkson or Lord Cameron's, inspired them to check their risk and in some cases saved their life.

View 4 Images Former England international John Barnes had his prostate removed (Image: Offside via Getty Images)

"We're extremely grateful to everyone who has publicly shared their experiences of prostate cancer, shining a light onto this disease that is much easier to treat when found earlier, and kickstarting many lifesaving conversations. "We know men need a safe and effective screening programme. Prostate Cancer UK's Transform trial will get us the evidence we need to make this a reality and give every man the chance for an early diagnosis. Until then, public figures telling their stories and inspiring men to check their risk are playing an important role in helping men and loved ones across the country, and we thank them for their vital work."

‌



Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men, with one one in eight expected to develop it within their lifetimes. The risk is double among black men, and is highest in men aged over 50.

Symptoms include difficulty passing urine or needing to go to the toilet more frequently, especially at night.

If you are over 50, or over 45 if you are Black or have a family history of the disease, you can arrange a PSA blood test by booking an appointment with your GP. This measures the amount of prostate-specific antigen, a protein made by the prostate gland, in a sample of your blood.

Article continues below

Targeted prostate cancer screening every two years is currently available for men aged 45 to 61 who have the high-risk BRCA2 gene - though campaigners are calling for mass testing for all men

News.title: Hair product health fears as one in three with Afro hair report physical impact
News.content:
Hair product health fears as one in three with Afro hair report physical impact

New World Afro day research has sparked fresh calls for scrutiny over products aimed at Afro hair, as campaigners and experts raise concerns about safety, regulation and the use of chemical treatments

View 4 Images Sarah began chemically straightening her hair aged 13 (Image: Getty Images for Bauer)

Sarah-Jane Crawford was just 13 when she first began chemically straightening her hair, inspired by the sleek styles of the R&B stars she grew up watching.

At the time, the TV and radio presenter gave little thought to the potential effects of the products she was using - something she now believes consumers should be better informed about.

Her experience comes as new World Afro Day research found one in three people with Afro-textured hair said hair products had negatively affected their physical health, compared with one in 10 without Afro hair. The findings, based on responses from 1,442 people, were released to mark the 10th World Afro Day.

View 4 Images World Afro day founder Michelle De Leon (Image: @‌LifeofTruly1/Instagram)

World Afro Day takes over Parliament for in hopeful bid to end Afro hair discrimination READ MORE :

Michelle De Leon, who founded World Afro Day in 2017, said: “You cannot argue with health evidence if something shows you in a quantifiable way that it impacts somebody’s health.”

She said: “We’ve got big beauty brands who have products that are aimed to introduce chemicals to children’s bodies to make them feel more beautiful and more acceptable to a European standard of beauty and that is wrong. I don’t even understand how we can justify chemical cosmetic treatments for children any children but actually for black children this has been going on for decades through chemical relaxers.”

Research in the US has also examined the possible health effects of hair straightener use from a young age. A 2025 study using data from more than 4,000 Black women in the US Sister Study found hair straightener use between the ages of 10 and 13 may be associated with young-onset uterine fibroids.

Sarah-Jane had a fibroid the size of a grapefruit removed in 2015 and said the research has made her reflect on her own health. The former Xtra Factor presenter told the Mirror: “One thing I do know is that the research time and time again keeps on pointing back to there being a link between regular relaxer use and things like fibroids, especially with the sister study that was done in the U.S.

“And I can’t say whether there’s definitely, it’s definitely been like hair relaxer use that’s caused the fibroids. I’ll never know that for sure.”

Michelle said: “But all the evidence, all the evidence shows that hair products aimed at Afro hair have higher levels of harmful chemicals in them. Just the evidence is there. Yet regulation has not responded to this.”

View 4 Images Parliament is examining whether UK rules adequately product consumers (Image: Getty Images)

Hair relaxers are regulated as cosmetics in Britain and must comply with cosmetic safety rules. But questions over whether existing protections and evidence go far enough have reached Parliament. Parliament’s Science, Innovation and Technology Committee launched an inquiry into hair and beauty products in December 2025, examining whether UK regulation effectively assesses scientific evidence and protects consumers from potential harm.

In 2023, Labour MP Chi Onwurah had also asked whether the Government had assessed the impact of lye-containing hair relaxers on Black women’s health and associated health inequalities. The Department for Business and Trade said such an assessment had not been carried out, while stressing that lye was already restricted under cosmetics regulations.

Sarah-Jane, who has also experienced endometriosis and is now in perimenopause, said she has wondered whether years of using straightening products could have affected her reproductive health. She said: “I feel like if I hadn’t been using certain products I may have been able to go on to have more children. I just can’t prove it.”

Looking back, Sarah-Jane wishes she had known possible risks from a young age. She said: “I think what’s disappointing is that if I had known the serious potential impact of these products, I definitely would have avoided them. But because there wasn’t that fear factor, I thought the worst that was going to happen is that I was going to have a scab on the side of my head.”

A 2023 study by researchers at Boston University, using data from almost 45,000 women in the Black Women’s Health Study, found long-term chemical relaxer use was associated with an increased risk of uterine cancer among postmenopausal Black women, although no such link was found among premenopausal women.

View 4 Images World Afro Day's latest research surveyed more than 1,400 people (Image: Getty Images)

Laura Waters, Professor of Pharmaceutical Analysis at the University of Huddersfield said: “Most worryingly to me is the availability of these products to children as they are easily available on the high street. It would be great if there is more awareness of just how dangerous these products can potentially be."

“Any chemicals will have been through rigorous toxicity testing to be included in such products so they are considered ‘safe’ to use but it doesn’t necessarily mean we should be relaxed about their use.”

The World Afro Day survey also found 84% of respondents said it was very important that people could trust hair product ingredients were not harmful. Sarah said: “I was using a lot of harsh chemicals to get a quick result: clean, flatten, burn, straighten. And so just thinking they had absolutely no impact. You know, it’s on the market. I can buy it. Why is it going to be unsafe?”

Her concerns eventually compelled her to start her own haircare company, Clean Curls.

World Afro Day was founded in 2017 and has since expanded beyond its celebration of Afro hair into research, education and campaigning. Reflecting on the milestone, Michelle said: "Celebration mission accomplished - 10 years of celebration but liberation, I hope it doesn’t take a a decade to get there.”

The 10th World Afro Day will be marked with a three-day ‘Fro Festival in King’s Cross, London, with community catwalks, free hair and scalp health checks, panels and other events celebrating Afro hair and culture..

News.title: Mitch McConnell seen for first time in 3 months after police swarm home
News.content:
Mitch McConnell seen for first time in 3 months after police swarm home

The US senator has been recovering at his residence after being hospitalised following a fall on June 14 - as calls mount for the 84-year-old to provide proof of his capacity to serve

View 3 Images Senator Mitch McConnell has not been seen in months (Image: Getty Images)

Video footage has captured the moment US lawmaker Mitch McConnell is wheeled onto the Senate floor for the first time in months.

‌



McConnell, 84, had been recovering at his residence after being hospitalised after a fall on June 14 and case of pneumonia, he said in previous comments provided by his office.

‌



View 3 Images Police at the residence of Republican Senator Mitch McConnell (Image: Nick Sortor)

‌



The Republican senator was seen on Monday, September 14, when his colleagues reconvened on Capitol Hill after a five-week recess.

His office remained largely quiet for most of the day.

‌



He has stayed out of the public eye since his fall and his office previously said that the Kentucky Senator would continue his physical recovery at home while working on official business.

View 3 Images Mitch McConnel being pushed in a wheelchair through the Senate Subway during the Senate War Powers vote on April 22, 2026 (Image: Getty Images)

McConnell has not participated in any interviews or made any public appearances since he was first hospitalised, but he has released three written updates on his health and two photos of him and his wife, which were distributed through his staff.

Article continues below

This has done little to quell speculation and pressure, with some calling for him to resign.

In July, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat, called on McConnell to "provide proof of his capacity to serve, or resign."

News.title: Lucy Letby public inquiry findings set to be published
News.content:
The findings from a public inquiry into how Lucy Letby was able to repeatedly murder and harm babies will be published later on Tuesday.

The Thirlwall Inquiry was set up to look into what happened at the Countess of Chester Hospital between 2015 and 2016, while Letby was working as a nurse in the neonatal unit.

Letby, now 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, including one baby whom she tried to murder twice.

The inquiry was not tasked with examining Letby's guilt. Instead, it investigated how concerns about the neonatal nurse were handled by the hospital and whether action could have been taken sooner to stop her.

Among the key questions the report may answer is whether any babies might have lived or avoided injury if action had been taken earlier.

Letby was moved from the neonatal unit to administrative duties in July 2016 after consultants expressed concerns about her to the hospital's executive team. But the inquiry has been examining whether alarm bells should have started ringing earlier, for example in June 2015 after three babies died in quick succession.

The inquiry, led by one of the country's most senior judges Lady Justice Thirlwall, involved six months of evidence and thousands of documents at a cost of more than Â£18.5m.

It is expected that the report will find there were significant safeguarding failures, and will recommend changes across the NHS.

The chairwoman of the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) - the only organisation with the power to send Letby's case back to the Court of Appeal - has told the BBC the CCRC would be paying close attention to the report.

Letby has previously been denied permission to appeal against her convictions on two occasions.

Her defence lawyer Mark McDonald told BBC Newsnight on Monday he had submitted "nearly 30 expert reports to the CCRC really undermining the whole safety of the convictions" - and that it was "more evidence" than "any other case" in the CCRC's history.

He added: "If she is innocent, as I believe, as 30-odd experts believe, then everything that has gone before the inquiry and every recommendation has operated on the wrong premise."

McDonald also said he "fundamentally disagreed" that his case had been undermined after two experts quit his team.

It emerged on Monday that that Prof Geoff Chase, from the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, and chemical engineer Helen Shannon, had withdrawn from Letby's defence team, after claiming some of the evidence being put forward was inconsistent with the available evidence and science.

McDonald told Newsnight he was "sad that they've gone" but insisted those experts still believed "Lucy Letby is innocent".

"What they're saying is: 'We think our argument's better than your argument and therefore we're coming out of it'."

News.title: AI 'kill switch' may need to be mandatory, Anthropic co-founder tells BBC
News.content:
Clark told the BBC that specifics around "kill switch" requirements and verification should be part of "the larger policy conversation" taking place around AI.

"Should you mandate for companies to definitely have a kill switch? Is that kill switch verifiable by a third party?" he asked.

"I think that's the kind of thing society is going to want to know and might want to eventually pass rules around."

Anthropic, which was formed in 2021 by a group of former employees of its rival OpenAI, is currently at the centre of a debate around AI safety.

Last week, a post from an artificial intelligence researcher who quit Anthropic over concerns AI could wipe out humanity went viral.

In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger said he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was ">10% within the next decade".

Computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC on Friday that a 10% chance of AI killing all humans was "not unreasonable", external.

He and others with similar concerns have suggested AI could do so by taking control of important systems connected to the internet and turning them on humans.

However, some in the AI industry have suggested the fears around it destroying humanity are overstated or may be designed to generate hype.

Clement Delangue, leader of the developer platform Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI bots, said last week: "Sorry, but asking Jacob [Coxon] about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change."

"Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."

George Arison, the leader of Grindr, said the fears going around AI tools were being used by the companies to support their business plans.

Anthropic, which was valued at $965bn (Â£713bn), is preparing for an initial public offering on the stock market, allowing people to buy shares in its firm.

OpenAI, which was most recently valued at $852bn (Â£630bn), had been expected to do the same, but OpenAI's Altman said on Friday this would not happen this year due to the current debate around AI safety.

Arison said: "The only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'"

Asked what percentage he would put on all humans being killed by AI, Clark said: "I don't think these statistics are that useful", but added that allowing AI to continue as a "totally unregulated industry" was a bad idea.

"We are rolling dice with immense risks," Clark said. "And the point is, we have to change the course of this industry."

News.title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet
News.content:
The Â£72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers from two British billionaires is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.

In short, how should political parties be paid for, and by who?

And, what is a legitimate donation and what isn't?

It is worth setting out the law, in broad terms, now and how the government hopes to change it.

Right now, there is no limit on how much anyone, living in the UK or abroad, can give to a British political party as long as the individual is registered to vote in the UK.

But the government has been planning a change in the law for months, which would limit donations from Brits abroad to Â£100,000 each per year, backdated to 25 March this year.

But, crucially, the law hasn't changed yet and some of the key details in that proposed new law - such as what residency requirements would need to be passed to be classified as no longer being abroad - haven't been decided yet.

The reason for that date, 25 March, ministers argue, is that is the day a review by the retired civil servant Philip Rycroft was published,, external the first recommendation of which was that there should be "an annual cap on political donations from British voters living abroad".

On that same day, the then-cabinet minister Steve Reed told the Commons, external that cap would be Â£100,000 per year. He also added that it would "apply retrospectively" from that date onwards, even though the law at the time, and indeed now, has not yet changed.

Two big questions arise from this plan: is it proportionate to limit what British folk abroad can donate to UK political parties, given they are arguably less invested in the country than people living here?

And is it unfair, even morally questionable, to pass a law, but then backdate when its impact begins?

Fast forward to the last few days and along come these colossal donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, two cryptocurrency billionaires who until recently lived in Hong Kong and Thailand respectively.

They have both now returned to the UK.

In his first interview since these donations became public, Nigel Farage told me unequivocally that the money from both men was legal under the law as it stands now.

But he was equivocal when I asked him if they would legal under the law the government hopes to pass shortly.

"Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever," Farage told me.

Ah, today, I pointed out.

"Retrospectively declaring donations illegal - that simply cannot be," he pressed on, adding "you cannot confiscate money that has been given legally within the law as it stands."

That is a political, perhaps moral argument, but not a legal one - if the government changes the law, the law of the land will have changed, possibly with consequences for whether those donations are legal.

News.title: Nato jets down drone that entered Lithuanian airspace
News.content:
Nato fighter pilots have shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace overnight, the Lithuanian president said.

Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.

Lithuanian President Gitanas NausÄda wrote in a statement on X: "A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets."

The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, a spokesperson for the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said.

Drone alerts sounded across the capital Vilnius and surrounding region earlier on Tuesday.

Lithuania's armed forces and Italian pilots serving in the Nato Air Defence Mission "showed a swift and responsible response" to the drone incursion, Lithuania's Ministry of Defence said.

NausÄda's post on social media added: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."

Moscow has not commented on the incident.

Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.

Drone sightings were reported in Lithuania on Sunday. The crisis management centre later said an object had "likely" entered from Belarus and travelled across the country's territory before entering the airspace of Russia. The 13 September incident did not trigger air threat alerts.

Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.

Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".

These actions are of a "preventive nature" and are aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions", it added.

Residents in Lithuania's capital were forced to take shelter across Vilnius in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.

Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.

Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members".

News.title: Watch: Selena Gomez, Zendaya and other stars light up Emmys red carpet
News.content: Selena Gomez, Dakota Fanning and Brett Goldstein were among the celebrities to pose for the camera on the blue version of the 78th Emmy Awards red carpet ahead of the ceremony in Los Angeles, California.

News.title: US has deployed a space weapon, air force secretary says
News.content:
The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities.

US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action.

Speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday, Meink said the US was ready for "evolving threats", but did not elaborate on the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.

Senior military leaders have previously said they planned to boost military capabilities in space, citing Russian and Chinese programmes developing ways to attack and disrupt US satellites in a future conflict.

The Trump administration has said that space-based capabilities - and interceptor missiles - are a crucial part of its planned "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US from missiles and other airborne threats.

A 1967 treaty banned weapons of mass destruction in orbit. Since then, key powers including the US, Russia, and China have been exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

Last year President Donald Trump issued an executive order underlining the US Space Force's role in not only defending assets, but also as an attacking force.

The US Space Force - the newest branch of the US military in more than 70 years - was launched in 2019 as a way to protect American assets in space, including hundreds of satellites used for communication and surveillance.

A US Space Force spokesperson said: "Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain â employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities through disruption, degradation and even destruction, if necessary.

"These capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes at the direction of combatant commands."

In early February, it was revealed that two Russian satellites have likely intercepted the communications of at least a dozen European ones since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Such interceptions may have allowed Russian intelligence services to read the sensitive data they transmit, or hypothetically, even to take control of the satellites.

In 2024, the US said Russia had launched a satellite which it believed may be capable of attacking other such probes. Russia did not publicly comment on the issue.

The US Space Force says China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernisation strategy," while Russia "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts".

News.title: Man admits drugging and raping wife over 20 years
News.content:
A man accused of drugging and raping his wife without her knowledge over a 20-year period has admitted 60 offences against her.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's legal right to anonymity, had already admitted some counts at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court, including rape.

The wife watched proceedings from the public gallery supported by members of her family.

The husband, in his sixties, became visibly emotional as he repeated the word guilty to dozens of charges - including multiple counts of rape, assault by penetration and administering a substance with intent - and at one point was invited to sit down in the dock by the judge.

Twelve other men deny multiple serious sexual offences against the same woman.

The husband, from the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, will be sentenced for the counts he has admitted at the conclusion of the trial.

A 13th man previously admitted sexual offences against the woman.

The husband's offending against his wife, who he was married to for decades, took place over a period going back to 2004, while the accusations involving the other men range from September 2018 to November 2025.

The other defendants are:

Philip Wild, 58, from Stockport

Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport

Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester

Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester

Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport

Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport

Mohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abode

Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich, Cheshire

Richard Townsend, 37, from Rochdale

Karl Lindsay, 55, Taunton, Somerset

Daniel Rayner, 42, from, Whitstable, Kent

David Graves, 59, from, Ilkeston, Derbyshire

The trial is due to continue in the coming weeks.

News.title: Harry and Meghan to have security review and children change school
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are going to be given a review of their publicly-funded security after their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

It has also emerged that the Sussexes have changed their children's school, only days after they first started, over security concerns about the school run.

The prince previously mounted an unsuccessful legal challenge over his police security when he was visiting from the US.

But the family's return to the UK has meant a different set of circumstances for their taxpayer-funded security, and last week Ravec - which stands for the Executive Committee for the Protection of Royalty and Public Figures - met to discuss their case.

This committee, which includes representatives of the Home Office, the police and the Royal Household, seems ready to review potential dangers.

This means a so-called Risk Management Board will consider the threats against them and the level of police protection they might need - although no final decision on the outcome has been reached.

The review will include security for their children Archie, aged seven, and Lilibet, aged five - and as first reported by HELLO! magazine, the children have switched schools from where they started earlier this month because of a security issue.

The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.

A source close to the couple said: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

It is understood that Prince Harry had a review of his potential risks earlier in the summer, but before it was known that he would be returning to live in the UK.

This will be the first such security review for Meghan since she and Prince Harry ceased being working royals when they moved to the US in 2020.

Meghan posted footage on social media of the family at the weekend, showing a family outing in the countryside.

Separately on Monday, Prince Harry was told that Uganda would now take part in the Invictus Games next year.

It had appeared that Uganda was going to withdraw from the games for injured servicemen and women, in the fallout from a letter sent on behalf of King Charles emphasising that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.

The King's private secretary had spoken on the phone to Uganda's military chief, reassuring him that he approved of Uganda's participation in the games.

News.title: Burnham cancels engagements after death of father
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has cancelled official engagements on Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's.

He had been due to host a meeting of business leaders in Downing Street on Monday, and was expected to speak at the annual trade union TUC Congress in Brighton on Tuesday.

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

He had also said his father's illness was so advanced that he did not know his son had become prime minister.

Burnham told the BBC that while his father could not be there when he entered No 10 to take up the role, he and his mother had "exchanged a few words about my dad and how proud he would be".

"That's a little hard, but then again I've said, it's their achievement", he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg in July.

"The emotion of that moment was, well, bittersweet - it was painful in one way but beautiful in another."

The prime minister later said care home staff had shown his father footage of him entering Downing Street, calling it a "wonderful" thing.

Burnham said he wanted to help "my dad and the millions like him" when setting out plans to reform adult social care.

He said he had been "overwhelmed" by the skills and professionalism of care workers supporting his father.

Burnham has described how his father, a former telephone engineer, had raised him with "laughter, love and support" alongside his mother Eileen in Culcheth, Cheshire.

In his 2024 book Look North, he wrote that neither of his parents had attended university, but could have done had they "grown up in a different time and different place".

"Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go."

Opposition politicians have offered their condolences to Burnham and his family.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.

"A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won't ever be the same again."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "My heart goes out to the prime minister on the loss of his dad.

"From our conversations he sounded like a wonderful man."

Green party leader Zack Polanski said: "There are moments in life such as this sad time that transcend politics and I join the whole country in sending condolences."

News.title: UK set to turn cooler as unsettled weather continues
News.content:
Much of the UK is set to feel cooler from Tuesday, as more changeable weather moves in.

Parts of the UK are also likely to see some spells of rain, especially to northern and western parts of the UK.

The rest of the week stays a little unsettled with further spells of rain.

It could turn more settled into next week with temperatures rising above average for some, though heatwave conditions are looking increasingly unlikely.

Tuesday will start off relatively warm and muggy across central and south-eastern areas of England but further north and west it will start to feel a little cooler.

That cooler air will be moving south-east behind a cold front that will also bring a spell of rain across England and Wales for a time.

Fresher north-westerly winds will develop across all areas bringing showers - some heavy - to Scotland, Northern Ireland and more north-western parts of England and Wales.

Maximum temperatures will be around five degrees lower than Monday's values with 17 to 22C across the UK.

This is closer to the average for the time of year.

News.title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age
News.content:
Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.

Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff.

Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list.

The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would.

The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work.

It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document.

The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it.

Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app.

The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age.

This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult.

Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'".

Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step".

He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector.

This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said.

News.title: Westminster's time is coming to an end, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish leaders say
News.content:
The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end".

The nationalist leaders from Plaid Cymru, Sinn FÃ©in and the SNP - who want their countries to leave the United Kingdom - signed an agreement on Monday which said no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy".

But while Scotland's John Swinney and Northern Ireland's Michelle O'Neill called for referendums at a joint press conference, Wales' Rhun ap Iorwerth declined to give a timetable for one in his country.

Labour and Reform accused Plaid of wanting to break up the UK.

Swinney and ap Iorwerth's governments later backed a separate agreement agreed to work together on pressing UK government on "fairness" in funding and powers.

For the first time since devolution began, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland all have first ministers who want to leave the United Kingdom.

All three met on Monday as representatives of their parties. Sinn FÃ©in president Mary Lou McDonald also attended.

The memorandum of understanding said: "For people watching across these islands - for people watching around the world - there could be no clearer sign that Westminster's time is coming to an end.

"No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future.

"We recognise that our parties have different constitutional positions and that each nation will determine its own future in its own way and in its own time."

News.title: Balaclava ban comes into force in Nottingham city centre
News.content:
A ban on face coverings in Nottingham city centre has officially come into force.

From today, police and community protection officers will be able to ask people to remove coverings if they "reasonably believe" they are being used to conceal their identity to commit crime or anti-social behaviour.

Anyone who refuses to comply could face a Â£70 fixed penalty notice or be prosecuted, with courts able to impose a maximum fine of Â£1,000.

The leader of Nottingham City Council, Neghat Khan, said residents had felt intimidated when they saw people wearing balaclavas, skeleton masks or other face coverings without a legitimate reason.

"Our residents should be able to live, work and spend time in Nottingham without feeling frightened or unsafe," Khan previously told the BBC.

"That is why we are taking decisive action and becoming one of the first cities in the country to introduce a restriction of this kind."

The enforcement will not apply to face coverings worn for legitimate reasons, including religious, cultural, health, work, weather or personal safety reasons.

It will be up to officers to determine whether or not coverings are being worn legitimately.

News.title: Speedboat killer jailed for attack on girlfriend
News.content:
Speedboat killer Jack Shepherd has been jailed for 20 months with a further four years on extended licence for violently assaulting his girlfriend, including hitting her chest with a set of hot barbecue tongs.

The 38-year-old had pleaded guilty to two counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and damaging property at Isleworth Crown Court in July.

The attacks happened in February and June last year and sparked Shepherd's recall to prison.

He was originally jailed in 2018 for six years and six months for manslaughter over the death of 24-year-old Charlotte Brown when his speedboat crashed during a first date.

Shepherd was jailed for a further four years at Exeter Crown Court in 2019 for a drink-fuelled attack on a barman in March 2018 at a Devon hotel.

He was released on licence in January 2024, but faced recall to prison in September last year after he was accused of violence towards the woman.

According to a prosecution summary of the case, Shepherd started dating his former partner in August 2024, but towards the end of the year she accused him of being abusive and threatening.

In February 2025, he admitted pinning down the woman and "punching her several times, causing bruising to her arm and top of leg" during an argument.

In the second incident, in June 2025, Shepherd got angry with her after she said that he had burned a pizza on the barbecue, and "proceeded to hit her with the barbecue tongs on her left breast which caused a permanent scar".

News.title: No police collusion in sectarian murder but multiple RUC failings included tip-off to suspect
News.content:
An inquiry into the sectarian murder of Robert Hamill has found police officers who were in a vehicle near the attack did not condone or collude with the attackers.

However, the inquiry said there were multiple police failings in the investigation, including a tip-off to a suspect to destroy the clothing he wore that night.

The report, published on Monday, external, highlighted multiple wrongful omissions in the subsequent murder investigation including a failure to properly search the home of a key suspect.

Robert Hamill was 25 when he died after he was beaten by loyalists in Portadown, County Armagh, in 1997.

The inquiry concluded in 2009 and its report was completed in 2011 but the findings could not be published until three prosecutions in connection with the case concluded.

The inquiry concluded: "We find that Robert Hamill had been assaulted before the Land Rover officers got out of their vehicle.

"However, they were not aware of the assault and after they had got out of their vehicle, they attempted to restore order.

"They did not in any way condone or collude with attackers."

Although the inquiry found that the four officers in the police Land Rover could not have prevented the murder, the police investigation was flawed â both at the scene and in the days that followed.

"The inquiry found that serving RUC [Royal Ulster Constabulary] officers were guilty of wrongful omissions and that those omissions arose both at the scene and during the initial investigation," it said.

The inquiry concluded that some of the mistakes in the investigation were negligent, while others were deliberate.

The 290-page report followed an inquiry which cost approximately Â£33m.

The actions of the officers in the Land Rover have been the subject of many claims and counter-claims in the past three decades.

Given how close they were to the scene, questions have been asked about why they did not intervene sooner.

The inquiry found that they were "distracted talking to two members of the public".

On whether they could have done more, the three-person inquiry panel did not have a unanimous view.

Two members concluded that the officers in the police vehicle were not guilty "of any wrongful act or omission in relation to the death of Robert Hamill".

However, on this issue the chairperson Sir Edwin Jowitt "expressed a dissenting view".

News.title: British Crown symbol was branded on enslaved Africans, research finds
News.content:
Enslaved African people were branded with an identifying mark that included an emblem of the British Crown, according to new research by a project documenting British involvement in the slave trade.

Prof William Pettigrew, who led the Register of British Slave Traders research, described the imprinting as a "dramatic and harrowing" symbol of the monarchy's relationship to slavery.

The register, external lists 13,000 individuals and hundreds of institutions known to have invested in Britain's role in slavery between 1563 and 1807, when the trade was abolished across the British Empire.

Researchers say it is the most comprehensive examination of a national community of slave traders ever undertaken.

Dr Nicholas Radburn, historian at Lancaster University and co-investigator in the project, told the BBC he first found the identifying mark - which is an image of the Crown, with the South Sea Company logo below it - while looking through the company's archives at the British Library in 2022.

Founded in 1711, the South Sea Company was set up as a public and private British company and trafficked thousands of enslaved Africans.

Radburn said it was "remarkable" to find records of the branding "buried in a very nondescript sounding volume: 'The Register of Instruments'".

In 2024, he found letters that helped piece the story together. They were from the company's director to their "factors" (slave traders) in the Spanish Americas, Radburn explained.

"The letters were full of very detailed instructions on how to conduct the slave trade," he recalled.

One letter from February 1714 was "exceptional because it laid bare so clearly the ways in which the London-based directors were personally involved in the violence that was committed against the enslaved in the Americas".

The directors sent irons made in England for slave traders to use to mark enslaved African people on their left shoulder with the emblem.

The purpose, the letter outlined, was to distinguish the company's slaves from others.

In an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Pettigrew - from King's College London - said there were all sorts of connections between the monarchy and slavery, not just this "brutal imprint".

"If you think about the history of the monarchy when it was at its absolute lowest ebb, when King Charles I was executed, members of the royal family relaunched the monarchy, its finances and its reputation, by investing in the transatlantic slave trade," he said.

He said it was important to draw a distinction between the monarchy as an institution, and the individuals who led it.

"The institution is the same as it was hundreds of years ago.

"So when we talk about the role of the slave trade in rehabilitating the monarchy or improving its position, we're talking about an institution that is still very much a part of British life today.

"In a court of law, the monarchy is the same institution today as it was in the 17th Century."

In a statement, Buckingham Palace said King Charles "has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today".

The King is "grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed".

Dolly Parton was honored at the 2026 Emmy Awards in an emotional segment just moments before a larger in memoriam tribute to those television actors who died within the last year.

Sally Field and Reba McEntire led the tribute to Parton, who died August 25 aged 80. Parton was notably a music icon, but did make numerous television appearances, including two different eponymous variety shows and guest stints on series including Hannah Montana.

“If there are truly angels on earth, then we just lost one,” Field said of her Steel Magnolias co-star. “I adored her from day one. How could you not?”

“I couldn’t see then what a real giant Dolly was, not just as an artist, but as a human,” Field continued.

“I am not the only one on earth who will love you forever and ever,” Field concluded.

open image in gallery Reba McEntire led a tribute to Dolly Parton during the Emmys ( Reuters )

McEntire, clad in a sparkly white gown, then took the stage to sing Parton’s song, “Appalachian Memories.”

“I love you Dolly. So much,” McEntire concluded her performance.

Moments later, Parton was included in a larger segment that paid tribute to the numerous television stars who died during the last year.

Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy began by paying tribute to Home Alone and Schitt’s Creek star Catherine O’Hara.

“She wasn’t just a wife and mother ... she was my mama. She was our mama,” an emotional Culkin said. “She always showed up when I asked her. We’re showing up for her.”

open image in gallery Macaulay Culkin (left), Annie Murphy and Dan Levy paid tribute to Catherine O'Hara during the Emmys ( AP )

Murphy and Levy also shared stories in remembrance of O’Hara, before Noah Kahan began singing “Bridge Over Troubled Water.”

Eric Dane, Hayden Panettiere, James Van Der Beek, Vincent Pastore, Anthony Head, Sam Neill, Tim Curry, Shelley Fabares, and Bob Mackie — who died earlier Monday — were just some of the dozens of names included in the tribute.

Jamie Lee Curtis then walked onstage to pay tribute to Cheers co-creator James Burrows and Rob Reiner, who posthumously won an Emmy for his guest starring appearance on The Bear.

The 2026 Emmy Awards are underway in Los Angeles, recognizing the year’s most acclaimed series.

Hosted by Law & Order star Mariska Hargitay, the 78th annual ceremony is airing live on NBC and streaming on Peacock from Los Angeles’ Peacock Theater.

The Pitt leads the crowd with a whopping 25 total nominations, followed by the final season of Hacks with 24 and newcomer Widow’s Bay with 19. This year’s ceremony has been spread across three nights, with several categories having been announced last weekend.

Just moments into the ceremony, Jean Smart made Emmys history, tying Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman for the most overall acting wins (eight) in Emmy history. With the win, Smart has officially taken home lead actress honors for every season of Hacks, marking the first time an actor has accomplished that feat.

Matthew Rhys made Emmys history later in the ceremony, becoming the first actor to win two leading actor categories in the same year; for lead actor in a limited or anthology series, and then for lead actor in a comedy series.

News.title: Watch: Taylor Swift makes surprise appearance at 2026 Emmy Awards
News.content:
Taylor Swift surprised viewers at the 2026 Emmy Awards with an unexpected cameo in a Law & Order-themed skit.

The pop star appeared in the middle of the telecast on Monday (September 14) night, as host Mariska Hargitay attempted to decode whether Swift will show up at the awards ceremony.

The singer then made her entrance dressed in a suit, joining the squad as a detective in the sketch.

Her appearance came after she skipped the Emmys to attend her husband’s Travis Kelce’s Kansas City Chiefs game, where she was seen sitting alongside Tom Cruise.

California Governor Gavin Newsom has revealed that he won’t run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris does.

Newsom is considered a top potential Democratic candidate in the next presidential election, which is a little more than two years away. While the governor is still weighing a potential run, he told CNN’s Jake Tapper in a new interview that he wouldn’t throw his hat in the ring if Harris was in the race.

“I wouldn’t run if she ran,” Newsom said while fly fishing in Montana with Tapper as part of a series where the news anchor chats with politicians in some of their favorite places. “Why would I? I wouldn’t do that to her. I wouldn’t do that to you. I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time.”

When Tapper asked Newsom to explain, the governor suggested that pitting two California Democrats against each other would force their shared base to choose between them, handing an advantage to the other candidates.

“Electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They’d enjoy the hell out of it — mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good,” Newsom said.

open image in gallery California Governor Gavin Newsom has revealed that he won’t run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris does ( Getty Images )

The governor endorsed Harris when former President Joe Biden dropped out of the 2024 presidential election, writing on X, “With our democracy at stake and our future on the line, no one is better to prosecute the case against Donald Trump’s dark vision and guide our country in a healthier direction than [Harris].”

Newsom, who has gained popularity during Donald Trump’s second term for mocking the president online, also has five other people to consider when deciding to run in 2028 — his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom, and their four kids.

“I know what matters in life,” Newsom told Tapper in a clip of their interview, which will air in full Tuesday. “I’ve got four kids. It’s the only thing that matters to me. They gotta be on board.”

When Politico’s Jonathan Martin asked Newsom in a March interview whether his kids would want him to run for president, the governor said, “It depends on the day of the week.”

Newsom then told a story of his teenage son asking him about running in 2028.

When Newsom denied that he had decided on a presidential bid, his son said, “Good.” The California governor then asked him what he meant by that, and his son replied, “We’re too young and you need to spend more time with us.”

open image in gallery ‘Electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They’d enjoy the hell out of it — mutual assured destruction,’ Newsom said of him and his fellow California Democrat running against each other ( Getty Images )

Other names widely floated as potential Democratic candidates in 2028 are progressive congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Biden’s Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who ran for president in 2020.

In a Bowling Green State University/YouGov poll of likely voters released earlier this month, Harris received 17 percent of support for the Democratic nomination and Newsom received 14 percent.

Buttigieg closely trailed Harris with 16 percent support and Ocasio-Cortez tied Newsom at 14 percent.

On the GOP side, Vice President JD Vance received 44 percent support for the Republican nomination and Secretary of State Marco Rubio received 21 percent.

News.title: Dead man found stuck in kitchen vent at Atlanta soul food cafe
News.content:

An unidentified man was found dead on Monday morning wedged through a kitchen HVAC vent at Walter’s Soul Food Cafe in southwest Atlanta.

Emergency personnel were dispatched to the restaurant at 394 Cleveland Avenue SW shortly before 9 a.m. on Monday, following a call logged at approximately 8:58 a.m., as first reported by 11 Alive.

Witnesses told police they observed the man’s head, arms and torso extending from the vent located over the kitchen’s frying area.

“All we seen was his head,” a restaurant worker told ABC affiliate WSB-TV. “That’s all. His head and his arms.”

Another employee, a cook, told reporters that a female colleague first spotted the person upon arriving for work.

open image in gallery An unidentified man was found dead Monday morning after becoming wedged in a kitchen HVAC vent at Walter’s Soul Food Cafe in southwest Atlanta ( Google Maps )

“She came in and was hollering and screaming and telling me, ‘Rick! Look, look, look,’” the cook recalled, adding, “All you seen was his head.”

The restaurant’s owner reportedly told responding officers that a staff member first discovered the man stuck inside the kitchen vent. Atlanta Fire Rescue personnel also responded to the location and pronounced the person dead at the scene.

Investigators stated that there were no immediate indications of foul play. Personnel from the Atlanta Police Department’s Homicide Unit and Crime Scene Unit deployed to the site with the Fulton County Medical Examiner’s Office.

Arriving customers found the establishment locked late Monday morning.

“I don’t even know how you can get on the roof,” one customer told reporters.

A nearby gas station sits on an elevated slope, making the roof accessible, and police used a ladder to reach the top of the building.

“That’s weird to break in,” another person at the scene said. “To do what? There’s not even any food made yet.”

The cause and manner of death are pending an investigation by the medical examiner. Family members arrived at the scene later in the day and told police they believed the man was their relative.

John Mulaney’s 2026 Emmys appearance has fans all echoing the same thing online.

Mulaney, 44, appeared to present the Lead Actor in a Drama Series category during Monday night’s ceremony. In doing so, he made several jokes in rapid succession, drawing hearty laughs from the crowd, and even garnering the broadcast’s first bleeped-out phrase. The comedian’s appearance lasted longer than several of the speeches so far during the ceremony.

Now, fans are all calling for Mulaney to serve as next year’s host — or to lead any awards show.

“Ok we really gotta get John Mulaney to host some of these awards shows. That was fantastic,” one person wrote on X while another agreed, “John Mulaney needs to host everything.”

“Oh my god why didn’t they just get John Mulaney to host the Emmys??” someone else wrote as another said, “Gotta get John Mulaney hosting one of these things.”

open image in gallery John Mulaney's appearance at the Emmys has fans all saying the same thing ( Getty )

“john mulaney shows up to these f***ing awards shows and every time, WITHOUT FAIL, demonstrates why he should just be hosting every single one of these. it's so refreshing and infuriating at the same time because WHY ARE THEY NOT HIRING HIM TO HOST,” another lamented.

“I need John Mulaney to stay as host for the rest of the ceremony. Don't let that other lady come back, please,” someone else said while another fan agreed, “Just keep John Mulaney on stage tonight.”

Law & Order star Mariska Hargitay hosted the 78th annual Emmys broadcast.

The 62-year-old, who has starred on the hit procedural for 27 years, pretended not to know the word “finale,” given that she’s never had one. She also poked fun at Law & Order creator Dick Wolf, joking that wisecracks about his name are unfair as his real name is “Richard Penis.”

open image in gallery Mulaney's Emmys appearance had fans calling for him to host future awards shows ( Getty )

She also spoofed Nicole Kidman’s famous  for AMC cinemas, only to be interrupted by Kidman herself. “Zip it movie lady,” Hargitay told her. “It’s TV’s turn tonight.”

Hargitay’s brief monologue came after an extended, extravagant musical sequence during which she sang “I love TV screens” to the tune of Joan Jett’s “I Love Rock ‘n Roll.”

The actor, who is hosting the Emmys for the first time, pointed out that she is the first female host for 15 years. She has been widely praised on social media, with one user writing: “Mariska Hargitay should host everything forever” and another adding: “Yes Mariska is killing it! I love this! I knew she would!!!”

Others, as seen on X, preferred Mulaney’s minutes-long stint.

Renowned Indigenous Chief Raoni Metuktire is receiving palliative care at home in the Brazilian heartland after being diagnosed with cancer at age 94, his institute said Monday.

The Raoni Institute said the cancer diagnosis in the chief's digestive system was confirmed after he was hospitalized in Sao Paulo in June due to a severe intestinal obstruction. He underwent surgery then and returned to the region of the city of Peixoto de Azevedo, in Brazil's Mato Grosso state.

“At this moment, our priority is ensuring that Chief Raoni is well cared for, comfortable, and close to his family and his people. We wish to share this information transparently, but we also ask for respect regarding his privacy, his need for rest, and his family’s decisions,” the institute said in a statement.

Raoni, one of the most renowned advocates for the protection of the Amazon rainforest and for Indigenous rights, traveled the world for decades to raise awareness about environmental preservation.

Doctors opted for palliative care given Raoni's advanced age, overall clinical condition, and the high risks associated with aggressive oncological treatments, the institute said.

“Palliative care does not mean an absence of treatment. The goal is to control pain and other symptoms, prevent complications, and ensure nutrition, hydration, medical supervision, nursing care, physical therapy, and the best possible quality of life,” it added.

Raoni is currently resting at home, surrounded by his family, community, and specialized health teams. The care plan also incorporates intercultural and spiritual support, the institute added, which honors his Indigenous heritage and allows traditional healers alongside medical professionals.
