World.title: Mali: The Success Mali Must Move Beyond
World.content:
Mali built a cotton sector capable of producing, ginning and exporting at scale. Mossadeck Bally argues that this success must now support a more demanding ambition: retain more fibre, begin with spinning and finance industry for the long term.

In Mali, cotton is everywhere except where its value multiplies. It supports between four and five million people and sustains transporters, banks, insurers and fuel distributors. The country has ranked among Africa’s leading producers for years. Yet, according to Mossadeck Bally, nearly 98 per cent of the fibre it produces still leaves the country without passing through a Malian spinning mill.

At first glance, this appears to be a story of industrial failure. Bally offers a more useful and more unsettling reading. The sector did not fail. It performed the mission for which it was designed: produce cotton fibre, gin it and export it. The problem is that Mali is now asking that architecture to accomplish a new mission without having built the ecosystem the new mission requires.

“We succeeded in making Mali one of Africa’s leading producers of cotton fibre. Now we need a vision of Mali as an industrial textile country.” — Mossadeck Bally

An agricultural success and an unfinished value chain

Bally speaks with the perspective of an entrepreneur who has invested across West Africa for nearly four decades. His diagnosis begins with history. Mali’s cotton sector was organised around farmer support and fibre exports. After independence, that orientation was consolidated with considerable success. Cotton became one of the country’s broadest sources of economic spillovers.

But producing fibre does not automatically lead to yarn, fabric and garments. The experiences of COMATEX, Fittina and ITEMA show why an isolated factory is not enough. Between a bale of cotton and a finished shirt stand reliable and competitively priced electricity, roads, technical skills, markets, guarantees and, above all, financing whose duration matches the life of the industrial asset.

AllAfrica Mossadeck Bally, President of the CNPM Â· Founder of the AzalaÃ¯ Hotels Group

Start with yarn

Bally is not proposing that Mali build an integrated industry overnight and attempt to compete with Asia at every stage. For a landlocked country located roughly 1,200 kilometres from some ports, sequencing matters. His first priority is spinning: convert fibre into yarn, even if the yarn must initially be exported.

The logic is industrial and logistical. Cotton fibre is bulky and flammable. Yarn is a higher-value product that is easier to transport and can attract textile manufacturers in a second phase. Once spinning capacity is established, Mali can progressively develop weaving and then garment production.

Public procurement can provide an initial market through military uniforms, school clothing and other government needs. Over time, Bally also sees scope for just-in-time production for Europe, using air freight when speed and proximity can offset some of the disadvantages of being landlocked.

“Instead of exporting cotton fibre, let us begin by exporting yarn. The yarn will then attract textile industries.” — Mossadeck Bally

When loan maturity programmes failure

The main barrier is not only the amount of capital. It is the form that capital takes. A spinning mill may require ten to fifteen years to amortise, while commercial banks rarely offer maturities beyond five to seven years. When repayment begins while a factory is still learning to produce efficiently, financing does not reduce risk; it organises failure.

Pixabay Cotton branch

Equity requirements create another barrier. For a textile plant costing CFAF 15 billion, Bally illustrates, a 30 per cent contribution represents CFAF 4.5 billion. Few entrepreneurs can immobilise that amount. When a project must raise US$20 million to US$50 million from a development finance institution, appraisal may take eighteen to twenty-four months—long enough to exhaust a promoter before the first machine turns.

Bally identifies four recurring disconnects between lenders and industrial operators: loan maturities that are too short; collateral requirements based on the promoter’s existing property rather than the future cash flows of the factory; lengthy appraisal processes; and a cost of credit incompatible with manufacturing margins. He adds a broader structural pressure: private borrowers can be crowded out when government securities offer banks attractive returns with fewer capital constraints.

“You have barely begun production when repayment starts. That means failure is guaranteed.” — Mossadeck Bally

Finance the project not only the promoter’s assets

The answer requires more deliberate financial engineering: first-loss guarantees, political-risk cover, equity investment and semi-concessional resources. Bally points to the World Bank’s Private Sector Window and to political-risk guarantees available through specialist institutions. These tools do not eliminate risk. They allocate it in a way that can make investment possible.

He also identifies Mali’s Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations, once fully operational, as a potential source of long-term capital. Pension funds can play a similar role because their liabilities extend over ten, fifteen or twenty years—the same horizon industry needs. Bally argues that the Private Sector Guarantee Fund should be capitalised more strongly so an institutional guarantee can replace at least part of the land title or other fixed collateral demanded from entrepreneurs.

AllAfrica The Economic Impact of Mali's Cotton Industry, Summarized in Three Key Figures

A strategic state and a private operator

For Bally, the model is not a state that owns and operates factories. It is a strategic state: one that defines the trajectory, secures land, organises infrastructure, simplifies tax and customs administration, and then attracts private capital and expertise through public-private partnerships.

The Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone in Benin is a reference point, but not a template to copy mechanically. Benin’s zone is close to a port; Mali must absorb the costs of being landlocked. A Malian textile zone would need to be designed around competitive energy, internal logistics, a single-window service and an initial specialisation in spinning.

Two public decisions recur in his argument. The first is a cotton single window bringing together government, power utilities, producers, investors, banks, development institutions and insurers. The second is a revised public-private partnership law that gives investors the stability and visibility required to commit capital for twenty or twenty-five years.

“The state must be strategic and visionary, but it must not be the operator.” — Mossadeck Bally

Risk viewed from a distance

Bally does not deny geopolitical tension or logistical constraints. He challenges the way those realities are converted into a risk premium. His experience across eight West African countries has taught him that external narratives often confuse difficulty with impossibility.

TCM / AllAfrica Large-scale spinning and yarn preparation: the first link in the industrial chain that Bally wants to prioritize.

His message to investors is direct. Cotton responds to enduring global demand. Despite crises and disruptions to transport corridors, Mali continues to produce, gin and export. If that chain functions in a difficult environment, local transformation is not a fiction. Investors must visit, examine the assets, assess the operators and follow the real flows rather than stop at a general story about African risk.

“If you stop at what you see on television or hear on the radio, you will miss an opportunity.” — Mossadeck Bally

A vision measured over thirty years

The industrial ambition Bally describes cannot be reduced to a five-year campaign promise. It requires a measurable trajectory over several decades: progressively reduce the share of fibre exported, expand spinning capacity, use public procurement to establish an initial market, and then attract textile and garment production as the ecosystem gains competence.

A long horizon is not an argument for waiting. It is an argument for beginning now. Mali already has the raw material, organised producers, entrepreneurial experience and a regional market. The failures of earlier factories should be treated as evidence for better design, not as a verdict against industrialisation.

The first chapter of Mali’s cotton story was about volume. The next will be about value. The passage between them is not a leap but a sequence of concrete decisions: power, yarn, a guarantee, a law and a market. Bobbin by bobbin, the success of yesterday can become the industry of tomorrow.

“We must come together around a thirty- or forty-year vision: move from a producer and exporter of cotton fibre to a country industrialised around cotton.” — Mossadeck Bally

World.title: Kenya: Can Kenya Turn Its Cotton Comeback Into A Genuine Industrial Revival?
World.content:
Kenya is growing cotton again. But the bigger question is whether it can turn the crop into an industrial engine and keep more of the value at home.

The machines have stopped. Inside Luanda Ginnery in Busia, the belts and rollers that separate cotton fibre from seed sit motionless. The noise that would normally fill the building has disappeared. For about four months, there has been no cotton to process.

Outside, however, the next story is already taking shape. Across the farms of Busia, cotton plants are about two months old. Farmers are watching the skies, waiting for the rains they hope will give the crop the push it needs.

The landscape is hot and dusty. The roads leading to some of the farms are rough, forcing farmers and visitors to rely on boda bodas (motorcycle taxis) to reach fields hidden away from the main roads. Yet there is optimism. The cotton is growing. And with it, the hope that the industry that once supported thousands of families can find its way back.

Vincent Akumu wants to expand. His ambition is to grow cotton on five acres, up from the one and a half acres he farms today. The problem is getting there. Land preparation remains difficult because machinery is scarce. Farmers often depend on county equipment, hire machines when available or resort to labour-intensive manual preparation. Then there is seed. A late delivery can push farmers outside the narrow planting window.

Vincent knows what that means. “The rainy season cannot wait for farmers,” he says.

That simple observation captures one of the biggest challenges facing Kenya's cotton revival. The country may have farmers willing to grow the crop. It may have ginneries. It may have textile mills. It may have a market. But all those pieces have to work at the same time. Because cotton is not really a story about a plant. It is a story about what happens after the plant is harvested.

Kenya's cotton industry has been here before. According to research by the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (KALRO), national cotton production reached an all-time high of about 70,000 bales in 1985/86. By 2001, production had fallen to about 20,000 bales. The collapse was not caused by one problem. KALRO's research points to a combination of factors, including poor agronomic practices and pest control, delayed payment to farmers, mismanagement of cooperatives, exploitation by middlemen, poor pricing and poorly managed ginneries.

Rising imports of second-hand clothes, known in Kenya as mitumba, also weakened demand for locally manufactured cotton garments. The result was a vicious cycle. Farmers stopped planting. Ginneries struggled for raw material. Factories lost reliable supplies. Investment became harder to justify. And the industry shrank further.

For communities that had once depended on cotton, the consequences were profound. Farmers switched to maize and other food crops. And the machines built to process cotton increasingly became monuments to an industry that had lost its way.

But Kenya is attempting another turnaround. This time, the ambition is considerably bigger.

The government's vision is to increase production while strengthening certified seed development, textile mills and garment manufacturing, with the private sector playing a bigger role in the value chain. But between the 500,000-tonne ambition and Vincent's one-and-a-half-acre farm lies the difficult part: production, processing, investment, markets, infrastructure, skills and time.

Small farms, big ambitions

In Busia, most cotton farmers are not operating on large commercial plantations.

That small scale creates a problem for an industry that wants predictable volumes. Luanda Ginnery can process cotton. But a ginnery cannot run on machinery alone. It needs farmers. And farmers need markets. Barasa puts it bluntly: “If they don't grow cotton, then we don't have raw materials. That means we won't move on.”

It is the central contradiction of the revival. Kenya needs more cotton to make its ginneries viable. But farmers need functioning ginneries, reliable markets and predictable prices to make cotton worth growing. That is why the cooperative is critical. It is the bridge between the smallholder and the industrial system.

Bernard Ojiambo, the union's chairman, says cotton has been grown in the region for decades. But years of delayed payments and weak markets pushed farmers towards maize. Today, he believes cotton can once again provide a stronger cash income. “Cotton is more of a value than maize,” he says. But farmers need support to expand.

AllAfrica The upgraded Luanda Ginnery in Busia county awaiting the next ginning season (2)

Ojiambo says a lack of machinery delays land preparation. “We delay because we don't have machines like tractors and other things to support farmers.” The cooperative has been seeking investment in machinery and transport to improve its ability to serve farmers. For Vincent, mechanisation would mean the opportunity to expand. For the ginnery, it would mean more raw material. For the textile mill, it would mean more cotton. And for the economy, it could mean another step towards rebuilding an industry.

For farmers such as Mama Aisha Mohammed, the change is not measured in tonnes. It is measured in school fees. Food. Livestock. And the ability to improve a household.

Aisha, from the Bajuni community, had largely grown maize and green grams for household consumption before cotton became a commercial opportunity. After her first harvest, she was able to pay school fees and provide for her grandchildren. Julia Njuguna tells a similar story. Income from cotton enabled her to build a new house and improve her family's living standards. She now sees cotton as a crop her children can build a future around.

These stories matter because they show what happens when the first link in the chain begins to work. But the real test comes after the farmer sells the cotton.

A garment can be assembled in Kenya using imported yarn or imported fabric. It is Kenyan-made. But the value chain behind the garment may stretch across several countries. Kenya's bigger opportunity is to shorten that chain. Cotton grown in Busia or Lamu. Ginned in Kenya. Spun in Kenya. Woven in Kenya. Dyed and finished in Kenya. Cut and stitched in Kenya. Sold in Kenya or exported. That is how one crop becomes an industrial ecosystem.

As Olweny puts it: “The more stages we keep in Kenya, the more employment we create.”

Those stages create opportunities far beyond the farm. Transporters move cotton. Engineers maintain machinery. Technicians operate textile equipment. Workers spin yarn. Others weave and dye fabric. Garment workers cut and stitch. Packaging companies supply factories. Retailers sell the finished product. Graduates of technical and vocational training (TVET) institutions and university researchers become part of the industrial workforce. The cotton plant may begin in a field. But its economic footprint can stretch across an entire country.

The import paradox

There is, however, a striking contradiction in Kenya's cotton story. While the country wants to dramatically increase domestic cotton production and rebuild its textile industry, it continues to import large quantities of cotton products.

A factory cannot plan production around uncertainty. It needs cotton when it needs it. It needs quality that can be predicted. It needs enough volume to justify machinery and workers. And it needs markets for the finished products.

That makes the problems farmers describe — delayed seed, inadequate machinery, limited finance and small acreage — industrial problems too. A farmer waiting for seed is not just an agricultural story. It is a textile factory waiting for raw material months later. A cooperative without a tractor is not simply a rural development issue. It is a supply-chain bottleneck. A silent ginnery is not merely an idle building. It is evidence that one link in the industrial chain is missing. And a textile mill relying on imported yarn tells another part of the story. The value chain remains incomplete.

KALRO's research demonstrates both the potential of cotton and the painful history of its decline. Farmers in Busia are returning to the crop. Lamu has demonstrated that farmers can respond when the economics improve. Cooperatives are asking for machinery and finance. Ginneries are waiting for raw material. Textile companies are asking for reliable supply and investment. And the government is talking about taking production from tens of thousands of tonnes of lint towards half a million tonnes.

As the sun sets over Busia, the cotton fields remain quiet. The plants wait for rain. Vincent waits too. He wants his five acres, and a crop that will educate another generation of his family. A few kilometres away, Luanda Ginnery waits for cotton. The machines will eventually start again. The challenge is making sure they never again fall silent because farmers have abandoned the crop. And beyond the ginnery, another set of machines waits at textile factories. Their future depends on what happens in fields like Vincent's.

"By doing so, because the company will be very, very large, we will be having 10 per cent of the total America's capacity," Mr Dangote added.

Africa's richest man aims to list his 700,000 barrel-per-day oil refinery, which commenced its initial public offering Monday morning, in the United States in the next three to four years, he told the investing public in Lagos during the Fact Behind the Offer event at the Nigerian Exchange.

"In the next three years, by the grace of God, three to four years or thereabouts, we will try and also list outside the African continent, most likely in the U.S," he said.

"By doing so, because the company will be very, very large, we will be having 10 per cent of the total America's capacity," he added.

The IPO hopes to democratise wealth creation across Africa by allowing the mass market that is dominated by retail investors to own a piece of the cake in the refinery, which is looking to increase capacity twofold by 2030 from the proceeds of the transaction.

Mr Dangote said the IPO is not out to raise money in the strictest sense of the word, given that it has other means of sourcing, with $46 billion already in the pipeline for the expansion of the plant and the actualisation of its 2030 strategic vision.

Rather, the share sale aspires to extend the ownership of the refinery to as many people as possible, he went further to say.

"Even if there is mishap, devaluation, the business you are investing in is a dollarized business. Don't let the train leave you at the station," he noted, assuring that the investment of local investors will be shielded from currency headwinds, with dividends planned to be distributed in dollars.

The $2.5 billion that was eventually raised from the private placement was the original size the refinery aspired to raise from both the placement and the IPO.

"We refused to take one single currency other than the dollar. With the private placement, we have already met our demand," he stated.

Come the end of the year, the refinery will be the largest company in Africa, not just in Nigeria, Mr Dangote remarked, adding that an asset of that magnitude should create value, not for a few people, but for millions of people.

The refinery and petrochemical plant is also looking to build the first train ever in the world of linear alkaline benzene, a major raw material in detergent making, with a capacity of 400,000 metric tonnes, surpassing Egypt's 50,000 tonnes and Algeria's 100,000 tonnes.

World.title: Gov Hochul's plan to opt New York into federal school choice program draws union opposition
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As New York teachers unions organize a protest against Gov. Kathy Hochul’s plan to opt into a federal tax-credit scholarship program, the CEO of Teach Coalition told Fox News Digital that opponents are spreading "misconceptions" about how the policy actually operates.

"It seems that they want to continuously spread these lies and the misinformation about this program on to anyone who will hear them," Sydney Altfield, CEO of Teach Coalition, told Fox News Digital on Monday. "But the people who actually want to help children, the people who actually want to see children succeed, they're not going to listen. They're going to understand that this is not the truth of what this program actually can do."

Tax-credit scholarships, historically operated at the state level, serve as a mechanism for school choice by allowing individuals or corporations to receive full or partial tax credits when donating to non-profit scholarship organizations. Unlike traditional voucher programs that draw directly from municipal or state education funds, tax credits allow taxpayers to redirect a portion of their tax liability toward non-profit funding for student scholarships.

NEW YORK JOINS FEDERAL SCHOOL CHOICE INITIATIVE DESPITE TRADITIONAL DEMOCRAT OPPOSITION

The federal iteration allows state governors to opt into the framework, enabling local families and educational programs to access federally incentivized scholarship dollars.

Emma Wallner, a spokesperson for Hochul’s office, confirmed in May that the governor intends to opt New York into the federal tax-credit scholarship program — making New York the 30th state to participate.

"Governor Hochul is supportive of the federal tax credit scholarship and its potential to help New York students and schools," Wallner told Fox News Digital. "Our office awaits information from the federal government on the program and will thoroughly review the details of the policy for poison pills that could harm New York’s education system."

For decades, school choice initiatives have remained a third-rail issue for many Democrats, who argue that choice models divert resources away from public education and undermine teachers unions. However, several high-profile Democrats have recently adjusted their stances.

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis became the first Democratic governor to opt his state into the federal program in January 2026. Dismissing critics at the time, Polis told local media he "would be crazy not to" join, noting that the credits empower parents to afford after-school, tutoring, or summer enrichment programs previously out of reach.

ARIZONA REPUBLICANS GIVE TEACHERS UNION AN EDUCATION LESSON THEY WON’T FORGET

Despite these arguments, major labor groups remain opposed.

Teachers unions and several allied interest groups plan to demonstrate on Wednesday at the United Federation of Teachers (UFT) headquarters in Manhattan. The coalition includes the UFT, its statewide parent organization, the New York State Union of Teachers (NYSUT), and their national affiliate, the American Federation of Teachers (AFT).

Together, the groups launched a public petition calling on state leadership to reject Hochul’s decision.

"Gov. Hochul plans to opt New York in starting in 2027. But most New Yorkers haven’t even heard of this program or know how it will affect New York," the petition states. "Tax dollars would help pay private tuition for families who never used public schools."

The petition further points to fiscal challenges in other states that expanded school choice models: "Florida couldn't account for $270 million in voucher funds in a single year. Arizona's $65M plan became a $1.4 billion budget hole — cutting water, highways, and community colleges ... We need to show the governor that New Yorkers stand for strong public schools and against any measure that would weaken them."

Union advocates argue that "every dollar diverted to private schools is a dollar taken away from the public schools that serve 90% of New York's kids."

Altfield, however, disputed the characterization that the program constitutes a traditional private school voucher.

"Why are we trying to take away opportunities for our children when they're included as well? Another thing that they call it is a ‘voucher’. And it is not a voucher. It is a tax credit," Altfield explained. "What we know as a voucher is when you take public funding from the public school system, and you allow it to follow the child — which works in many states — but that's not what this is."

On their online campaign website, union organizers argue that labeling differences are purely rhetorical: "The branding changes — ‘Education Savings Accounts,’ ‘tax-credit scholarships,’ ‘school choice’ — but the mechanism is the same: public money flowing to private schools."

TRUMP ADMIN URGES RETURNING EDUCATION TO STATES, CITING $3 TRILLION OF TAXES SPENT AND POOR PROFICIENCY SCORES

The union FAQ page also claims that funds do not go directly to families: "Funds flow to private SGOs [Scholarship Granting Organizations], which decide who receives the money. These organizations aren't required to be transparent or accountable to the public, and the private schools they fund can turn away students based on disability, academic record, behavior, religion, or almost any other criteria they choose."

Altfield strongly denied that public school operational budgets would suffer under the program.

"This money does not come out of state budgets. It does not come out of state public school resources," Altfield said. "Which is one of the things that the misinformation is trying to tell you — that this is going to drain public school resources and funding. This money does not come out of that bucket."

"Those buckets remain untouched," Altfield added. "One of the things that they like to peddle is that this is going straight into the pockets of private school parents. Well, yes, private school parents and students can access this funding, but they also forget to tell you that public school students can also get this funding and get these scholarships."

The New York State Union of Teachers, American Federation of Teachers and United Federation of Teachers did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

World.title: UK breakup push escalates amid historic pact after Trump backs reunification of Ireland
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland called Monday for the British government to "prepare for, plan and facilitate" constitutional change that could lead to the breakup of the United Kingdom, with the remarks coming days after President Donald Trump said he would "love to see" Irish reunification.

"Westminster’s time is coming to an end," Scottish First Minister John Swinney, Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth and Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill said in a historic joint declaration issued in Cardiff.

The nationalist party leaders had met Monday to strengthen cooperation among Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland and advance what they described as "constitutional change."

KEIR STARMER REPORTEDLY CONSIDERING STEPPING DOWN AS PM AND COULD ANNOUNCE TIMETABLE FOR DEPARTURE

The declaration, signed during the summit in Cardiff, signals an unprecedented challenge to Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the U.K.’s constitutional settlement.

Trump spoke about the status of Northern Ireland over the weekend, saying Saturday during a visit to Dublin: "It’s going to happen eventually. It might as well happen now."

On Sunday, Trump repeated his support for a united Ireland, saying it made sense to merge the Republic of Ireland with Northern Ireland.

"It just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland, and it would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is put them together," Trump said in Doonbeg.

NIGEL FARAGE RESIGNING FROM UK PARLIAMENT

"You asked about Scotland. That one I won't talk about yet. I'll save that for another day," he added.

By Monday, the nationalist leaders had released a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to drive constitutional change.

They said no Westminster government has the right to block democratic decisions made by Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.

"Each of our nations has the right to determine its own future, through democratic means and in accordance with the wishes of its people," the three leaders wrote.

"For the first time ever, people across these islands have First Ministers in Scotland, in Wales and in the North of Ireland who are all committed to independence from the United Kingdom. For people watching across these islands – for people watching around the world – there could be no clearer sign that Westminster’s time is coming to an end," the statement continued.

MEET 'COUNT BINFACE,' THE TRASH CAN-CLAD COMEDIAN CHALLENGING NIGEL FARAGE

"We call for the British Government to prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change in each jurisdiction," the memorandum said.

According to GB News, Burnham was told Monday that he could not stop the breakup of the U.K.

Sinn Féin, the largest party in the Northern Ireland Assembly, issued the warning after signing the memorandum with the SNP and Plaid Cymru.

O’Neill said the three nations shared a "common cause" because "Westminster does not and will never serve our people well."

She added during a news conference that Burnham would not be able to "hold back the tide" of nationalism.

"We’re certainly living in times of enormous change, change that is unstoppable, change that, no matter what is said by any British prime minister, will not be able to hold back the tide of what’s happening in front of our eyes right now.

"Our common cause here is the understanding that Westminster does not and will never serve our people well," she added.

KING CHARLES FOLLOWS QUEEN ELIZABETH'S PLAYBOOK WITH A TWIST DURING TRUMP STATE VISIT: EXPERT

The memorandum commits the parties to cooperation on economic policy, renewable energy and rebuilding ties with the European Union, among other areas.

It also calls for greater self-determination and states that the nations should work together as equals.

A spokesperson for Burnham said: "The Prime Minister is committed to delivering change across all four nations of the United Kingdom and believes strongly in the Union.

World.title: Oklahoma State might have known which plays Oregon Ducks were running during upset win
World.content:
While Week 2 of the college football season was filled with drama, the typical chaos, and the game of the year with Texas-Ohio State, the most shocking result of the weekend was Oklahoma State's upset win over the Oregon Ducks.

This preseason, most analysts expected the Ducks to be one of the top few teams in the country. Oregon was once again a playoff team in 2025, with their only losses coming to eventual National Champion Indiana. They had another typically excellent recruiting class, with four five-star high schoolers joining an already loaded roster.

Quarterback Dante Moore surprisingly returned for another season, and while head coach Dan Lanning had to replace two coordinators, expectations were that the transition would be seamless thanks to picking internal promotions.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Through two games however, no team has been more disappointing. Oregon struggled to put away Boise State in Eugene in week one, ultimately winning 34-27. Week two was far worse.

Several turnovers forced by the Ducks' defense papered over what was a dominant performance by the Cowboys. Oklahoma State ran a whopping 83 plays for 554 yards, a solid 6.7 yards per play. They averaged nearly six yards per carry on the ground, good for 237 total rushing yards.

NEW AP POLL TOP 25 PUNISHES OHIO STATE, OKLAHOMA, OREGON, TEXAS JUMPS TO NO 1 AFTER BIG COMEBACK

Meanwhile, Oregon could never get much going offensively. The Ducks' vaunted offensive line was frequently overwhelmed, leading to an anemic 3 yards per carry and just 281 total yards with 4.8 yards per play. Sometimes upsets are fluky, with some pivotal breaks going the underdogs' way. Not this time. The Cowboys dominated and deserved to win. If anything, the ultimate final margin was misleadingly close.

Beyond the shock of a team that had lost 12 straight games, that lost to Tulsa in week one, dominating an opponent that had national championship aspirations, it raised several questions. Namely, how the heck did this happen? And according to a postgame report out of OK State, the Cowboys might have had some help from the Ducks themselves.

"We were noticing earlier in the week that their (Oregon’s) offensive line had tendencies that helped us key into run (or) pass and a couple areas we could take advantage of," said linebacker Tate Romney. "and obviously our defensive line was keyed into that. That was one big thing that gave us a big advantage."

Well then. That's interesting, isn't it? It's like in baseball, when a pitcher tips his pitches and lets hitters know what's coming.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

That might not have been all their telegraphing either. Landon Tengwall on his show this week added to what Andrew Nemec found on quarterback Dante Moore.

Essentially, Moore against Oklahoma State had two different stances in his pre-snap setup, using the same configuration before runs, and then a different configuration against the pass.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

It's not clear whether the Cowboys were aware of that "tell" too, or if it was just the offensive and defensive line movement that tipped them off. But it presents an interesting possibility: is Oregon's poor performance due, at least partially, to giving the defense free clues as to what's coming?

Maybe. But it's always easy to point to these types of things when you're losing. And even if they were telegraphing their plays, individual Oklahoma State players would still have to win their battles against their matchups. You can know a pass is coming, but if your defensive line is overmatched, there's no guarantee you get to the quarterback. Not to mention that the Cowboys offense moved the ball seemingly at will against Oregon's defense. And nobody's said anything about the Ducks "play tipping" their coverages and blitzes.

Oregon plays Portland State this coming weekend, so any "corrections," or lack thereof, won't matter given the massive talent gap. World.title: Ole Miss and LSU will deliver cinema, but the next week for each team could be their most pivotal tests
World.content:
The most-anticipated game of the college football regular season will take place in Oxford, Miss., on Saturday night, with a gold-and-purple-clad Lane Kiffin returning to town to take on the team and fanbase he abandoned just 10 months ago.

On paper, the LSU-Ole Miss matchup features everything a college football game could ever want. For starters, it's a historic rivalry matchup featuring two Top 10 teams with huge SEC Championship and College Football Playoff implications on the line. You add in the Kiffin of it all, and the contest goes from just a great college football game to a full-blown spectacle.

If Kiffin's first game against Ole Miss as the head coach at LSU were being held in Baton Rouge, it wouldn't have nearly as much of a mystique around it. Thankfully, the football gods had it made that this game would be played in Mississippi.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

If you're an LSU fan, there has to be something at least slightly unsettling about Kiffin and his $50 million Tigers roster coming to Oxford to take on an Ole Miss team headlined by quarterback Trinidad Chambliss and running back Kewan Lacy, two players Kiffin and his staff fought to come join them on the bayou. Leaving Oxford without a win would deliver a dose of reality to both Tigers fans and Kiffin himself that perhaps things aren't quite as they seem, at least not yet.

On the other sideline, you have an Ole Miss team that not only lost key pieces from last season, but is also being coached by a man in Pete Golding, who is entering just his sixth game as a head coach. You also have a fanbase foaming at the mouth to see Kiffin squirm on the opposing sideline inside the stadium he coached in for six seasons.

In terms of question marks, Ole Miss has the most between the two teams heading into Saturday, but they could also have the answers in the form of Chambliss and Lacy, two Heisman Trophy candidates.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

The angles of what makes Saturday's game simply so massive are virtually endless, and while the game itself will undoubtedly deliver, the contests that both teams will have to play in just seven days later could very well be the most pivotal ones of their respective seasons.

Ole Miss travels to Gainesville to take on Florida in Week 4, and if the Gators take care of Auburn on the road this Saturday, The Swamp will be absolutely jumping when the Rebels arrive. That statement will be true whether Ole Miss beats LSU or loses by three touchdowns. Florida head coach Jon Sumrall will be looking to catch an Ole Miss team at the right time, with the Rebels coming off an unbelievably emotional week.

LSU has the luxury of returning home to Death Valley in Week 4, but has to welcome Texas A&M to town. The Aggies play Kentucky at home in Week 3, meaning they'll likely arrive in Baton Rouge unbeaten and as a Top 10 program in the nation. Many would argue that Texas A&M is the most overlooked team of the young college football season up to this point, but taking down LSU in Baton Rouge would certainly flip that narrative.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In a world where college football chatter has become more focused on court cases and NIL money, it's these sets of factors and matchups that still make the sport so great. The SEC adding an additional conference game to the slate this season is also being felt in this particular scenario, and it's going to be fascinating to see how teams respond to an extra, very stiff test.

Nothing would be more college football than seeing the winner of the Ole Miss-LSU throwdown turn around and lose just seven days later. Whatever happens, we'll all be watching.

World.title: Trump calls Nvidia CEO to talk AI — and gets put on speakerphone in all-hands meeting
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Monday called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during a company all-hands meeting and gave another full-throated defense of artificial intelligence after Huang put the call on speakerphone.

Trump characterized concerns about AI safety as a “hoax,” while telling Huang that the U.S. had to beat China in AI innovation and development.

“The robots will not be taking over. The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax,” Trump said, suggesting that critics are “just playing right into the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen. That could be political people, that could also be China.”

Trump also lauded politically unpopular data centers, calling them “great” and saying they make people and states “wealthy.”

“It’s the oil of the next 20, 25 years, it’s bigger than the internet and AI, you know, much more so,” he said, while adding that people “have to be a little careful” and do things “prudently.”

A video of Trump’s call, posted on X, was reposted by the Trump War Room account, which is associated with a Trump-aligned PAC. The call is also included in a podcast that Huang was recording at the time.

Nvidia said it had no comment on Huang’s exchange with Trump or whether they will be meeting soon to discuss these issues.

Trump’s comments to Nvidia, one of the world’s biggest manufacturers of AI chips and hardware, come as AI leaders have called for slowing down development of the technology.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay over the weekend that AI development needed safeguards, which was quickly endorsed by Tesla CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, among others. It came after researchers at leading AI companies stepped down from their jobs last week and spoke out over safety concerns, some describing them as an existential threat to humanity.

Former President Barack Obama urged Democrats last week to prioritize the development of an AI agenda.

Trump, however, has firmly stood by his support for AI development. In a flurry of social media posts Monday, Trump described AI concerns as a “SICK conspiracy” and a “hoax.”

During the Nvidia phone call, Trump said he assumed Huang was on the same page as him regarding AI development; Huang said they were.

“We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race in America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people,” he told Trump during their call.

The Nvidia CEO, who helped persuade Trump last year to not send National Guard troops to San Francisco, sits on Trump’s council of science and technology advisers. He has lobbied lawmakers to allow sales of Nvidia around the world, which lawmakers have said could advantage China and undercut U.S. leadership in technology.

His conversation with Trump came as House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who had been urged by House Democrats to end recess early so the lower chamber could take legislative action regarding AI safety, said this week that industry leaders should be the ones taking the lead on safety.

Johnson said Monday that Trump would call a meeting with AI leaders. A source familiar with the matter told NBC News that a meeting between Trump and the leaders was “in the works,” but no clear timing had been nailed down.

World.title: The 2026 Emmys air tonight. Here’s what to expect, how to watch and who’s hosting.
World.content:
The Primetime Emmy Awards, Hollywood’s biggest night in television, is back after a year of new beginnings and heartfelt endings.

Several shows in their first seasons have garnered multiple nods, with “Widow’s Bay” up for 19 awards, “Pluribus” 18, “DTF St. Louis” 13, “Spider-Noir” 11 and “The Beast in Me” nine.

Follow live coverage of the 2026 Emmys

“The Pitt” leads the overall pack with 25 nominations, followed closely by the final season of “Hacks,” with 24.

Fan-favorite “The Late Show with Stephen Colbert” has nine nominations. CBS announced the end of the franchise last year, and the final episode aired in May.

Many other familiar shows are back this year, too, including “Beef,” with 16 nominations; “Shrinking,” with 10; “Slow Horses,” with nine; “The Bear,” with eight; “Abbott Elementary,” with seven; and “Only Murders in the Building,” with five.

Whether you plan to tune in live or track the winners online, here’s what to expect from this year’s Emmys.

When are the 2026 Emmy Awards?

The Emmys will take place starting at 8 p.m. ET Monday at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles.

Where can I watch or stream the Emmys?

Viewers can watch the broadcast on NBC or stream the event live online with a Peacock subscription.

Who is hosting the Emmys in 2026?

“Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” star Mariska Hargitay will host this year’s Emmys. Hargitay is coming off two wins this season for the documentary “My Mom Jayne.”

Hargitay follows 2025 host Nate Bargatze, who made a splash with charity donations for too-long speeches — a stunt with major returns for the Boys & Girls Clubs of America and mixed reviews from audiences for its execution.

When does the red carpet start?

E! will host red-carpet events throughout the night, with a preshow starting at 5 p.m. Live red-carpet coverage will kick off at 6 p.m. — but fans should expect a blue carpet, instead.

Which shows have the most Emmy nominations this year?

HBO’s “The Pitt” leads the nominations with 25, followed by “Hacks” with 24. Apple TV+ trails with 19 for the first season of “Widow’s Bay” and 18 for Season 1 of “Pluribus.”

Who is predicted to win in 2026?

This year’s Emmys pit longtime favorites against breakout stars, and shake-ups can be expected.

“The Pitt” is likely to take home a decent amount of hardware, and “Widow’s Bay” is poised to make a splash in its first year.

Jean Smart is looking for her fifth win in a row for the role of Deborah Vance in “Hacks,” another Emmys favorite. The win would be her eighth, tying her with Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman for most acting Emmys for a single performer.

Meanwhile, Rhea Seehorn is expected to win her first Emmy as the star of Vince Gilligan’s “Pluribus.”

“The Late Show with Stephen Colbert” is also expected to win. It won best talk series to raucous applause last year, just months after its fate was announced.

Longtime Emmys darling “The Bear” has already earned its first win for best guest actor in a comedy, which went posthumously to Rob Reiner.

World.title: EPA to repeal limits on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants
World.content:
The Environmental Protection Agency announced Monday that it will roll back emissions limits on coal- and gas-fired power plants — one of the Trump administration’s most significant moves yet to undo the climate policies enacted under Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama.

The change would overturn a 2024 rule requiring power plants to use carbon sequestration equipment to control pollution; it was one of the biggest climate change rules implemented by the Biden administration’s EPA.

The agency also proposed eliminating all other greenhouse gas emissions rules, arguing that under the Clean Air Act, it doesn’t have the authority to regulate those emissions as they pertain to climate change.

In February, the EPA similarly repealed emissions rules for vehicles, which account for the most pollution in the U.S. today. The agency repealed greenhouse gas emissions standards for vehicles, as well as the legal conclusion that underpins its obligation to regulate such emissions in the first place, known as the endangerment finding. The moves announced Monday would essentially do the same thing for power plants, which are the second-biggest source of U.S. emissions.

If the newly announced rollbacks survive the expected legal challenges, they could prevent future administrations from requiring coal and gas power plants to limit planet-warming pollution.

“It’s part of a thematic effort to roll back air quality standards,” said Charles Driscoll, a professor of environmental systems and engineering at Syracuse University. “Trump has said he doesn’t believe in climate change, so he’s been working hard to try to roll back any sort of carbon control measures that have been implemented previously or might be implemented in the future.”

The announcement came during a meeting of energy ministers about “energy abundance” at the G20 summit in Houston.

The EPA said repealing the 2024 power-plant rule would save industry more than $300 billion in costs and help “unleash” American energy.

“The Trump administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a statement.

Industry groups cheered the announcement.

“Overturning these examples of EPA overreach will help preserve and strengthen the U.S. coal fleet, protect grid reliability, and shield electricity consumers from higher costs at a time of surging demand from data centers, artificial intelligence, and advanced manufacturing,” Michelle Bloodworth, a spokesperson for America’s Power, a trade organization for the country’s fleet of more than 400 coal-fired power plants, said in a statement.

Environmental groups have already sued the Trump administration to challenge its repeal of the endangerment finding. They promised to sue in response to the changes announced Monday, as well.

“This is full-throated climate denial,” said Patrick Drupp, the climate policy director at the Sierra Club. “It’s going to mean more pollution, more extreme weather, higher electricity bills because we’re going to continue to rely on fossil fuels. ... This is the administration doubling and tripling down on old fossil-fueled coal and gas.”

The Biden administration’s 2024 rule was designed to be phased in over time. It would have required power plants to sequester and store at least 90% of the carbon pollution they produced by 2032.

The administration said at the time that the requirement would benefit the climate and public health in ways that would far outweigh the implementation costs. The administration estimated that in the year 2035 alone, the rule would be responsible for preventing 1,200 premature deaths, 360,000 cases of asthma symptoms and 47,000 lost workdays.

The Trump administration is reversing the policy when the consequences of climate change — intense heat waves and stronger storms, for example — are becoming more obvious.

Extreme heat has baked much of the world this summer. July was the hottest month on record in the U.S., according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and many locations set all-time records. Overall, the three months from June through August were the warmest ever recorded for the contiguous United States.

Last year was the third-hottest in modern history, according to Copernicus, the European Union’s climate monitoring service. The past 11 years have been the 11 warmest on record, Copernicus data shows.

The litigation over the new EPA policy changes could take years and might not resolve before President Donald Trump leaves office.

“These cases proceed relatively slowly in the courts of appeals,” said Meghan Greenfield, a partner at the law firm Jenner & Block who oversaw the EPA’s Supreme Court docket for rulemaking during the Biden administration. “It’s not clear to me at this point that this repeal, the one that’s being finalized today, will be before the Supreme Court by the end of this administration.”

World.title: Gavin Newsom says he won’t run for president in 2028 if Kamala Harris does
World.content:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom made a surprise announcement that he won’t launch a 2028 White House bid if former Vice President Kamala Harris decides to run again.

“I wouldn’t run if she ran,” Newsom told CNN in an interview that aired Monday evening.

Newsom said running against Harris, a fellow California Democrat who was the state’s attorney general before she became a senator, would be an electoral “gift” for everybody else.

“They’d enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good. Why would I do this if I wasn’t trying to serve some greater good? There would be no upside whatsoever,” said Newsom, who has been considering a White House run.

Newsom, who has not run for president before, acknowledged that an “approach to the campaign” would be to say Harris, who ran in 2020 and 2024, had had a shot and has previously run for president.

Kamala Harris in New York on April 10. Angelina Katsanis / AP file

“That would be the case you’d make. Pretty good one, actually. You know, that’s objectively true,” Newsom said, adding that the Venn diagram between them had too much crossover.

“I know her base of supporters; I know her friends,” Newsom said. “I wouldn’t do that to people.”

Harris’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Newsom’s remarks.

Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment on his CNN remarks.

Harris has not said whether she will launch a bid for 2028. She said in July that she has “not made a decision” and that she is focused on the midterm elections.

Harris said this year that she was weighing making a third presidential run, telling the Rev. Al Sharpton at an April event that she was “thinking about it.”

Newsom, whose term as governor is up in a few months, had previously said he would decide whether to run after the midterms, telling CBS News last year that he would seriously consider the notion after the 2026 elections. He recently traveled to South Carolina — the first state to hold a Democratic primary in 2028 — and confirmed he was considering a presidential run.

World.title: Pentagon inspector general says Iran war has led to a shortfall of U.S. munitions
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Defense Department’s inspector general released its first report on the war with Iran on Monday, saying the conflict has resulted in a shortfall of U.S. munitions and “bottlenecks” in supply chains as the Trump administration works to replenish weaponry.

“To mitigate these constraints,” the report said, the Pentagon is “working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times, and to stockpile critical materials, components, and selected munitions to respond rapidly to a contingency.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has denied reports that the U.S. is running low on munitions.

President Donald Trump said Monday on Truth Social that the U.S. is “producing more Exquisite and Elite Weapons than at any time in our History. They are being delivered on a daily basis to our Forces in the Middle East and beyond.”

Two weeks ago, Trump posted that the U.S. had “virtually unlimited” amounts of ammunition and lashed out at reports of munitions shortfalls.

The congressionally mandated report covers from the start of the war on Feb. 28 through June 30. It is one of the first public accountings from any government agency detailing the cost, scope and scale of the U.S.- and Israel-led conflict to the U.S. military, the State Department and other agencies. It follows reports of low morale among U.S. troops deployed to the Middle East, a depleting stockpile of key munitions and extensive damage to American military and intelligence assets in the region.

Among the findings, the report provides one of the first government confirmations that Iran targeted the U.S. Navy’s main logistics hub in the region, in Bahrain, with drones and ballistic missiles.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.

It does not address what was most likely a U.S. strike on an elementary school in Iran during the initial hours of strikes. The military has yet to release an internal investigation into the bombing; NBC News reported in June that a report was being finalized.

The watchdog’s report details the damage to military equipment, aircraft and other materiel over the first four months of the war, including the destruction of at least 30 large U.S. drones.

It says the war with Iran has cost roughly $33.4 billion, which does not account for repairing damaged facilities. It does include $22.3 billion in expended munitions, $3.7 billion for equipment losses and $7.4 billion in other expenditures.

NBC News reported in July that the war had so far cost $80 billion to $100 billion, according to three U.S. officials and three people familiar with the internal cost estimates. The Pentagon publicly said in July that the war cost $37.5 billion. Its estimate does not include the cost of replacing aircraft, repairing U.S. bases and replenishing critical weaponry.

Trump initially said the war would last for only weeks. But over the weekend, he said it might not end until “right after” November’s midterm elections or perhaps before.

Strike-damaged residential buildings in Karaj, southwest of Tehran, in April. Atta Kenare / AFP via Getty Images

The report also finds that the war has displaced more than 20,000 U.S. military and diplomatic personnel, who were relocated at the outset of the conflict and in the days and weeks after.

Most medical evaluations of injured U.S. forces were carried out on the ground, some by local ambulances, and the patients were taken to local treatment facilities because airlift capabilities had been moved because of concerns.

And U.S. forces flew as many as 5,000 flights from European bases in support of the war, though Trump has bitterly complained that European allies have not done enough to help support the war.

Sailors conduct flight operations aboard the USS George H.W. Bush in July. Seaman Apprentice Lucas Krug / U.S. Central Command

The report catalogs some of the damage to U.S. aircraft and other military gear, as well as some of the American bases in the region. Aircraft costs, for example, include destruction or extensive damage to four F-15E jet fighters, an F-35A Joint Strike Fighter and an A-10 Warthog, which was also destroyed, according to the report. Twelve KC-135 refuelers and nine other aircraft were also destroyed, the report says. More than 30 MQ-9 drones had also been destroyed as of June, according to the report, citing the Congressional Research Service.

The State Department sustained more than $208 million in damage in four countries — Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — according to the report. That includes $184 million in damages to “diplomatic facilities” and $25 million more due to delays in construction projects, the report says.

The damage Iran inflicted on U.S. military bases had been far more extensive than is publicly known, NBC News reported in April. Iran also caused more damage to America’s intelligence and surveillance assets in the region than U.S. spy agencies have ever endured, and it is estimated to cost billions to repair, NBC News reported last month.

The report does not touch on the morale of U.S. troops who have been deployed as part of the war effort.

In recent weeks, concerns about deteriorating conditions for troops serving in the Middle East on the USS Abraham Lincoln during an extended deployment had escalated, and the Pentagon announced it was replacing the aircraft carrier.

The Lincoln is en route back to its port in San Diego after a stop in Thailand.

World.title: Bob Mackie, legendary designer who dressed Cher and Diana Ross, dies at 87
World.content:
Legendary fashion and costume designer Bob Mackie, whose sequined gowns for Cher, Diana Ross, Tina Turner and other stars dazzled red carpets for decades, has sewn his final stitch.

Mackie died Monday at 87, according to a post on his Instagram account.

“He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do,” the post read. “His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world.”

His longtime publicist Jenelle Hamilton confirmed that he died of pneumonia Monday morning in Palm Springs, California.

Known as the “sultan of sequins,” Mackie dressed some of Hollywood’s biggest names over more than 50 years. His creations for celebrities like Carol Burnett, Liza Minnelli and Barbra Streisand stunned both performers and fans alike and remain some of the most iconic costumes ever worn.

Mackie poses with two of his iconic designs worn by Cher. Kirsty Wigglesworth / AP file

“Every time I put something on that Bob made, I felt very, very special,” Sir Elton John said on social media Monday. “His costumes were works of art, and he will go down as one of the most legendary designers ever in Hollywood.”

“He loved glamour like I love glamour, but more than anything, we shared the same sense of humour and had so much fun together,” he added.

Born and raised in the San Gabriel Valley east of downtown Los Angeles, Mackie was a fan of movies early on. Dave Karger, a Palm Springs friend of Mackie’s, as well as a host for Turner Classic Movies, said Mackie recalled taking a cable car to downtown L.A. at age 5 to see Judy Garland in “Meet Me in St. Louis” in 1944.

“He, from the youngest of ages, was a true fan of great actors and actresses and singers and performers,” Karger said in an interview with NBC News on Monday. “So I think the fact that he then got to live his dream and be an important figure in that industry meant a lot to him.”

Mackie first attended nearby Pasadena City College before he transferred to what would become the California Institute of the Arts, according to his Television Academy biography. He dropped out to work as a costume sketch artist in 1961, which included sketching the skintight, beaded dress Marilyn Monroe wore in 1962 when she sang “Happy Birthday” to President John F. Kennedy.

A year later, he was hired by the man who would become his lifelong romantic and creative partner, Ray Aghayan, to work on “The Judy Garland Show.”

The pair went on to win the first Emmy Award for costume design in 1967.

Aghayan died of kidney failure in 2011 at 83.

Mackie was briefly married to Marianne Nicholson, an actor known as Lulu Porter, according to her IMDb bio. Their son, Robert Gordon Mackie Jr., who worked as a makeup artist, died from complications related to AIDS in 1993.

His work with actor, singer and dancer Mitzi Gaynor in 1966 caught Burnett’s attention, according to a short biography on his website. Her producer hired him to design the complete wardrobe for “The Carol Burnett Show,” a post he held for 11 seasons.

A star was born.

Mackie and Carol Burnett at one of his fashion shows in 1969. Max B. Miller / Getty Images file

Karger, who interviewed Mackie for a forthcoming book on Hollywood, said one of the designer’s most iconic costumes was made for a Burnett sketch lampooning “Gone With the Wind,” in which Scarlett O’Hara’s dress is fashioned from drapes and curtain rods, transforming her into Burnett’s Starlett O’Hara.

Karger said Mackie called it the “Wind Dress.” It’s now part of the collection at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History.

He said Mackie didn’t enjoy attention but deserved recognition that came later in life.

“When you think of Bob Mackie, you think of his loud, vibrant designs,” Karger said. “You think of the clothes that he designed for Carol Burnett to wear on her show or for Cher to wear at the Oscars or in a music video. When you knew Bob Mackie, you quickly learned that wasn’t him at all. He dressed in a very conservative way, almost kind of, like, preppy with a lot of tweed.”

Mackie created bold looks for Streisand for the 1975 film “Funny Lady.” She posted a photo of a dress she wore for the movie on her Facebook page Monday.

“Bob Mackie was an incredible talent,” Streisand said in a statement that accompanied the photo. “He designed one gorgeous outfit after another for me in Funny Lady. He might continue designing creations for the angels.”

National Comedy Center Executive Director Journey Gunderson said Mackie found a potent communications channel in costumes.

“Throughout his extraordinary body of work, Bob Mackie understood the unique power of costume in comedy — to help create a character and become part of the creative energy that drove the comedy itself,” Gunderson said in a statement.

His work with Burnett, Cher, Joan Rivers, Bette Midler and Lucille Ball “helped shape some of comedy’s most memorable moments on television and stage,” he added.

In 1982, Mackie launched a ready-to-wear collection and a line of collectible Barbie dolls, which featured red carpet-ready dresses complete with headdresses, dramatic long trains and his signature sequined glow.

Throughout the decades, his designs took on an increasingly universal appeal despite — or perhaps because of — their sheer scale and luminosity. One of his most famous pieces, the flame dress, has been worn by pop icons Beyoncé and Turner, as well as Cher, with whom he also shared a lengthy creative partnership.

The dress, a version of which debuted in 1968 on “The Fred Astaire Show,” initially featured large gold paillettes. By the time Cher and Turner donned matching versions on “The Sonny & Cher Show,” the paillettes were replaced by smaller sparkly sequins that came to typify his work.
