” … If something very important happens in the country, it doesn’t appear [in the media],” Sheinbaum claimed.

She subsequently accused media outlets of “distorting reality in a way that agrees with their propaganda.”

“… They seek to distort everything, adapt everything to what they want, create political propaganda for the right,” Sheinbaum said.

The president also accused media commentators of coordinating their attacks on the government.

“They have a [group] chat where they talk about what everyone is going to say during the week,” she said.

“This week, the INE. The INE is not an institution that guarantees clean elections,” Sheinbaum said, referring to the National Electoral Institute and seeking to provide an example of the kind of coordination she believes occurs.

In the context of alleged media bias and distortion, the president portrayed her accountability tour as a presentation of the truth, although her administration also faces allegations of bias.

“What do we do? Disseminate [information], talk. Why do I go to all the states to report [to the people]? So that they hear what we’re doing in all the federal entities,” Sheinbaum said, asserting that if citizens relied solely on the media, it would be difficult for them to find out what her government is actually achieving.

Sheinbaum: There is ‘deep pride’ in being Mexican

Citing poll results, Sheinbaum highlighted that pride in being Mexican is much more prevalent today than it was in 1990.

“The other day we brought out an El Financiero newspaper poll where it said that in 1990, 58% of Mexicans felt proud of being Mexican. Today it’s 90%,” she said.

🗣️ “El 90% está orgulloso de ser mexicanas y mexicanos” 🇲🇽 Claudia Sheinbaum resaltó que el trabajo de la Cuarta Transformación ayudó a que la población sea más orgullosa del país; “algo que no lo dio el neoliberalismo”, agregó pic.twitter.com/kfTuPxe3hH — El Universal (@El_Universal_Mx) September 14, 2026

“I like the poll [result] precisely because it’s what I see every day, especially when I go out on tour,” Sheinbaum said before asserting that there is “deep pride” in being Mexican.

“This didn’t happen during neoliberalism in Mexico,” she said, referring to the period between 1982 and 2018.

Rather, “deep pride” in being Mexican became more prevalent with “fourth transformation” (4T) governments in office, said Sheinbaum, who now leads the 4T movement founded by former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

“And it’s very powerful — very powerful because when a people knows their strength and their history, there is nothing that can stop them,” she said.

World.title: Western Cape Storm Warning Puts the Karoo at Level 4
World.content:
SOUTH AFRICA · WEATHER

Key Facts — What is happening A cut-off low, a slow-moving weather system that parks over a region and rains on it.

— Where the worst is The Central Karoo, in the interior of the Western Cape, not the coast.

— The warning level Yellow Level 4 for disruptive rain there, valid to late on Monday 14 September.

— How much rain 25 to 50 millimetres, locally 60 to 80.

— Cape Town itself Yellow Level 2 for severe thunderstorms, with hail, lightning and localised flooding.

— At sea Waves of four to four and a half metres south of Table Bay.

The heaviest warning this week is not for Cape Town. It is for a semi-desert 400 kilometres inland, where 80 millimetres of rain has nowhere to go.

Western Cape Storm Warning Puts the Karoo at Level 4

A cut-off low over the Western and Northern Cape has triggered warnings across the region. The highest of them covers the Karoo rather than the coast.

What the Weather Service Issued

The South African Weather Service issued a Yellow Level 4 warning for disruptive rain. It covers the Central Karoo in the Western Cape and eastern Namakwa in the Northern Cape.

It ran from six on Sunday evening to just before midnight on Monday 14 September.

Expected rainfall is 25 to 50 millimetres, with 60 to 80 in places. In a semi-arid region that is a large amount of water arriving at once.

The service warned it may displace communities, flood settlements and low-lying areas, and close bridges and roads.

It also flagged possible interruptions to water, electricity and schooling.

What Cape Town Is Actually Under

The City of Cape Town sits under a Yellow Level 2 warning for severe thunderstorms. So do the West Coast, Cape Winelands and Overberg districts.

That covers hail, excessive lightning and localised flooding. It is a real warning and it is two levels below the Karoo.

At sea, waves of four to four and a half metres are expected south of Table Bay.

A separate warning for damaging winds and waves covers KwaZulu-Natal, from Port Edward to Richards Bay. That is on the other side of the country.

The Level 4 warning covers the Karoo, 400 kilometres inland from Cape Town.

Why a Cut-Off Low Does This

Most weather systems in the Cape arrive from the Atlantic, rain and move on. A cut-off low detaches from the main westerly flow and stalls.

That is what turns a wet day into a flood. The same clouds sit over the same catchment for 24 or 36 hours.

Cut-off lows have caused some of South Africa’s deadliest flooding, including the KwaZulu-Natal disaster of April 2022.

Senior forecaster Tokelo Chiloane gave the practical advice for the coast. Avoid the beach area whenever there is a warning, he said. Gale-force winds are very dangerous, and the rough seas are also dangerous.

What It Means on the Ground

The Central Karoo is sparsely populated, and its towns sit along the N1, the main road between Cape Town and Johannesburg.

Road closures there have national consequences for freight, not just local ones.

In Cape Town itself, the expected disruption is the ordinary kind: surface flooding, delayed flights and traffic.

Informal settlements on the Cape Flats flood readily in any sustained rain. A Level 2 thunderstorm warning still matters there.

Cut-off lows have caused some of South Africa’s deadliest flooding.

What Comes Next

The Level 4 disruptive rain warning for the Central Karoo continues into 15 September.

Level 2 thunderstorm warnings remain for the West Coast, Cape Winelands, Overberg and the City of Cape Town.

No specific wind speeds were published for the Western Cape. Figures circulating in kilometres per hour did not come from the weather service.

For anyone travelling in the region this week, the warnings are updated daily and the inland routes are the ones to check.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Western Cape warning?

A Yellow Level 4 warning for disruptive rain over the Central Karoo and eastern Namakwa, valid into 15 September 2026.

Is Cape Town under the same warning?

No. The city is under a Yellow Level 2 warning for severe thunderstorms, two levels lower.

How much rain is expected?

25 to 50 millimetres in the warned area, with 60 to 80 in places.

What is a cut-off low?

A low pressure system that detaches from the main westerly flow and stalls. It rains over the same area for a day or more.

What about the sea?

Waves of four to four and a half metres are expected south of Table Bay.

Which roads are at risk?

Routes through the Central Karoo, including the N1 between Cape Town and Johannesburg.

Sources: South African Weather Service, SAnews, EWN, The Citizen.

World.title: Ethiopia Rebels Warn Mining Firms After Tulu Kapi Attack
World.content:
ETHIOPIA · MINING

Key Facts — Who issued it The Oromo Liberation Army, an insurgent group operating in Oromia, Ethiopia’s largest region.

— What it said Mining companies must consult local communities properly and meet verifiable environmental standards.

— The word it used Non-negotiable.

— Where it appeared A post on the group’s official account on 13 or 14 September, reported by Addis Standard.

— What it points to An attack on 4 September at the Tulu Kapi gold project in West Wollega, in which several people died.

— Who operates Tulu Kapi KEFI Gold and Copper, a London-listed company.

An armed group has told mining companies in Ethiopia how it expects them to behave. It pointed at a deadly attack as the consequence of not listening.

Ethiopia Rebels Warn Mining Firms After Tulu Kapi Attack

The Oromo Liberation Army has issued what it calls an urgent notice of requirement to companies working in Oromia’s mining sector. It arrived nine days after a fatal attack at a gold project.

What the Notice Says

The statement was posted on the group’s official account and reported by Addis Standard on 14 September.

It addresses foreign and domestic companies operating in the extractive sector in Oromia.

Companies must hold what it calls thorough and transparent deliberations with local communities. They must implement verifiable environmental standards.

Both requirements are described as non-negotiable.

No spokesperson is attached to the statement. Accounts attributed to the group have been impersonated in the past.

The Attack It Points To

On 4 September, gunmen attacked the Tulu Kapi gold project in West Wollega zone.

Several security personnel and community members were killed, including one company employee.

The operator, KEFI Gold and Copper, declined to give further detail, citing the sensitivity of an ongoing matter.

The group’s statement invokes Tulu Kapi as the consequence of non-compliance. It does not claim responsibility for the attack in the published text.

Who the Oromo Liberation Army Are

Oromia is Ethiopia’s largest region by population and area, and the Oromo are its largest ethnic group.

The Oromo Liberation Army broke from the older Oromo Liberation Front in 2018. The front had returned from exile to join mainstream politics.

It has fought the federal government ever since. The conflict has never attracted the attention given to the war in Tigray.

The Ethiopian government designates it a terrorist organisation. Talks in Tanzania in 2023 produced nothing.

What Tulu Kapi Was Supposed to Be

Tulu Kapi is one of the larger gold developments in Ethiopia and has been in preparation for more than a decade.

Ethiopia has been trying to build a mining industry to earn foreign currency it badly needs, having spent years short of dollars.

A project of this kind depends on a security guarantee the state provides. That guarantee is what the attack called into question.

For any investor weighing Ethiopian mining, the risk is not a tax rate or a licence. It is whether a site can be operated at all.

Why Companies Cannot Simply Leave

Mining licences are long, and the money is spent up front. A developer that walks away from a project like this loses everything it has put in.

That asymmetry is what gives an armed group leverage over a listed company.

It is also why statements of this kind are rarely answered in public. A company that negotiates openly with an insurgency has a different problem.

Ethiopia has been courting foreign miners for a decade, and this is the constraint the marketing does not mention.

One Word Worth Getting Right

The notice concerns mining, and mining only.

Ethiopia does have oil exploration, but it is in the Somali region in the east, a different theatre with a different insurgency.

Oromia has no producing oil. Descriptions of a warning to mining and oil companies extend the statement further than it goes.

Neither the federal government nor the Oromia regional administration had responded publicly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who issued the warning?

The Oromo Liberation Army, through a post on its official account reported by Addis Standard on 14 September 2026.

What does it demand?

Transparent consultation with local communities and verifiable environmental standards, both described as non-negotiable.

What happened at Tulu Kapi?

An attack on 4 September 2026 killed several security personnel and community members, including a company employee.

Who operates Tulu Kapi?

KEFI Gold and Copper, a London-listed company. It declined to comment in detail.

Did the group claim the attack?

Not in the published text. It invokes the attack as a consequence of non-compliance.

Does this affect oil companies?

No. Oromia has no producing oil. Ethiopia’s oil exploration is in the Somali region.

Sources: Addis Standard, KEFI Gold and Copper, BSS.

World.title: Algeria’s Economy 2026: Gas Dependence, Deficits and the Slow Turn to Diversification
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio.

Key Facts — Hydrocarbon dependence: Oil and gas account for 92–93% of Algeria’s exports and roughly 40% of GDP, according to the IMF’s 2025 Article IV consultation.

Oil and gas account for 92–93% of Algeria’s exports and roughly 40% of GDP, according to the IMF’s 2025 Article IV consultation. — External accounts: The current account is projected to swing to a deficit of about US$11.4 billion in 2026, after surpluses of US$19.1 billion (2022) and US$6.0 billion (2023).

The current account is projected to swing to a deficit of about US$11.4 billion in 2026, after surpluses of US$19.1 billion (2022) and US$6.0 billion (2023). — Budget: President Abdelmadjid Tebboune signed a US$135 billion budget for 2026 in December 2025, extending the post-2020 spending expansion.

President Abdelmadjid Tebboune signed a US$135 billion budget for 2026 in December 2025, extending the post-2020 spending expansion. — Energy diplomacy: 2026 brought a bigger gas deal with Germany’s VNG and a reinforced pipeline track with Spain via Medgaz.

The Hydrocarbon Engine — and Its Limits

Algeria enters the second half of the 2020s as Africa’s third-largest economy, with GDP projected at roughly US$285 billion in 2026 and growth of about 3.4% in 2025, or around US$6,095 per capita. The engine is unchanged: natural gas and oil. Hydrocarbons fund the state, the import bill and the generous subsidy system that underpins social peace — and they leave the country exposed to every swing in energy prices.

The IMF’s 2025 Article IV consultation laid out the arithmetic. The windfall years of 2022–2023, when Europe’s scramble to replace Russian gas filled Algerian coffers, are over. The current account is projected to widen to a deficit of about US$11.4 billion in 2026, and the Fund warns that the fiscal deficit remains elevated without strong policy action. Algerian economist Abderrahmane Mebtoul has estimated the 2025 budget gap at roughly US$61 billion — about 21% of GDP — an unofficial figure, but one that captures the scale of the revenue-expenditure mismatch.

A US$135 Billion Bet on Continuity

The government’s answer, for now, is spending. The 2026 budget, signed by Tebboune in December 2025, comes in at about US$135 billion — continuing the expansionist course set after 2020. Subsidies, public wages and infrastructure keep domestic demand alive, but they are funded by hydrocarbon revenue that depends on declining legacy fields and volatile prices.

State energy giant Sonatrach is the regime’s counter-move: a US$40 billion investment program for 2023–2027 spanning exploration, refining and renewable integration. New output from the Hassi R’mel and Touat fields has expanded natural gas production, buying time for the rentier model even as planners talk about life after gas.

Sonatrach, Algeria’s state energy company, is the backbone of the country’s gas exports to Europe.

Europe Is Buying: Germany and Spain Deepen Gas Ties

Algeria’s strongest card in 2026 is geography. In July, during Tebboune’s official visit to Berlin, Sonatrach signed an agreement with Germany’s VNG that increases pipeline gas deliveries to Germany from January 2027 and adds cooperation on a future green hydrogen corridor — a signal that Europe’s second-largest gas supplier to the EU intends to stay relevant in the energy transition, not just the gas era.

The Spain track advanced in parallel. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s July 2026 visit to Algiers reinforced the Medgaz pipeline arrangement — the direct subsea link that makes Algeria Spain’s top gas supplier — and scheduled the eighth high-level bilateral meeting for October 2026. Italian firms, meanwhile, are moving into Algerian agriculture and agri-mechanisation, a quieter but telling diversification of the relationship map.

Farms on the Mitidja plain near Algiers — agriculture sits at the center of Algeria’s diversification push.

The Diversification Question

Every Algerian government for two decades has promised to diversify away from hydrocarbons. The 2026 reality is mixed. Non-hydrocarbon exports remain marginal; the private sector operates in the shadow of the state; and periodic import-restriction drives — including a fraud inquiry into import requests this year — show how defensive the economic reflexes still are. Mining (notably iron ore at Gara Djebilet), phosphates, agriculture and renewables are the designated growth sectors, but none yet moves the macro needle.

The stakes are generational. Algeria’s median age is under 30, and the labor market cannot absorb new entrants without growth outside the state-energy complex. The gas rents of 2022–2023 financed a grace period; the deficits of 2026 are the bill. How Algiers sequences subsidy reform, private-sector opening and energy-transition investment — against a watchful security establishment — is the central economic story of North Africa’s largest country.

Frequently Asked Questions

How big is Algeria’s economy in 2026?

GDP is projected at roughly US$285 billion in 2026, with growth of about 3.4% in 2025 and GDP per capita around US$6,095 — making Algeria one of Africa’s three largest economies.

How dependent is Algeria on oil and gas?

Extremely: hydrocarbons account for 92–93% of exports and roughly 40% of GDP, according to the IMF’s 2025 Article IV consultation. The current account is projected to swing to an US$11.4 billion deficit in 2026 as energy windfalls fade.

Who buys Algerian gas?

Europe is the anchor market. Spain receives gas via the Medgaz subsea pipeline, Italy via the Transmed link, and a July 2026 agreement with Germany’s VNG increases pipeline deliveries to Germany from January 2027, with added cooperation on green hydrogen.

What is Sonatrach investing in?

Sonatrach, the state energy company, is running a US$40 billion investment program for 2023–2027 covering exploration, refining and renewable integration. New production from the Hassi R’mel and Touat fields has expanded gas output.

World.title: Belgium Sends Semlex to Trial Over Congo Passport Fees
World.content:
DR CONGO · CORRUPTION

Key Facts — The company Semlex, a Brussels firm that printed biometric passports for the Democratic Republic of Congo.

— The allegation That passport fees were inflated and the difference went offshore.

— How it worked The price of a Congolese passport roughly doubled to US$185. Civil parties say US$60 of each one went to a company in Dubai.

— The total About US$60 million over a decade, on the civil parties’ estimate.

— What just happened A Brussels court sent Semlex and 13 others to stand trial on 31 August.

— When the trial starts Unknown. No date has been set.

For a decade, Congolese citizens paid one of the highest passport prices in the world. A Brussels court has now decided that fourteen defendants must explain where the money went.

Belgium Sends Semlex to Trial Over Congo Passport Fees

A Belgian court has ordered Semlex and thirteen other defendants to stand trial over the Congolese passport contract. The investigation began at an airport nine years ago.

What the Court Decided

On 31 August, the Brussels council chamber referred Semlex and thirteen co-defendants to the city’s criminal court.

That is a committal, not the opening of a trial. It means a judge has found the case strong enough to be heard.

The charges are bribery of foreign public officials, money laundering and tax fraud. They relate to Congolese biometric passport production between 2015 and 2025.

Reuters, which reported the referral, could not establish when the trial will begin. No date exists.

The Passport That Cost US$185

The mechanism at the centre of the case is simple enough to explain in a sentence.

The price of a Congolese passport roughly doubled, to US$185. Of that, civil parties allege US$60 per passport went to LRPS Ltd, a company registered in Dubai.

Reuters reported in 2017 that LRPS was linked to a relative or close associate of Joseph Kabila, then president of Congo.

Over a decade, the civil parties put the total diverted at around US$60 million.

That figure is their estimate. No court has made a finding on it.

Who Is Involved

Semlex was founded and is led by Albert Karaziwan, a Belgian businessman whose company has supplied identity documents across Africa.

The identities of the thirteen co-defendants have not been disclosed. Congolese reporting describes them as Semlex executives and figures close to the Kabila-era presidency.

Entities named in that reporting include Semlex itself, its Congolese subsidiary Locosem, and LRPS.

Semlex has previously said it is the target of a smear campaign. The allegations are unproven.

The price of a Congolese passport roughly doubled, to US$185.

How It Started

The case began with money. In 2016, suspicious funds were found at Brussels Airport.

The investigation that followed has run for what campaigners call nearly nine years.

In May 2020, fifty-one Congolese citizens joined the proceedings as civil parties. They are supported by FIDH, the Belgian League for Human Rights, Transparency International and its Belgian chapter.

The Congolese state itself is not among the civil parties.

Fifty-one Congolese citizens joined the case as civil parties in 2020.

Why Belgium Is on Trial Too

Transparency International Belgium and FIDH call it a first. No Belgian company has had to answer in court before for bribing foreign public officials.

Belgium has been criticised repeatedly by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development for weak enforcement of foreign bribery law.

That is why the case carries weight beyond the passports. It is a test of whether Belgian courts will prosecute Belgian companies for what they do abroad.

Congo and Belgium have a particular history. A Brussels courtroom weighing what Congolese citizens paid for their own passports sits inside it.

The trial date is the thing to watch. A committal without a hearing date can sit for a long time.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Semlex?

A Brussels-based biometric identity document company, founded and led by Albert Karaziwan.

What is it accused of?

Bribery of foreign public officials, money laundering and tax fraud over Congolese passport production from 2015 to 2025.

How much money is involved?

About US$60 million, on the civil parties’ estimate, from roughly US$60 of each US$185 passport fee.

Has the trial started?

No. A Brussels court referred 14 defendants to trial on 31 August 2026 and no date has been set.

Who brought the civil claim?

Fifty-one Congolese citizens, supported by FIDH, Transparency International and other organisations. Not the Congolese state.

Why is the case significant?

Campaigners say it is the first time a Belgian company has faced court over bribing foreign officials.

Sources: Reuters, FIDH, Transparency International Belgium, Congo Quotidien.

World.title: Libya and Washington Talk Elections, Budget and Oil
World.content:
LIBYA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — The problem Libya has had two rival governments since 2014 and no national election since 2014.

— What happened The Tripoli prime minister met the senior American diplomat for Libya on Sunday 13 September.

— What they discussed An election framework, a single national spending plan, and keeping the oil flowing.

— Why now Eastern and western negotiators signed an accord on 30 August covering elections within 24 months.

— The oil Libya’s only real revenue. The National Oil Corporation kept pumping through the war and still does.

— What is not settled Everything else. No election date exists and the two governments remain separate.

Libya has spent a decade holding meetings about elections. The difference this time is that the two halves of the country signed something first, and Washington is now inside the room.

Libya and Washington Talk Elections, Budget and Oil

Libya’s Tripoli government met the senior United States diplomat for the country on Sunday. The agenda was the three things that have to move together: a vote, a budget and the oil.

Who Met

Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, prime minister of the Government of National Unity, received Jeremy Berndt in Tripoli on Sunday 13 September.

Berndt holds two roles. He is United States chargé d’affaires to Libya, and since July also senior policy adviser for Libya policy at the State Department.

The Libyan readout covers three files. The political track, a unified spending agreement, and support for the oil sector.

Berndt met the chairman of the National Oil Corporation, Masoud Suleiman, on the same day.

The Accord That Made the Meeting Worth Holding

On 30 August, a body known as the 4+4 Committee signed an accord at United Nations headquarters in Tripoli.

It has four representatives from eastern Libya and four from the west. That is what makes it different from most Libyan negotiating formats.

The accord reshapes the High National Elections Commission under a new chairman, Dhou Al-Hamali, with Sana Al-Lishani as deputy.

It separates presidential and legislative results, and it commits to elections within 24 months.

A separate body, the older 6+6 committee from the 2023 Bouznika process, was revived under an Ankara agreement on 11 September. The two are different mechanisms.

Why Money Is Part of the Conversation

Libya has one national institution that never split: the central bank holds the oil revenue, and the National Oil Corporation earns it.

Two governments spending from one pot is the mechanism through which the division has been financed for a decade.

The unified spending agreement, brokered with American involvement, is an attempt to impose one budget on both.

It covers fiscal discipline, transparency and equitable distribution. Those three words describe exactly what has been absent.

The accord commits to elections within 24 months, without setting a date.

The Oil Nobody Wants to Interrupt

Libya holds Africa’s largest proven oil reserves. Production has recovered to well over a million barrels a day despite everything.

The National Oil Corporation has functioned through blockades, rival boards and armed standoffs at the terminals.

Berndt’s meeting with Suleiman covered budget implementation under the spending agreement, and the position of American companies.

Both halves of the political class have an interest in the oil continuing to flow. It is the one thing they agree on.

The central bank holds the oil revenue both governments spend from.

What This Does Not Solve

No election date exists. A commitment to elections within 24 months is not a schedule.

The eastern government under Osama Hammad continues to operate separately, with its own institutions and its own policies.

In June it barred nationals of Sudan, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia from territory under its control. Diplomats and some contracted workers were exempt.

That decision was taken without reference to Tripoli, which is the shape of the problem in miniature.

For foreign companies and residents, the practical test is whether one budget actually funds one set of institutions. Until then Libya remains two countries sharing an oil account.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who met in Tripoli?

Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah and Jeremy Berndt, the US chargé d’affaires and senior policy adviser for Libya, on 13 September 2026.

What did they discuss?

The electoral process, a unified national spending agreement and stability in the oil sector.

What is the 4+4 Committee?

A body with four representatives each from eastern and western Libya. It signed an accord on 30 August 2026.

When will Libya hold elections?

No date exists. The accord commits to elections within 24 months.

Why does the budget matter?

Libya has two governments spending from one oil revenue pot. A unified spending agreement would change that.

Is Libya still divided?

Yes. The eastern government under Osama Hammad operates its own institutions and sets its own policies.

Sources: Libya Observer, Al-Saa24, North Africa Post, UNSMIL, National Oil Corporation.

World.title: Tunisia Moves to Rewrite a Drug Law That Filled Its Prisons
World.content:
TUNISIA · DRUG POLICY

Key Facts — The law Law 52 of 1992, which made drug use a prison offence in Tunisia with almost no judicial discretion.

— What changed in 2017 Judges were allowed to consider mitigating circumstances. Use stayed criminal.

— The pressure now Drug cases rose from about 5,000 in 2020 to more than 15,000 in 2025.

— Arrests More than 27,000 in 2025, against roughly 10,000 in 2020.

— What is spreading Cocaine, ecstasy and pregabalin, sold under the brand name Lyrica.

— The seizure that shocked Tunis Twelve million pregabalin tablets at Radès port in September 2025.

Tunisia jailed young people for smoking cannabis for thirty years. The argument now is not about whether to change that law, but about which direction to change it in.

Tunisia Moves to Rewrite a Drug Law That Filled Its Prisons

Two very different plans to replace Tunisia’s 1992 drug law are moving at the same time. One would give police more powers. The other would treat users as patients.

The Law That Defined a Generation

Law 52 of 1992 made consumption of illegal drugs a prison offence. It carried a mandatory minimum and left a judge little room to disagree.

For three decades it filled Tunisian prisons with young men convicted over cannabis. It became shorthand in Tunisian politics for a state that punished rather than governed.

A partial amendment was adopted on 25 April 2017 by 133 votes to 140 cast.

It allowed judges to apply mitigating circumstances and avoid prison in some cases. It did not decriminalise use, and it was billed at the time as provisional.

Nine years later the full revision it anticipated has still not happened.

The Numbers Behind the New Push

The figures come from Mohamed Ali Chaïbi, who heads the anti-narcotics service at the El Gorjani judicial police directorate. He gave them in a television appearance on 10 September.

Drug cases rose from over 5,000 in 2020 to more than 15,000 in 2025. Arrests went from around 10,000 to over 27,000 across the same period.

The 27,000 is an annual figure for 2025 rather than a running total.

The drug mix has changed too. Cocaine and ecstasy are spreading, with ecstasy arriving across the Libyan border along a route from India through Turkey.

The Pill That Changed the Conversation

Pregabalin, sold as Lyrica, is a prescription drug for nerve pain and epilepsy. In North Africa it has become a street drug.

Tunisian seizures went from about 60,000 tablets in 2020 to twelve million at Radès port in September 2025.

That was described as the largest interception in Tunisian history.

A pharmaceutical arriving by the container load is a different problem from cannabis. It is the one driving the police case for new powers.

Arrests rose from around 10,000 in 2020 to more than 27,000 in 2025.

Two Reforms, Pulling Apart

The version that has reached parliament is not the police version.

Fifteen deputies filed a private members’ bill on 25 February 2025. It went to the Commission of General Legislation, chaired by Faouzi Daas, on 10 April 2025.

That text runs to 17 articles and balances enforcement with a therapeutic approach, moving away from imprisoning users. Special investigation techniques, including wiretapping and undercover work, appear within it.

The interior ministry is arguing for the enforcement half. There is no published government bill.

So Tunisia has a police service advocating tougher tools and a parliamentary committee holding a text that would treat users more gently. Neither has become law.

Tunisia sits between Libya and the Mediterranean, on a transit route.

Why This Matters to Foreign Residents

Tunisia is a transit country. It sits between Libya and the Mediterranean, within reach of European markets.

That geography shapes how its police operate and how seriously possession is treated, including for visitors.

Until a new law passes, the 1992 statute as amended in 2017 remains in force. Consumption is still a criminal offence.

For anyone living in or travelling to Tunisia, the practical position has not changed. What has changed is that both directions of reform are now on the table at once.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Tunisia’s Law 52?

A 1992 statute making drug consumption a prison offence with little judicial discretion. It was partially amended in 2017.

How many drug cases does Tunisia have?

More than 15,000 in 2025, up from over 5,000 in 2020, with more than 27,000 arrests in 2025.

What drugs are spreading?

Cocaine, ecstasy and pregabalin, sold as Lyrica. Twelve million pregabalin tablets were seized at Radès in September 2025.

Is there a government bill?

No. A private members’ bill filed in February 2025 sits with a parliamentary committee.

What would that bill do?

It runs to 17 articles, balancing enforcement with a therapeutic approach and including wiretapping and undercover powers.

Has the law changed yet?

No. The 1992 law as amended in 2017 remains in force and consumption is still criminal.

Sources: Tunis Afrique Presse, La Presse de Tunisie, Directinfo, Tunisian Assembly of the Representatives of the People.

World.title: Morocco Votes on 23 September With Turnout the Real Test
World.content:
MOROCCO · ELECTIONS

Key Facts — What is being elected All 395 seats in Morocco’s Chamber of Representatives, the lower house of parliament.

— When Wednesday 23 September, after a campaign that began on 10 September.

— Who is standing 7,288 candidates on 1,850 lists, from 28 political formations.

— How the seats work 305 are local constituency seats. The other 90 come from regional lists reserved for women.

— Who is staying out Al Adl Wal Ihsane, the largest Islamist movement, which has called on its supporters to abstain.

— What the king does Morocco is a monarchy where the king holds real power. Parliament governs within limits he sets.

Morocco votes for a parliament that governs but does not rule. The number the palace will read afterwards is not the winner’s share, but how many people bothered to turn up.

Morocco Votes on 23 September With Turnout the Real Test

Moroccans elect a new parliament on 23 September. Twenty-eight political formations are competing, and the country’s largest Islamist movement is telling people to stay home.

The Mechanics

Polling day is Wednesday 23 September, set by decree. The campaign period runs 13 days, from 10 to 22 September.

The Chamber of Representatives has 395 seats. Of those, 305 are elected in local constituencies.

The remaining 90 come from regional lists that are reserved entirely for women, a quota built into the electoral law.

The interior ministry counts 7,288 candidates across 1,850 lists. Women make up 36.47% of them.

About 15.8 million voters are registered.

Who Is In and Who Is Out

Twenty-eight political formations are fielding candidates, including alliances formed for this election. Twenty-seven were allocated broadcast time, which is where the smaller figure in circulation comes from.

The Justice and Development Party is contesting, led by Abdelilah Benkirane. It governed Morocco from 2011 to 2021 and then lost more than 90% of its seats in a single election.

Al Adl Wal Ihsane announced on 9 September that it would boycott. It called the system incapable of genuine democracy and cited what it described as the renewal and expansion of authoritarianism and corruption.

That movement is not a registered party and could not have stood in any case. It rejects the constitutional order and the monarchy’s religious authority.

Its boycott is therefore a call to voters rather than a withdrawal of candidates, and it is aimed squarely at turnout.

About 15.8 million voters are registered.

Why Turnout Is the Number That Matters

Morocco is a constitutional monarchy. King Mohammed VI appoints the prime minister from the largest party, and keeps authority over religion, defence and foreign policy.

Parliament makes law and manages the economy. It does not decide the direction of the state.

That arrangement depends on elections being seen as meaningful. Low turnout undermines it more effectively than any opposition victory.

Turnout was 50.35% in 2021 and 42.29% in 2016. A movement with the reach of Al Adl Wal Ihsane calling for abstention is aimed at exactly that number.

The Western Sahara Backdrop

Morocco’s central foreign policy objective is recognition of its autonomy plan for Western Sahara, the territory it has controlled since 1975.

On 4 September in Copenhagen, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen received his Moroccan counterpart Nasser Bourita and called the plan credible.

He described it as a good basis for a mutually agreed solution, and as a serious contribution to the United Nations process.

Denmark first endorsed the plan in September 2024, so this was a reaffirmation rather than a shift.

The timing has weight anyway. Security Council Resolution 2797 renewed the UN mission to 31 October 2026, so a renewal debate is due in late October.

Turnout was 50.35% in 2021 and 42.29% in 2016.

What to Watch on the Night

The first figure to appear will be participation. It will be read as a verdict on the system rather than on any party.

The second is whether the Justice and Development Party recovers any of the ground it lost in 2021.

The third is the shape of the coalition. No Moroccan party has won a majority alone in the modern era, and the palace has a role in what follows.

Foreign residents and businesses will see little immediate change. Economic policy in Morocco has been notably consistent across governments of different colours.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does Morocco vote?

Wednesday 23 September 2026, after a 13-day campaign that began on 10 September.

How many seats are contested?

395 in the Chamber of Representatives: 305 local seats and 90 from regional lists reserved for women.

How many parties are standing?

Twenty-eight formations are fielding candidates. Twenty-seven received official broadcast campaign time.

Who is boycotting?

Al Adl Wal Ihsane, the largest Islamist movement. It is not a registered party and could not have contested.

Is the PJD standing?

Yes, led by Abdelilah Benkirane. It governed from 2011 to 2021 before losing over 90% of its seats.

What power does parliament have?

It legislates and manages the economy. The king retains authority over religion, defence and foreign policy.

Sources: Maroc.ma, Moroccan Interior Ministry, Le Matin, Le Desk, Morocco World News, UN Security Council.

World.title: Eritrea Accuses the UAE of Port Imperialism in Africa
World.content:
ERITREA · RED SEA

Key Facts — Who is speaking Osman Saleh, foreign minister of Eritrea, one of the world’s most closed states.

— What he said That the United Arab Emirates is practising what he called port imperialism across Africa.

— Where In an interview in Asmara, published on 12 September.

— The ports he means Berbera in Somaliland and Bosaso in Puntland, both run by Dubai’s DP World.

— What Eritrea did Refused. It turned down a UAE proposal for a military facility in its Dahlak islands, around a decade ago.

— Why anyone should care These ports sit on the approaches to the Red Sea, through which roughly a tenth of world trade passes.

Eritrea rarely explains itself to anyone. Its foreign minister has now set out why his government keeps turning down offers from the Gulf.

Eritrea Accuses the UAE of Port Imperialism in Africa

Eritrea’s foreign minister has given a rare interview about Gulf ports. The United Arab Emirates, he says, is building a chain of them around the Horn for reasons that are not commercial.

What He Actually Said

Osman Saleh spoke to Middle East Eye in Asmara. The phrase he used was port imperialism.

The UAE has port facilities everywhere in the region, he said, and African countries have to ask why. Is it just for economics? No.

On his own country he was categorical. We didn’t want DP World in Eritrea, he said. We do not want any foreign power to have a hub in Eritrea.

He extended the question to Israel. Why is Israel running to control the Horn of Africa, he asked. Why do they need a base in Somaliland?

The Ports in Question

DP World, the Dubai state-owned operator, holds 51% of the Berbera concession in Somaliland under an agreement signed in 2016. Somaliland holds 30%.

Ethiopia took 19% in 2018 and then forfeited it for failing to meet the investment conditions. Reporting since 2022 treats that stake as lapsed.

Bosaso, in Puntland, is run by P&O Ports, a DP World subsidiary, under a 30-year concession signed in 2017.

Both agreements were signed with regional administrations rather than with the federal government in Mogadishu.

The Somali federal parliament voted the arrangements null and void in 2018. They remain legally contested.

The Offer Eritrea Turned Down

Saleh disclosed that Eritrea rejected a UAE proposal. It was for a shared Emirati and Israeli military facility on an island in the Dahlak Archipelago.

That was around 2016, roughly five years before the Abraham Accords made Israeli and Gulf cooperation public.

Eritrea did allow something else. The UAE operated a base at Assab from 2015 for the Saudi-led campaign in Yemen, and later wound it down.

So the refusal is a decade old and is only now being described publicly. It reads as an explanation of Eritrean policy rather than as a new dispute.

Eritrea turned down a proposed foreign military facility in its Dahlak islands.

Why the Horn Attracts This Attention

The Bab al-Mandab strait, between Djibouti and Yemen, is one of the world’s critical shipping chokepoints.

Roughly a tenth of global trade passes through it, and Houthi attacks since 2023 have shown how quickly that can be interrupted.

The coastline from Djibouti round to Puntland is therefore some of the most militarily and commercially contested in the world.

Djibouti alone hosts American, French, Italian, Japanese and Chinese military facilities within a few kilometres of each other.

A port concession in that geography is never purely a port concession, which is the argument Saleh is making.

Both port deals were signed with regional administrations, not with Mogadishu.

What It Means for Somalia

The accusation lands in the middle of an unresolved Somali dispute about who may sign away a coastline.

Somaliland declared independence in 1991 and is recognised by no country. Puntland is an autonomous federal member state.

Both signed port deals directly with Dubai. Mogadishu says they had no authority to do so.

Eritrea, which has its own long history of conflict with Ethiopia over sea access, has an interest in keeping that question open.

The United Arab Emirates has not responded to the interview.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Eritrea accuse the UAE of?

Its foreign minister, Osman Saleh, said the UAE is practising port imperialism across Africa, in an interview published on 12 September 2026.

Which ports are involved?

Berbera in Somaliland and Bosaso in Puntland, both operated by Dubai’s DP World or its subsidiary.

Does Mogadishu accept those deals?

No. The Somali federal parliament voted them null and void in 2018 and they remain contested.

Did Eritrea reject a UAE base?

Yes. It turned down a proposed shared UAE and Israeli facility in the Dahlak islands, around 2016.

Was there ever a UAE base in Eritrea?

Yes, at Assab from 2015 for the Saudi-led Yemen campaign. It was later wound down.

Why does the Horn of Africa matter?

It controls the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which roughly a tenth of world trade passes.

Sources: Middle East Eye, Shabelle Media Network, Reuters, The National.

World.title: Collin Francis sentenced to 16 years for manslaughter of Nestor Vasquez, 10 years for attempted murder of nurse
World.content:
Collin Francis sentenced to 16 years for manslaughter of Nestor Vasquez, 10 years for attempted murder of nurse

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Seven years after Nestor Vasquez, 60, was fatally beaten inside a police holding cell, Collin Francis, 33, has been sentenced to 16 years in prison for manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.

High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim also sentenced Francis to 10 years for the attempted murder of psychiatric nurse Augustina Elijio. The sentences will run concurrently and take effect from June 6, 2019, meaning the time Francis has already spent in custody will count toward his sentence.

Francis pleaded guilty earlier this year to both offences after psychiatric evidence established that he had been suffering from schizophrenia and was experiencing an acute psychotic episode at the time of the attacks. He had initially faced a murder charge for Vasquez’s death, but the Crown later accepted manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility.

Elijio was attacked on June 4, 2019, at the Port Loyola Health Centre, where Francis had gone seeking mental-health treatment. Public reports at the time said he returned to the facility in an agitated state and stabbed Elijio multiple times.

Francis was subsequently detained at the Queen Street Police Station. Two days later, Vasquez was placed in the same holding area with him and was brutally beaten. Vasquez suffered massive blunt-force trauma and died at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital on June 8. Police later acknowledged serious failures surrounding the incident, and three officers were placed on interdiction and faced disciplinary proceedings.

Vasquez was the brother of Channel 7 News Director, Jules Vasquez, who attended Monday’s sentencing. Speaking about the case, Jules said he believes police failed his brother by placing him in a cell with Francis despite Francis’s mental condition and the fact that he had attacked Elijio only days earlier.

The case was delayed for years because of questions surrounding Francis’s fitness to stand trial. Justice Pilgrim found Francis unfit to plead in February 2024 and ordered that his condition be medically reviewed every six months. A psychiatrist later assessed Francis as fit to stand trial in 2026.

In his sentencing decision, however, Justice Pilgrim strongly criticized the failure of prison authorities to carry out the court-ordered periodic psychiatric assessments. The judge noted that several reviews should have occurred before Francis was eventually reassessed and said the failure created uncertainty over whether Francis may have regained fitness much earlier.

Justice Pilgrim ruled that it would therefore be unfair to exclude the period during which Francis was deemed unfit from his time served, saying the failure by the authorities to comply with the court’s order should not operate to Francis’s disadvantage.

“There is no excuse for failing to fulfil a court order,” the judge said, while also stressing the State’s constitutional responsibility to provide adequate resources, including psychiatric services, for the proper functioning of the criminal justice system.

Justice Pilgrim also raised the broader issue of how Belize handles accused persons suffering from severe mental illness and recommended that lawmakers examine the need for an appropriate facility to accommodate and treat persons in circumstances such as Francis’s.

World.title: Man detained after wife reports that he burned down their house in Paraiso
World.content:
Man detained after wife reports that he burned down their house in Paraiso

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained Gregorio Espirito as they investigate allegations that he deliberately set fire to his own house, the home he shared with his wife.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Hilberto Romero, Head of the National Crime Investigation Branch, said police responded on Saturday to a fire at a residence in Paraiso Village, where an approximately 18-by-20-foot building was engulfed in flames.

According to Romero, Espirito’s wife reported that she was in the area when she saw her husband enter the house. Shortly afterward, the building went up in flames.

Gregorio Espirito was subsequently detained and remains in police custody pending the outcome of the investigation.

Romero confirmed that the couple lived together and that police have received previous reports of domestic violence involving them.

Police are continuing their investigation to determine whether criminal charges will be laid.

World.title: Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry: 30th Expo Belize Market Place draws almost 10,000 visitors
World.content:
Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry: 30th Expo Belize Market Place draws almost 10,000 visitors

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BCCI) is celebrating the success of the 30th Annual Expo Belize Market Place, held September 12–13 at the Marion Jones Sports Complex in Belize City.

This year’s milestone event was held under the theme, “Expo Belize Market Place® – The Original Expo: 30 Years of Connecting Business, Creating Opportunities.”

The BCCI said the weekend attracted close to 10,000 visitors, surpassing last year’s attendance despite early-morning rains and midday heat. The Chamber also reported strong purchasing activity and increased consumer spending throughout the weekend, reflecting continued support for local businesses. The large turnout, however, also highlighted the need for a fully indoor and weather-proof venue as the Expo continues to grow.

The 30th anniversary edition featured several new attractions, including the “30 for 30” Expo Shopping Challenge and hourly giveaways.

Visitors also enjoyed performances throughout the weekend, with the Expo House Band and Super Furia providing entertainment alongside headline performances by Belizean artists Supa G and Vida Magz. The opening ceremony featured remarks from BCCI President Giacomo Sanchez, Belize City Deputy Mayor Elude Miller and Mena Group of Companies Director and Ambassador for Trade in Belize Emile Mena.

Sanchez emphasized the broader role of the Expo in supporting Belizean businesses, stating, “The Expo is more than a trade and consumer show; it is a platform where consumers can discover and support local products and services, entrepreneurs can build relationships, and the wider community can come together to celebrate Belizean enterprise.”

The BCCI also recognized outstanding exhibitors through its Best Booth Awards, with Smart Belize taking Overall Business Excellence and Marketing Excellence, while Taste by Tess won Most Outstanding Micro Entrepreneur, Zesty Squeeze took Most Outstanding Youth Entrepreneur, Pickle La Cochinita Pibil Tacos won Most Outstanding Food Booth, and Digi Belize received Most Innovative Excellence.

To mark three decades of the Expo, the BCCI also honored 13 Legacy Partners whose support has helped anchor the event since its inception in 1996.

World.title: Belize Is Not A Real Place? Croc caught in viral Southside brawl rescued; charges may follow while larger croc remains in neighborhood
World.content:
Belize Is Not A Real Place? Croc caught in viral Southside brawl rescued; charges may follow while larger croc remains in neighborhood

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A crocodile seen tied up as a brawl unfolded in a viral video posted by Breaking Belize News on Belize City’s Southside was safely rescued and relocated Sunday night, but police say charges may follow from the incident, while wildlife responders warn that a second, larger crocodile may still be in the Dolphin Street neighborhood.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Hilberto Romero, Head of the National Crime Investigation Branch, confirmed Monday that police have seen the video and that the matter has been referred to the department’s Cybercrime Unit.

Romero said police can investigate potentially criminal acts captured in videos circulating online even without waiting for someone to make a formal complaint.

He said investigators will seek to identify the persons involved and determine whether any offences were committed.

Police are also reviewing the handling of the crocodile, which is a protected animal in Belize, and Romero said persons involved could face charges if investigators determine that an offence was committed.

The Crocodile Research Coalition (CRC) became aware of the incident after the video began circulating online and members of the public contacted and tagged wildlife organizations.

Dr. Marisa Tellez, founder and Executive Director of the CRC, said the footage appeared to show that the crocodile had been captured but was not properly restrained and was being teased or harassed.

Tellez said such treatment of a protected animal could potentially result in charges under Belize’s wildlife laws.

CRC volunteers Erica Holding and Austin Bennett subsequently responded to Dolphin Street on Belize City’s Southside at around 10:15 p.m.

Holding said that by the time they arrived, police were already at the location and the crocodile had been moved into a shed.

Residents had restrained the animal using electrical wire, cable and a cloth.

The volunteers removed those restraints, properly secured the crocodile and transported it from the area with assistance from police.

Despite the chaotic circumstances seen in the viral video, Holding and Bennett said the crocodile did not appear to have suffered injuries during the incident.

Bennett said the animal had minor wounds which appeared to have been caused by previous encounters with other crocodiles.

The crocodile was subsequently released into suitable habitat away from the heavily populated area.

The CRC does not reveal such specific locations where animals are released as doing so could place relocated wildlife at risk.

Holding also revealed that residents reported seeing two crocodiles frequenting the neighborhood.

CRC believes both animals may be males and may have been involved in an ongoing territorial fight.

The crocodile captured Sunday night was reportedly the smaller of the two, while the larger animal left the area after its rival was caught.

That means the second crocodile may still be somewhere in or around the Dolphin Street area.

Holding said she collected contact information from residents and asked them to provide photographs or videos if the larger crocodile reappears.

She and Bennett will then assess whether the animal needs to be captured and relocated or whether removing the smaller male from the area has resolved the problem.

Romero said investigators will meanwhile review both the fight captured in the viral footage and the circumstances surrounding the crocodile’s handling.

No charges had been announced as of Monday.

World.title: World Meteorological Organization warns of very strong El Niño with extreme weather risks into 2027
World.content:
World Meteorological Organization warns of very strong El Niño with extreme weather risks into 2027

By Zoila Palma: El Niño is expected to intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, increasing the risks of extreme weather around the world, according to a new update from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

The climate phenomenon is already firmly established and is expected to have significant effects on rainfall and temperature patterns, with heightened risks of floods, drought and extreme heat.

WMO forecasts indicate an “exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100%” that El Niño will persist through February 2027. The agency said this is the first time one of its El Niño/La Niña updates has been so unequivocal, reflecting strong agreement among forecasting centres and climate experts worldwide.

The phenomenon is being fueled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific.

According to WMO, El Niño is expected to strengthen further during the coming months, reaching a very strong intensity before peaking toward the end of 2026, while its climate impacts are expected to continue into 2027.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned of the growing global risks associated with the event, saying, “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes.”

He added that rising sea surface temperatures and increasing global temperatures are placing the world in a dangerous period of extreme weather, reiterating the need for stronger climate action and preparedness.

WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said communities and economies could face significant impacts as El Niño intensifies. “El Niño in Spanish means boy child – but it has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world,” Saulo said, noting that droughts and floods are already causing disruption and devastation and could worsen.

Saulo said the exceptional strength of the event requires increased preparation and response, with national meteorological and hydrological services playing a critical role in protecting lives and livelihoods.

WMO said it is working with United Nations and humanitarian partners to provide climate information to support disaster management and climate-sensitive sectors, including agriculture, health, energy and water resources, emphasizing that “we have no time to lose.”

World.title: Two men killed after truck crashes into vehicles stopped near fallen tree on Hummingbird Highway
World.content:
Two men killed after truck crashes into vehicles stopped near fallen tree on Hummingbird Highway

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating Wednesday’s deadly collision on the Hummingbird Highway in which two men were killed after a heavy-duty truck crashed into vehicles that had stopped near a fallen tree.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Hilberto Romero, Head of the National Crime Investigation Branch, identified the deceased during Monday’s police briefing as Irvin Gutierrez and Jaheed Lopez.

Romero said police responded between miles 51 and 52 of the Hummingbird Highway, where they found a truck overturned and four other vehicles damaged.

Investigators determined that several vehicles had stopped along the highway while persons worked to clear a tree that had fallen across the roadway.

According to Romero, the truck was travelling toward Belmopan and was unable to stop in time, colliding with the vehicles before overturning.

Gutierrez and Lopez were trapped beneath the truck and were pronounced dead at the scene.

Romero said police have recorded several statements and taken measurements as part of the investigation. A sample was obtained from the truck driver, who was also served with a Notice of Intended Prosecution.

The completed case file will be submitted to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions for directives.

Public reporting has confirmed that Lopez was among those who had stopped to help clear the fallen tree. He was also a footballer and University of Belize student who had recently received a sports scholarship.

The accident occurred near Armenia Village at around 4:30 p.m. and involved an 18-wheeler carrying sand and gravel.

World.title: Thieves got some ‘Belize Local Deals’ after Blake Building break-in; phones, laptops and tablets among stolen items
World.content:
Thieves got some ‘Belize Local Deals’ after Blake Building break-in; phones, laptops and tablets among stolen items

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating another burglary at Belize Local Deals, located inside the Blake Building in Belize City, where thieves made off with several cell phones, laptops and tablets.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Hilberto Romero, Head of the National Crime Investigation Branch, said the burglary was reported at around 7:10 a.m. on Sunday.

According to Romero, a security guard made checks inside the business establishment after becoming suspicious and discovered that locks had been broken.

Further checks revealed that a number of electronic devices, including laptops, tablets and cell phones, had been stolen.

Romero said investigators are reviewing surveillance footage from the property in an effort to identify the persons responsible.

Police did not have a final count or value for the stolen merchandise at the time of Monday’s briefing.

The Blake Building has been targeted before. In August, burglars broke into Belize Local Deals at the Hudson Street property and stole a large quantity of electronics. Surveillance footage from that incident reportedly showed six persons entering the establishment.

Police investigations continue.

World.title: Galen University celebrates 2026 Eagle Scholarship recipients
World.content:
Galen University celebrates 2026 Eagle Scholarship recipients

By Zoila Palma: Galen University celebrated its 2026 Eagle Scholars on Friday, September 11, recognizing students who received the institution’s prestigious scholarship awards for their achievements, dedication and commitment to excellence.

The 2026 recipients were recognized under four scholarship categories: the Eagle Merit Scholarship, Eagle Athletic Scholarship, George Price Scholarship, and the Dr. Dorian Allan Barrow Memorial Scholarship.

The university congratulated all recipients and said their accomplishments represent the true spirit of a Galen Eagle.

Galen University continues to provide scholarship and financial assistance opportunities to students from across Belize.

Established in September 2003 as Belize’s first independent university, Galen University has grown to offer a range of undergraduate and graduate programs through hybrid online and face-to-face learning.

Over the years, the institution has introduced several programs and initiatives that have contributed to Belize’s higher education sector, while providing students with opportunities to pursue their academic and professional goals.

World.title: Balford Henry, award-winning veteran journalist, dies at 74
World.content:
Veteran journalist Balford Henry (right) being conferred by Governor-General Sir Patrick Allen with the Order of Distinction (Officer Class) for distinguished service to journalism.

KINGSTON, Jamaica – Award-winning veteran journalist Balford Henry, whose career spanned more than five decades of reporting, has died at the age of 74.

He died on Monday after a short illness.

Henry entered journalism in 1971 as a trainee reporter with the Gleaner while in sixth form at Wolmer’s Boys’ School in Kingston.

Early in his career, he reported on sittings of the Kingston and St Andrew Corporation (KSAC) before making his name as a labour relations reporter and later a parliamentary journalist.

He also covered major social and cultural activities and historical events, including Bob Marley’s funeral in 1981.

Henry also served as a senior reporter with the Jamaica Observer and a consulting editor at the Jamaica Information Service (JIS).

A recipient of a number of professional awards, Henry was the winner of the Press Association of Jamaica (PAJ) Honorary Award for a series on the social and economic problems facing Jamaican youths in Britain’s inner cities, based on his own experience while living in the country in 1977, according to the JIS.

He also won the PAJ Best Story award for his coverage of Marley’s funeral as well as the PAJ’s first Cultural Story Award for the feature on reggae singer Junior Byles entitled, ‘Fall of a Superstar’.

In 2011, Henry was conferred with the Order of Distinction (Officer Class) for distinguished service to journalism.

He leaves behind two sons and two daughters.

World.title: Sigh of relief
World.content:
ARCHIBALD... had been identified by investigators as one of the main organisers of robberies and break-ins targeting automated teller machines, remittance agencies, and other cash-intensive businesses

THE Chinese business community is breathing a sigh of relief after the fatal shooting of Dewar Archibald — who police sources say was part of an organised criminal network operating across several parishes — during a reported gun battle with cops in St Andrew early Sunday morning.

According to a highly placed source, Archibald, otherwise called Max, was a thorn in the side of several Chinese individuals as he preyed on their businesses and homes.

“He and his cronies were on their way to hit the home of a Chinese man in the Corporate Area when they were intercepted by the police Sunday,” the Jamaica Observer source said.

Police reported that Archibald, whom they described as a “high-risk criminal target linked to two murders and a series of major robberies and break-ins across Jamaica”, was among three people fatally shot during an operation by members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Specialised Operations Branch along Red Hills Road about 1:45 am.

According to the police, the Specialised Operations team was on patrol in the Red Hills area when information was received that a group of armed men travelling in two vehicles — a red Honda HR-V and a white Toyota Probox — was allegedly preparing to carry out criminal activity in the St Andrew North Police Division.

A preliminary police report said the cops attempted to intercept the vehicles but the drivers did not stop. The Probox eluded the police.

“Police subsequently intercepted the Honda HR-V in the vicinity of Knightsdale Drive. Occupants of the vehicle reportedly opened fire at members of the police team, who then discharged their service weapons,” the police said.

Three people, one of them a woman, were subsequently found with gunshot wounds. The two men were identified as Archibald, 44 years old of Mountain View, Lincoln, Manchester; and Damian Byfield, 39 years old of Fraser’s Content, St Catherine. Police sources said the woman, who was unidentified at press time, was of brown complexion, approximately 5 feet seven inches tall, with braided hair, and was clad in a black dress.

Two firearms along with ammunition were recovered, the police said.

Police said Archibald was a member of the Speculation Gang and had been identified by investigators as one of the main organisers of robberies and break-ins targeting automated teller machines (ATMs), remittance agencies, and other cash-intensive businesses.

According to police sources, the woman is critical to the criminals’ modus operandi as “they use her as a lookout or a distraction”.

Archibald has also been implicated in two murders committed within the past nine months — Chevardo Messam at Galleon Beach in Crawford district, St Elizabeth, on December 21, 2025; and Kemar Brown, otherwise called Mars, in Bristol, Alexandria, St Ann, on January 9, 2026.

A woman was shot and injured during the second incident.

Police also reported that Archibald had been linked to a shooting during an attempted theft of an ATM in Drax Hall, St Ann, in April.

Additionally, investigations had further implicated him in a series of robberies and break-ins in Linstead, St Catherine, in February and June; Kingston in April; and Croft’s Hill, Clarendon, in May.

World.title: Ministry targets book list abuse
World.content:
There have been mounting complaints annually about lengthy and expensive book lists.

JAMAICA’S education authorities are moving to rein in controversial school book lists after a special review found that some lists issued to parents do not match those approved by the ministry.

Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon says an electronic system is being developed to prevent such discrepancies, amid mounting complaints annually about lengthy and expensive book lists.

The issue has dominated the news over the past few weeks, resulting in the ministry indicating that it would review schools’ textbook lists to ensure that only essential, high-quality texts are required, given agitation about escalating back-to-school costs.

Following on those indications Morris-Dixon, in a recent interview with the Jamaica Observer, said the measures contemplated will address not just the expense but also waste.

“Sometimes the books are not used. I have seen it too where you look through the book at the end of the year and you are like ‘Wait a minute, I spent all this money on this book and it was not being used’, and so I sympathise with parents,” Morris-Dixon said.

“I spoke to the ministry team, they put together a team to relook the book lists — because book lists have to be approved by the ministry — and we have seen some instances where the book list that the parent gets is not necessarily looking like what we have approved, so we are actually putting in place an electronic system that the schools will have to upload their book lists to. We will go through it and we will make the necessary adjustments,” Morris-Dixon disclosed.

She said the ministry is also mulling whether it could further absorb more of the costs which parents now bear.

“We are also looking at whether or not it is possible — we already spend about a billion dollars on books — to add some more books in terms of the [government-provided book] programme to support students, but obviously that’s another financial expense,” the education minister told the Observer.

Noting that the ministry, at present, provides textbooks for core subjects for grades four to six students in primary schools, Morris-Dixon said the intent is to explore whether or not it “could add to the number of books that are already provided”.

“So we are exploring it, and we are looking at all different methods that we can use, but what we are thinking is: The approval process for the book list, it’s important that we tighten that up and change the process so that we in the ministry review it prior to it getting to the parents, and we can look to see whether it’s an unnecessary burden, and also looking at the extent to which we could probably give more books to the schools,” she explained.

Recently, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness addressed the issue, saying that he had received complaints from parents.

“Many parents have said, ‘Prime Minister, why am I being asked to purchase so many books that my child who is in the grade below… when I purchased them last year… didn’t use at all? When I see the book list for this year, it’s a totally different book list and I can’t use those books again,’ ” Holness said during the Office of the Prime Minister and Office of the Cabinet Primary Exit Profile Awards Ceremony.

“Then there are other parents who said to me, ‘Prime Minister, I have family who live overseas and nobody’s using books. All the books are on tablets and computers; they’re all e-books.’ So there has to be a consideration of a more economical approach without losing the value of books,” he added.

The prime minister emphasised that books remain an essential part of the learning process and stressed that the Government is not seeking to diminish their importance in education.

The education minister, in the meantime, told the Observer that the use of the electronic books sourced by the Government in 2022 has also been contemplated in the search for solutions, but said this measure would need more thought.

“We do have e-books but what we found, we did some work and the e-books are not being used, and so we know probably the students don’t have the devices to use it, and we also want to limit device use in schools, so it’s a delicate balance. We know the e-books could solve one problem, but you may create other problems, so we are obviously trying to be very balanced in the way we move forward,” Morris-Dixon told the Observer.

World.title: Gun law credited with decrease in murders, says Chuck
World.content:
CHUCK... the mandatory minimum sentence is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck signalled Sunday that while legislators are set to review the mandatory minimum sentences under the 2022 Firearms Act, a repeal is unlikely as security forces and other key stakeholders are crediting the law for the sharp decline in murders and shootings in recent times.

According to the Serious Crimes Report published by the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), up to July this year Jamaica recorded 275 murders, 23 per cent less than the 335 reported during the same period in 2025. It said overall, Category One crimes declined by 15 per cent, with 322 fewer major crimes reported than last year.

According to the JCF, the reduction in murders formed part of a broader decline in serious crimes, with shootings falling by 27 per cent, robberies by 25 per cent, while both rapes and break-ins declined by 10 per cent over the comparative period.

In January this year the country reported its lowest monthly murder figure since national crime data collection began in 2001 with 33 homicides, representing a 55 per cent reduction when compared to January 2025 which recorded 74 murders.

“I am aware that in the Firearms Act you have mandatory [minimum] sentences. It is a matter that is being examined but I can tell you that ,from where I sit, the security forces and a number of my colleagues feel that the Act is working and it is bringing down murders and shootings. It is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms. But it is under consideration,” Chuck told members of the judiciary attending the 2026 Assize Church Service at East Queen Street Baptist Church.

The Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, which prescribes a mandatory 15-year sentence for violations, took effect in November 2022 and, among other things, provides penalties ranging from 15 years to life imprisonment for possession of illegal weapons, and establishes a dual regime — distinguishing between prohibited weapons or unregulated firearms and connected activities, and firearms that are duly authorised or registered.

However, members of the bench have telegraphed that the provision is problematic. In 2024, Appeal Court President Marva McDonald Bishop revealed that there would be a full court sitting soon to hammer out issues with aspects of the new Act which, she said, have been proving a pain to lawyers and judges alike.

“The Firearms Act is giving problems to prosecutors, it’s giving problems to trial judges, and surely at the Court of Appeal. We might have seen other cases where the court might seem inconsistent in its approach, and we have taken the decision that we have to take steps to put the court in a position where we can declare conclusively what the position of the court is on a particular area of the law so to avoid confusion,” the Appeal Court president said in presiding over a special sitting of the court marking the opening of the Michaelmas Term — her first since being appointed in July that year.

Additionally, concerns have been that the mandatory minimum provisions in the Act counteract the Plea Negotiations and Agreements Act (plea bargaining legislation), with many accused opting to head to trial rather than plead guilty at their first appearance.

On Sunday, the justice minister’s remarks about the provision came in the course of his comments about the deluge of criminal matters awaiting trial before the island’s circuit courts.

Said Chuck: “Probably one of the main criticisms of our justice system is not access to justice but the inordinate and unnecessary delays in the delivery of justice. In truth, there are non-contentious matters which really should be dealt with in weeks rather than months and years, and it’s a major complaint which we need to address. And then… there are trials that must be heard and must be determined… we cannot try all cases, it’s just impossible, and so over the next many months I will be, literally, not only advocating but on a missionary zeal to urge persons in dispute to really settle matters by mediation.

World.title: Double impact for I-Octane
World.content:
I-Octane.

Recording artiste I-Octane is maintaining his musical momentum with two female-focused singles, Balance Pan Yuh Hand and Whine Up, which are gaining traction in different markets.

Balance Pan Yuh Hand, produced by long-time collaborator Seanizzle, was released on July 22, while Whine Up, produced by Costa Rican producer DJ Kendo, followed on August 12.

The entertainer, whose given name is Byiome Muir, told the Jamaica Observer his relationship with Seanizzle dates back to the early stages of his career, making their latest collaboration a natural one.

“Seanizzle is my brother and a producer I’ve always worked with from day one. He called me and said he had a song that he wanted us to work on, so he linked me in New York City with the idea and we completed it together right on the spot,” he shared.

Balance Pan Yuh Hand has been reportedly generating encouraging feedback from listeners and is also making an impact in the dancehall space. However, he believes there is still considerable room for the song to grow.

“I love the feedback it’s getting from the fans, plus the impact in the dance. We still have a far way to go in terms of promotion, but we’re doing it stage by stage with this song because it’s a big song, so we have to stay consistent,” he said.

Meanwhile, Whine Up has been expanding I-Octane’s reach in the Latin American market, reaching #1 on the Shazam Costa Rica charts. According to the artiste, the song has also been gaining traction in other Spanish-speaking countries.

The track has also found an audience online, particularly on TikTok, where numerous women have been using the sound in their videos.

“This achievement is great because it’s a great look when you have a big song in different markets worldwide. Plus, it extends the I-Octane brand globally,” he said.

Consistency has remained a major part of I-Octane’s strategy as the way audiences consume music continues to evolve.

“We live in a time now where people’s attention spans are very short, so most of the time you have to stay consistent within the algorithms,” he explained.

He described the year so far as a positive one but said his focus remains on finishing even stronger.

“It’s a very good start, but we’re working so we can end it great. We have a lot of new projects coming soon, plus more shows,” he said.

Among those projects are a new album, additional singles, and a new branding line, which the artiste said he is particularly excited about.

On the performance front, I-Octane’s team is currently putting together a winter European tour, which he described as his next major move.

World.title: ‘Dellmar’ remembered as loyal, considerate bespoke photojournalist
World.content:
