World.title: Abkhaz president voices blacksmith in cartoon
World.content:
Abkhaz President Badra Gunba has voiced a character in the animated film Nart Sasrykva, dedicated to a hero of the Abkhaz epic. Gunba provided the voice of one of the film’s characters, the blacksmith Ainar.

Work on the 36-minute animated film, which has taken five years to complete, is nearing its end, with its official premiere due in a month. Director Astamur Kvitsinia adapted the heroic epic, which has several versions, into a format designed to be engaging and accessible to children.

It is unclear why the president became involved in voicing the film. One possible explanation is the longstanding friendship between Badra Gunba and Astamur Kvitsinia, dating back to Gunba’s time as Abkhazia’s culture minister from 2011 to 2014.

Astamur Kvitsinia is widely regarded as the father of Abkhaz animation and has created more than a dozen animated films based on Abkhaz fairy tales and myths.

Versions of the Nart epic, about warrior brothers who battle giants, are found among many peoples of the Caucasus. Most scholars date the epic to the 8th-7th centuries BC.

Each people’s version has its own distinctive features and reflects its particular worldview. In the Abkhaz version, the Narts are a family of 100 brothers and their only sister. Sasrykva, the youngest of the brothers, is the epic’s main hero.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: “Injustice prevails under oligarch Ivanishvili” — video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: EDB notes increase in Kyrgyzstan’s goods imports
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. Kyrgyzstan’s goods imports increased to $1.4 billion in June 2026.

This was announced in a report published by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB)

The EDB noted that goods imports stood at $956 million in January 2026 and declined to $933 million in February.

According to the bank, imports increased to $1.06 billion in March and further to $1.27 billion in April. The indicator then declined to $1.2 billion in May before increasing to $1.4 billion in June.

Furthermore, the EDB added that goods imports in 2025 stood at $898 million in January, $991 million in February, $1.22 billion in March, $1.21 billion in April, $1.183 billion in May, $1.083 billion in June, $1.02 billion in July, $972 million in August, $1.03 billion in September, $1.174 billion in October, $1.16 billion in November and $1.28 billion in December.

The bank noted that goods imports increased in the first half of 2026 despite some monthly fluctuations, with the strongest level recorded in June.

Trend’s analysis indicates that Kyrgyzstan’s goods imports are likely to remain elevated in the coming months, supported by the strong upward momentum seen during the first half of 2026.

Based on the current trajectory, monthly imports could remain in the range of around $1.2–1.5 billion in the near term, although fluctuations are likely depending on domestic demand and import requirements.

The trend suggests that imports may continue to exceed exports by a significant margin through the remainder of the year. If current dynamics persist, the trade deficit could remain under pressure in the second half of 2026.

World.title: Türkiye's construction costs rise below inflation in July 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. Türkiye's construction costs increased at a lower annual rate than consumer prices in July 2026, while labor costs in the sector recorded a growth rate closer to overall inflation.

This was reported in a publication by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TURKSTAT), compared with the consumer price index (CPI) published separately by that agency.

According to TURKSTAT, the construction cost index increased by 28.33% year-on-year in July, compared with annual consumer price inflation of 31.75% for the same month.

Trend's calculations show that the overall construction cost index was 3.42 percentage points below annual CPI inflation in July. The difference was mainly related to material costs, which increased 27.13% year-on-year, or 4.62 percentage points below consumer inflation. At the same time, the construction sector's labor cost index increased 30.51% annually, leaving a difference of 1.24 percentage points compared with CPI inflation, according to Trend's calculations.

A similar pattern was recorded in civil engineering. Trend's calculations reveal that labor costs in the segment increased 31.65% year-on-year, while material costs rose 26.50%. The difference between civil engineering material cost growth and consumer inflation amounted to 5.25 percentage points. The comparison shows that labor-related components of construction costs moved closer to overall inflation than material-related components in July 2026.

For reference, TURKSTAT's construction cost index tracks changes in material and labor costs across residential building construction and civil engineering projects. The index provides data on cost developments in the construction sector and is published separately from consumer price statistics.

World.title: Azerbaijan reports increase in lending to households
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 15. As of August 1 of this year, the volume of loans extended by banks and nonbank credit institutions in Azerbaijan to the real sector totaled 34.155 billion manat ($20.09 billion).

According to Trend’s calculations, based on data from the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA), this figure increased by 3.897 billion manat ($2.2 billion), or 12.9%, compared to the same period in 2025.

Households accounted for the largest share of the loan portfolio. Thus, during the reporting period, the volume of loans issued to households totaled 20.341 billion manat ($11.9 billion). This is 2.369 billion manat ($1.3 billion), or 13.2%, more than in the same period last year.

Next on the list were the trade and services sectors. The volume of loans directed to this sector totaled 4.490 billion manats, representing an increase of 284.2 million manat ($167.1 million), or 6.8%, year-over-year.

The volume of loans to the transportation and communications sector totaled 2.512 billion manat ($1.4 billion). This figure increased by 610.4 million manat ($359.06 million), or 32.1%, compared to the same period last year.

The volume of loans issued to the construction sector totaled 2.561 billion manat ($1.5 billion). This is 774.1 million manat ($455.3 million), or 43.3%, higher year-over-year.

The volume of loans issued to the industrial and manufacturing sectors totaled 1.652 billion manat ($970 million). This figure increased by 54 million manat ($31.7 million), or 3.4%, compared to the same period in 2025.

The volume of loans issued to the mining, electric power, gas, steam, and water management sectors totaled 553.6 million manat ($325.6 million). This is 184.4 million manat ($108.4 million), or 25%, less than last year.

The volume of loans to the agriculture, forestry, and fisheries sectors totaled 512.8 million manat ($301.6 million). This figure decreased by 53.3 million manat ($31.3 million), or 9.4%, compared to the same period last year.

In addition, there are reports of further opportunities for expanding lending in the banking sector.

At a July 31 press conference on interest rate corridor parameters, CBA Chairman Taleh Kazimov stated that excess liquidity in the banking sector, excluding required reserves, amounts to 6 billion manats.

"The banking sector fully complies with all of our liquidity requirements. Even taking these requirements into account, according to general estimates, the banking sector has 4.6 billion manat ($2.7 billion) in available funds. Banks can allocate these funds toward both capitalization and lending," the Chairman of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan noted.

According to Trend’s analysis, the growth in lending to Azerbaijan’s real sector points to continued expansion in financial support for economic activity. Strong increases in credit to construction, transportation and communications highlight growing financing flows into key productive sectors of the economy. At the same time, the banking sector’s available liquidity creates additional room for expanding lending and supporting further economic growth. Overall, the data indicate that Azerbaijan’s financial sector retains significant potential to sustain economic activity through increased credit financing.

World.title: The moment this Knights finals rookie will hold onto forever
World.content:
Last Friday's semifinal win over South Sydney was one of the great nights in Newcastle's recent history, and nobody had a better time of it than Jermaine McEwen.

In his first finals match, the 21-year-old had the game of his young life, inspiring the 20-10 upset victory that has the whole Hunter dreaming big ahead of Sunday's sudden-death clash with the Warriors.

McEwen scored the first double of his NRL career and ran for 187 metres, the best mark of his 37 first-grade matches, and set the tone for the Knights' right-edge defence with a physical brutality that would make a mafia kingpin proud.

Knights win is proof the future has come Stars were born under the finals lights as Newcastle knockout finals win over South Sydney announced the dawn of a new tomorrow.

On a night of many highlights, McEwen's personal favourite was his second try that helped Newcastle kick clear in the second half, as he backed up winger Dom Young to score right in front of the Knights faithful.

McEwen crawled the last few metres before slamming the ball down so hard it's a wonder they could dig it out of the turf.

"The only reason I slammed it was because my parents and my family were right in front of me. I just looked at them, and I was like, 'hell yeah,'" said McEwen.

"That was the best moment I have ever had in my footy career. That moment right there, that's something I will hold forever. So I am just super grateful and so happy."

McEwen's first try of the evening helped get things started as he again trailed Young after the Englishman claimed a bomb inside the first five minutes.

It brought Newcastle into the match and gave the team the start they needed en route to their first away finals win since 2013 and just their third since their last premiership 25 years ago.

Repeating the dose in Auckland is a tall order, but even before the win over Souths, McEwan and his teammates did not lack for belief.

"The Knights have given me everything, and I believe in the coach, Justin (Holbrook). He's allowed me to be the greatest version of myself on that field," said McEwen.

"But when I put the ball down and looked up and saw all the fans, I was (thinking) how happy I am to be a Knight. I'm just so grateful.

"We just wanted to go out there and play with energy and lift each other up."

Newcastle's right edge did a fine job shutting down South Sydney's attack. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

McEwen spent much of the week thinking of how the Knights would shut down South Sydney's left edge, which is just about the most dangerous attacking weapon in the NRL.

Between them, Alex Johnston, Latrell Mitchell, Tallis Duncan and Cody Walker scored 63 tries in 2026, two more than Newcastle managed as an entire club last season.

But McEwen, Sandon Smith and Dane Gagai rose to the occasion magnificently, locking onto the superstars and refusing to let go, moving and defending as one.

Souths did end up scoring down the left through Jye Grey, but only after McEwen had left the field late on.

"When you have challenges, you get more prepared in it. You think about it more. When you're at home or training, you get flashbacks of what you have to do," said McEwen.

"When I have Cody Walker and their left edge — they do it the best in the whole comp. Cody Walker, he is just so good at that stuff.

"Us in D, we had a big job to do, and we just went out there and did it."

Jermaine McEwen and the Knights will look to pull off another finals ambush this Sunday against the Warriors. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The journey through this year to Sunday's knockout final has not always been smooth for McEwen.

He was suspended for one match in June after being charged with low-range drink driving, an incident for which he apologised unreservedly and left him "deeply ashamed".

At the time, McEwen said he let his community down, and he's been trying to make amends ever since.

"Bro, at the end of the day we're all human and just because I play footy doesn't mean I'm special," said McEwen.

"In those circumstances, with the rollercoaster (of this year), that has taught me a lot in life.

"I feel like people can either shy away from it or own up to it. I wanted to show up for the fans and show them what I could do, and repay them in that way."

"Because I know how much the town speaks to this club and the hold this club has on the town. I wanted to repay them with good footy."

A sellout crowd is expected at Eden Park on Sunday, and a win would send Newcastle to just its second preliminary final in the last 25 years.

They'll again be underdogs against a Warriors side that beat them just three weeks ago, and the match marks the biggest game of McEwen and several of his teammates' careers.

But the same was true last Friday and by leaning on the experience of men like Gagai and prop Tyson Frizell, McEwen was inspired to make a difference, and all he wants is to do it all over again.

"These are experienced boys who have been in the game for a lot of years, and when you have them talk to you, it makes you more comfortable," said McEwen.

"You're not nervous. You're going out there to do a good job."

World.title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour over pro-Palestinian comments
World.content:
American rapper Macklemore says he has been dropped from pop star Ed Sheeran's US tour after his pro-Palestinian comments and Free Palestine remarks during a September 4 concert at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium.

Macklemore, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, wrote on Instagram he and Sheeran had "some difficult conversations this past week".

Messina Touring Group, promoter of the US leg of Sheeran's Loop Tour, told Rolling Stone that venue owners on the upcoming US tour dates notified the promoters they would not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore in the line-up.

"After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates," Messina Touring Group said.

Sheeran had no immediate comment.

The Loop Tour is scheduled to resume on September 19 in Philadelphia. (AP: Andy Kropa/Invision/File)

"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine,'" Macklemore said earlier this month.

"I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza, to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them," Macklemore had said during the concert.

Macklemore, a Grammy-winning artist, was on the bill to perform at eight of the 10 shows Sheeran has left on his stadium tour, which will resume on September 19 in Philadelphia, according to Variety.

The Israeli-American Council started a petition urging Sheeran to remove Macklemore from the tour.

Macklemore said on Instagram that New England Patriots owner and billionaire Robert Kraft rallied support among some stadium owners and told Sheeran they would not allow him to perform at their venues if Macklemore stayed on the tour.

In a statement to US media, Mr Kraft said much of his time was dedicated to fighting hate and antisemitism and he felt "a responsibility to stand up when I believe that line has been crossed".

Macklemore denies being antisemitic and said that conflating antisemitism with criticism of Israel's actions aimed to avoid Israeli accountability.

World.title: Police deny targeting LGBTQIA+ community after weekend nightclub raids
World.content:
A Sydney NSW MP is referring weekend drug raids on the city's LGBTQIA+ nightlife district to the police watchdog, saying the incident left the community feeling targeted and intimidated.

Video taken by James Twigg, who was in one club raided by police, shows more than a dozen officers and a drug detection dog entering an Oxford Street venue on Saturday night.

Mr Twigg told 702 ABC Sydney the officers went through the whole venue, prompting many club-goers to leave out of discomfort.

"I happened to be standing at the entrance of the nightclub and about 20 officers sort of stormed the entrance with the drug dog, kind of making us feel very, very uncomfortable," Mr Twigg said.

"You kind of think of those images of the 1970s and the way that the police dealt with the LGBT community there.

James Twigg says about 20 officers entered the club when the raid took place. (Supplied: James Twigg)

"You can only imagine the amount of money that would have been lost by the hospitality venue."

NSW Police says officers searched 65 people during the night's "intelligence-led" operation, resulting in 28 drug detections, 12 fines issued, six cannabis cautions and one move-on direction across multiple venues in the area.

NSW Police Deputy Commissioner Peter McKenna rejected claims the queer community was targeted, saying the weekend's operation went to 14 different licensed premises.

"Five, maybe six of those may consider themselves a place that LGBTQIA+ communities frequent," Deputy Commissioner McKenna told 702 ABC Sydney Mornings.

Deputy Commissioner Peter McKenna says five or six venues raided on Saturday are frequented by members of the LGBTQIA+ community. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

"The same night, we had a drug dog operation in the King's Cross Precinct and across all of those licensed premises.

"I think there has been considerable exaggerations and I would say histrionics around this particular matter.

"We have to go everywhere. Otherwise, we would encourage drug suppliers."

Deputy Commissioner McKenna said he personally reviewed police body-worn camera footage of Saturday's raid and that officers were "polite, professional [and] unobtrusive".

MP questions police priorities

However, NSW Member for Sydney Alex Greenwich questioned police priorities and what intelligence they relied on, noting similar raids in June during Pride Month.

"Why so many police resources were deployed at LGBTQ venues that resulted in a handful of cautions and fine?" Mr Greenwich said.

"James and a number of other people contacted me throughout Saturday night and throughout yesterday, talking about how they felt intimidated going out.

" I think we really need a bit of a fresh approach because the police actions on the weekend really work against the government's vibrancy agenda. "

Mr Greenwich and Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore referred the June searches to the Law Enforcement Crime Commission (LECC), during which some club-goers reported being shoved, pushed against walls and forced to remove clothing in full public view.

Alex Greenwich says he will refer the latest raid to the Law Enforcement Crime Commission. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

NSW Police did its own investigation into the June 13 raids and found there was no aggression or unlawful conduct, according to Deputy Commissioner McKenna.

However, the police watchdog forced the misconduct investigation to be reopened, invoking statutory powers to direct NSW Police to investigate.

Premier rejects accusation of community targeting

Premier Chris Minns told a press conference on Monday he did not believe NSW Police was "picking on any particular group" as part of the operation.

"They do have to confront what is often trade in illegal substances," Mr Minns said.

"If there's going to be trade in illegal narcotics in Sydney institutions, then you can expect a response from police."

In a statement, a spokesperson for NSW Police said the Surry Hills Police Area Command remained committed to working collaboratively and respectfully with the local community, including the LGBTQIA+ community.

World.title: I'm childless not by choice, but I do have biological children
World.content:
People would often tell Brett he'd make a great dad.

"I'd always go, 'I appreciate that,"' the 49-year-old from NSW says. "But to know I couldn't … that did hurt."

After trying to have a baby for many years, Brett (not his real name) and his wife were told by a fertility specialist they would be unlikely to conceive naturally. The couple decided not to pursue IVF.

Brett had been considering becoming a sperm donor. But, fearing it would upset his wife, he never shared his desire.

Then, after learning his cousin used an egg donor to get pregnant, it was his wife who suggested he consider donating.

"I nearly fell over," Brett says.

We spoke with Brett about how assisting others with infertility has helped his own grief with childlessness.

These are his words.

Kids weren't going to happen for us

We'd tried on and off over the years to get pregnant.

The grief of childlessness on Father's Day Michael Hughes had always imagined being a dad, but it didn't eventuate for him. Father's Day is especially painful, as it was the day his wife had a miscarriage almost two decades ago.

When we went to a fertility clinic, they did some tests and said it would take a lot of IVF and even then, may not be successful.

My wife also went through early menopause. So that put a full stop on the biological aspect.

I love my wife very much and she loves me, and we always thought we'd like to have a little one of us at home to grow and nurture.

It was a very sad thing to know that wasn't going to happen for us.

I'd had the thought about donating for years. But knowing that my wife couldn't get pregnant, I thought it would be unfair of me to mention that.

Then my cousin fell pregnant with a donor egg and my wife said, "I wouldn't mind if you donated."

My wife is a lovely person and always has other people in mind.

I was so happy and said, "Honestly, I've been thinking about it for a while."

A looming deadline

What I didn't know at the time was that 45 is the cut-off for donation. Which is how old I was when my wife and I discussed it.

So I got onto it straight away.

I contacted a donor program operated by a fertility care provider in Australia.

There were some forms to fill in. You have some blood tests and genetic screening done.

What to consider before donating sperm While donating sperm can be considered a generous act, there is a lot to consider before doing so.

The process also involved a questionnaire for things like books I've read, my favourite movies, any hobbies I have. It asked about jobs and education, a little bit about family.

You also share details like your eye colour, cultural background. This all helps the recipient have a bit more understanding about you.

I provided photos of when I was three and six years old.

The other component was a psychological screening in the form of speaking to a counsellor.

And if you're married, you need to let them know. My wife had a separate conversation with the counsellor.

She really coached us through what a big deal this is; not something to be taken lightly.

You're not a father, you're a donor.

You don't have any legal obligation or attachment to the child you help create.

I would welcome a donor child contacting me

The counsellor also asks about how you would feel if the children were to make contact.

[Donor-conceived individuals can access a donor's identifying information when they reach between 16 to 18 years of age, depending on state legislation.]

I said I would more than welcome it. It would be a wonderful thing to meet any of them.

But I also understand you have to be prepared for no-one to contact you ever. You have to be comfortable with that.

As a donor, you really have to park all personal things like "I'd love to see what that child looks like."

You can think about it, of course, but you can't expect that curiosity to be satisfied.

September 14 to 20 is World Childless Week. If you have a story about childlessness, we'd be honoured to hear from you

A fulfilling experience

When I first heard a child was born, that was when I actually told my parents.

They were so happy, they weren't even shocked.

Initially, I didn't broadcast it to people.

Now when it comes up in conversation, like when people ask, "Do you have any kids?", I say no, then as I get to know them better, I might share that I have donated.

It's been good to get people's reactions and let them know parts of the process they might not have been aware of.

On my last check there were five children born using my sperm.

I would say after accepting being childless, this has given me a bounce in my step.

It's fulfilling to know there are children out there. It's helping people, I feel good about that.

World.title: Bilby capital of Australia turns mascot into 300kg cement sculptures
World.content:
One of Australia's most beloved tiny marsupials has gone larger than life, with six sculptures set to take over a town in outback Queensland.

Artists have unveiled six cement bilby sculptures in prominent spots across Charleville, outback Queensland, to celebrate the marsupial's national day on Sunday.

The "bilby release" highlights the town's title as Australia's bilby capital and aims to educate visitors about the endangered species.

Visitors and locals celebrated the trail's launch on National Bilby Day, including Murweh Shire Mayor Shaun "Zoro" Radnedge (right). (Supplied: Bilby Art Trail Charleville)

Trail brings together art and nature

Charleville Cultural Association Arts project manager Carmel Williams said six artists were selected to paint the 300-kilogram cement casts based on their proposals.

"It just all came together beautifully, and each one is unique, with their different style," she said.

Six artist proposals were accepted to paint the bilbies, with the three unsuccessful applicants encouraged to apply for a future bilby release. (Supplied: Carmel Williams)

Ms Williams adapted the idea for the project after visiting the Kooka! Trail in the Brisbane suburb of Paddington in 2022.

But it was then a journey of raising money to create a cement mould and finding artists who would decorate the bilbies.

An exhibition at the Mulga Lands Gallery features local artists and those who worked on the bilby trail. (Supplied: Carmel Williams)

Bilbies released into Qld National Park With the population booming inside a predator-proof fence, conservationists have set the bilbies free. But can they survive on the outside?

The cement bilbies are positioned in busy parts of town, including the airport, railway station and courthouse.

Over the coming years, it is hoped the trail will grow to 18 bilbies and include other towns in Murweh shire.

"It gives us an opportunity to shine the light on Save the Bilby Fund and the plight of the bilby," Ms Williams said.

Richard Ranson chose to paint in a bold abstract theme. (Supplied: Bilby Art Trail Charleville)

Abstract and traditional artists decorate bilbies

While most of the artists had to travel to Charleville to paint their bilbies, Richard Ranson had the luxury of taking his time and waiting for the right conditions to paint.

Now he walks past his bilby every day, displayed in Graham Andrews Parklands.

The bilby trail takes visitors through prominent and scenic places in Charleville. (Supplied: Richard Ranson)

"We've tried to place them so that when they take the photo, they've got a nice backdrop," Mr Ranson said.

"They're a great design. You can't look at them and not smile."

He said it showed what the town could do.

"It really does bring together the community, and it brings together the arts and the children. Children love them."

Louise Dean (left) travelled to Charleville to paint her bilby in four days. (Supplied: Bilby Art Trail Charleville)

Pentland artist Louise Dean was inspired by the Charleville Cosmos Centre, the Moreton Bay Ash gum tree and the town's red dirt.

But she said she felt the pressure as she worked to finish her artwork during a brief visit to Charleville, about 800 kilometres from her hometown.

"Presenting a two-dimensional picture to an art exhibition like that is different to actually going and painting a three-dimensional," she said.

Louise Dean practised her design on a paper mache and wire model built by her husband. (Supplied: Louise Dean)

"I have to admit it was a challenge. It was damned hard work, but it all came together in the end, and then they were very thrilled with it.

"It's the most fantastic feeling to have your artwork on display like that and to have a town think that your artwork is worthy enough to put on display."

World.title: Worker hit by vehicle after pipe blast in underground mine
World.content:
Queensland's mining regulator has issued a safety alert after a man was critically injured at a central Queensland mine.

A 71-year-old male worker was treated for significant chest, facial, arm and abdominal injuries after emergency services were called to the Crinum underground mine around 10am on Saturday.

He was taken to Emerald and Rockhampton hospitals before being flown to the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital on Monday morning, where he remains in a critical condition.

The Gregory Crinum complex is made up of the Gregory open-cut operations and Crinum underground mine. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

The mine is part of the Gregory Crinum Complex, which contains an open cut and underground mine, located 60 kilometres north-east of Emerald in the Central Highlands and owned and operated by company Sojitz Blue,

Initial investigations by Resources Safety and Health Queensland (RSHQ) found the worker was carrying out maintenance work on a pipe system when he was hit by a mine vehicle.

RSHQ's report stated the man was standing on the front bumper of a mine vehicle, known as a drift runner, to access the pipework and as he tightened the clamp, the pipe blew, causing pressurised air to blast, creating dust and reducing visibility, and the man fell.

It is then understood the operator of the drift runner, for unknown reasons, moved the vehicle, which struck the man on the ground, the regulator's report said.

In the publication of its safety alert, RSHQ said before starting work on pressurised systems, coal mine operators should ensure workers isolate and depressurise systems, not stand in an area where an unplanned release of energy could occur and establish an exclusion zone.

The safety alert also stated work should be undertaken using suitable work platforms, and not use mobile equipment for that purpose.

RSHQ is continuing investigations into the incident, has isolated the scene and "suspended certain operations until they can be performed to an acceptable level of risk".

The Mining and Energy Union's (MEU) industry safety and health representatives are also involved in the investigations.

"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the injured worker, his family, first responders and his workmates following this serious incident," an MEU statement said.

"We will continue to support our members and the broader workforce as the full circumstances of the incident are established."

World.title: HYROX apologises after Aussie athlete soils herself mid-race
World.content:
A founder of HYROX has apologised after an athlete who suffered sudden faecal incontinence mid-competition was allowed to continue, with the incident sparking rule changes after backlash online.

Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk experienced the medical episode during the competition that she went on to win in Beijing at the weekend.

The incident went viral on Chinese social media, with videos of her competing while visibly soiled shared widely.

HYROX sees competitors combine running with multiple workout station challenges, including sandbag lunges, burpees, sled pushes and rowing using shared equipment.

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) holds the HYROX Women's Solo Pro world record. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

Following the incident, many online criticised HYROX's health and safety standards, while some also questioned athlete responsibility.

"Blast HYROX. Blast the race director," Chris Hersh posted on a HYROX community Facebook page.

"But please leave the athlete alone or have a tiny bit of empathy for someone that really just was in a horrible situation and got zero assistance from anyone in a high pressure, make a decision on the fly scenario."

HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste took to Instagram to apologise "to all who were directly or indirectly involved".

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race," Fürste said in a statement on Instagram.

"In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not."

He said that new event procedures and rules were being drawn up to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

The rules now state that if a "racer's blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers, a Race Director may withdraw the racer from the race on medical grounds".

Before the rule change, competitors were penalised for littering, spitting, or clearing their nostrils onto the race course, which some online described as a double standard.

Following the event in Beijing, HYROX World issued a statement saying that "protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".

HYROX China said the competition area was cleaned after the competition finished and relevant equipment was removed.

It also said it would replace the floor at the venue to protect future athletes.

The incident went viral in China, with many taking aim at HYROX organisers and rules. (Weibo, RedNote and Douyin)

Wietrzyk, an elite HYROX athlete, was invited to compete at the Beijing event.

She has been contacted for comment.

The ABC has also contacted HYROX for comment.

HYROX is held in indoor venues, with a consistent race format that lets athletes compete against each other worldwide.

Organisers say it suits both elite athletes and people trying to improve their general fitness.

World.title: Man breaks into RAAF Base Darwin and steals vehicle
World.content:
A man who allegedly unlawfully entered a defence base in the Northern Territory, assaulted a defence force member and stole a car is still on the run from police.

In a statement a defence spokesperson said the incident occurred at RAAF Base Darwin yesterday afternoon and "lockdown procedures and protocols were implemented".

They said RAAF Darwin security, the Joint Military Police Unit, Northern Territory Police and Australian Federal Police attended the incident.

"The individual allegedly assaulted a defence force member and proceeded to leave the base in a stolen vehicle," the spokesperson said.

Northern Territory Police confirmed officers responded to a report of a stolen vehicle in Winnellie about 4:30pm yesterday.

Police said officers pursued the car after it was spotted travelling southbound on the Stuart Highway, but officers eventually lost sight of the vehicle.

Police investigations are continuing.

Police investigations into the incident at RAAF Base Darwin are continuing. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

It is the second incident on the base in recent weeks, with a lockdown triggered by a training exercise early last month.

More than half a dozen military and civilian police cars swarmed the base in Winnellie about 9pm on August 4 following reports of a security incident.

Eyewitnesses said the alarm lasted for about an hour, with the word "lockdown" repeatedly broadcasted in an automated message.

In a statement at the time, the Australian Defence Force said the lockdown was the result of "military personnel conducting training with specialist equipment" and it was resolved within half an hour.

World.title: Macklemore dumped from Ed Sheeran’s tour over pro-Palestine comments
World.content:
CultureCelebrityIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Macklemore dumped from Ed Sheeran’s tour over pro-Palestine comments Kayla Olaya Updated September 15, 2026 — 12:32pm ,first published September 15, 2026 — 9:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US rapper Macklemore says he was dropped as the support act for Ed Sheeran’s American tour after making pro-Palestine comments on stage this month. The Thrift Shop rapper stood by his “Free Palestine” comments, made during a performance at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium this month, in a detailed Instagram post that attracted criticism from a US-based pro-Israel activist group and the singer Pink. Macklemore has been dropped from Ed Sheeran’s tour after onstage support for Palestine. Getty In the post, Macklemore said Sheeran had told him that New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft called him to say Macklemore was banned from performing in a stadium owned by his business group. “Ed also told me that Kraft had rallied some of the other stadium owners, and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues,” he said in the post.



Sheeran, who is a famously apolitical artist, was forced to pick a side. While Macklemore says the pair remain friends, how did this controversy arise? Who is Macklemore? The Grammy Award-winning artist, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, broke records with his 2013 hit Thrift Shop with Ryan Lewis and featuring Wanz, becoming the second independently distributed song to reach number one on Billboard’s Hot 100. It came off the back of 2012 hit Same Love – also with Lewis – supporting same-sex relationships and marriage equality, three years before the US legalised it.



Known for independently producing and distributing his music, Macklemore has never been coy about his advocacy. When he sang at the NRL Grand Final in 2017, he called for marriage equality during an emotional performance one month before it was legalised in Australia. On Tuesday morning (AEST), the artist said via Instagram, after he was barred from Sheeran’s Loop tour of North America, that he had expressed support on stage for Palestine for the past three years. Macklemore, performing in Dublin last year, has proclaimed “Free Palestine” on stage. Redferns “What I said at MetLife, I have been saying on stages around the world for almost three years. So why is it an issue now?” Macklemore said, adding that he believed his comments during concerts had become a “resistance” and thus it “became so important to silence me”. “I’m sharing a stage with one of the biggest artists in the world, in some of the biggest stadiums in America. At a certain level of exposure, ‘Free Palestine’ becomes too much of a risk. If I kept doing the shows, saying Free Palestine, with Ed implicitly supporting it, the crowd getting loud and showing undeniable support for Palestinian liberation, what artist might speak out next?”



Sheeran has not commented, and a replacement opening act for his tour is yet to be confirmed. How did we get here? The controversy began at MetLife Stadium on September 4, during his support spot for Sheeran, when Macklemore exclaimed “Free Palestine” while introducing his protest song Hind’s Hall, and showed footage of the devastation in Gaza on a screen. Macklemore and Sheeran, pictured in 2014, have been longtime friends. Getty Written after the 2024 campus protests supporting Palestinians, the song is named for Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed after Israeli forces opened fire on her family’s car in Gaza City. (Macklemore also performed the song during his 2024 tour of Australia.)



Related Article Gaza Strip She was five years old and under fire. In this film, we hear her last words “A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine,” Macklemore said during the performance in New Jersey. The following night, he returned to the stage and said: “To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it in no way is criticism of you. “This message is for peace, love, for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.” In his Instagram post, Macklemore said he held no ill will toward Sheeran, who he considered a friend of 13 years. “As I told Ed multiple times on the phone, our friendship can’t change my responsibility to tell the truth about what happened,” Macklemore wrote.



Despite this, the controversy has wedged Sheeran into a position where he must make a political choice – as an apolitical singer. “Ed was in a f----ed-up position. He knew it. His typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before,” Macklemore said on Instagram. UK singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran performing at Melbourne’s Marvel Stadium in February during his Loop tour. Richard Clifford “He told me that the words ‘Free Palestine’ and the image of the Palestinian flag were hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with. “I told him that if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood. But he couldn’t get past his public-facing ‘don’t take sides’.”



A growing chorus of organisations and experts say Israel’s wartime actions in Gaza amount to genocide – an accusation Israel vehemently rejects. Pink and other critics lash out Macklemore’s tour comments drew criticism from fellow singer Pink, who is Jewish. She then attracted backlash herself. Singer Pink criticised Macklemore’s performance in New Jersey. AP “Last weekend [Macklemore] stood in front of a stadium full of music-loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens, dedicated a song to the movement of his choice, and then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn’t about them.



Related Article ★★★★

Sydney live reviews Macklemore brings Gaza protest song to Sydney “You don’t get to decide that for us,” she said. Pink also pointed out that in 2014, Macklemore apologised for a costume he wore which included a black wig, beard and a fake hooked nose, which critics labelled antisemitic. Macklemore addressed Pink’s comments in his Instagram post, saying the real victims were Palestinian people “who have been killed, starved, displaced and forced to live through unimaginable violence”. His post on Tuesday attracted support from activist Greta Thunberg, Irish band Kneecap, British singer Bob Vylan – who have each expressed support publicly for the Palestinian cause – and the Australian singer-songwriter Tones and I, who is friends with Macklemore and has collaborated with him previously.



US-based campaign group StopAntisemitism criticised Macklemore after his recent performances, saying “Jewish fans bought tickets to see Ed Sheeran sing ... [and] not to be ambushed by Macklemore’s anti-Israel propaganda”. According to its website, StopAntisemitism reaches nearly “one billion” people and transforms “awareness into action and advocacy into measurable change, including hundreds of firings, suspensions, expulsions, and arrests”. Who is Robert Kraft? Among the venues to bar Macklemore is Gillette Stadium – home to the NFL’s New England Patriots – in Foxborough, Massachusetts, south of Boston. Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the NFL team and stadium, said the decision to cancel Macklemore was a result of his recent comments “and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.



Owner of the New England Patriots, Robert Kraft. Getty Images “This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf. Their pain and loss are real,” Kraft said in a statement Monday. Macklemore’s advocacy “should not come at the expense of the Jewish community or obscure the responsibility of Hamas”, Kraft said. The tour’s promoter, Messina Touring Group, said in a statement to Rolling Stone that venues had notified it that “they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the line-up, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans”. Macklemore had been scheduled to perform at several stadiums owned by NFL-affiliated groups as part of Sheeran’s tour.



Related Article War Are we in World War III, and just don’t know it? While Macklemore did not name other stadiums that decided to bar him from performing, earlier this year, Ye – best known by his former name, Kanye West – performed in Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium (home to the Los Angeles Rams and the Los Angeles Chargers) and Florida’s Raymond James Stadium (home to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers). This was despite Ye’s long history of antisemitic remarks, praise of Adolf Hitler and the selling of merchandise depicting swastikas. with AP Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Complainant ‘M’ evidence to resume after court hears former 2GB broadcaster bought flowers weekly for former athlete
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent relating to six male complainants over a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the alleged physical acts occurred.

Jones, pictured on Monday, is standing trial on 22 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. Steven Siewert

Yesterday, the third of the six complainants, a former athlete dubbed “M”, started giving evidence.

“M” returns to the witness box today. Yesterday, he told the court:

Jones kissed him on the corner of his mouth at an event in Sydney about a decade ago. “I think I froze at that time,” “M” said.

The court heard Jones texted him that night: “Great to see you. Sorry I didn’t catch up after, had to go back to work. You looked great. I love you, I hope you can feel my kisses darling xxxx.”

“M” replied: “Nice to see you too. I had a very long day today and I am pleased to be in bed now; thanks mate xoxo.” The conversation ended in “M” saying “let me know when we can catch up. Lots of love” and Jones replying: “I will darling. Big kisses forever.”

The court heard that Jones texted “M” on another occasion, after receiving a photo: “I love the photo. I love you. I want to kiss you for hours. That is beautiful. We must catch up darling [name] xxx”. “M” said he did not respond immediately. Hours later, Jones wrote: “I hope my message did not upset you. I love you.” The man said he responded the next day, writing: “Not at all mate. It’s nice to be loved.”

The complainant said he had used the word “mate” for many reasons. “I know I’d made it very clear that ... it wasn’t moving into a relationship, so ‘mate’ was my way of pushing back, I guess.”

Reflecting on the messages, “M” told the court that he believed “it’s a person that is in love with me”, adding that he did not return those feelings.

“M” said that on the last occasion he visited Jones at his harbourside apartment, the broadcaster kissed him repeatedly on the cheek towards his lips and said words to the effect of, “I love you so much, you don’t know how much I love you.” The complainant said he could feel Jones’ genitals on his leg .

The complainant said he pushed the broadcaster away and said, “OK, mate”, in a tone intended to convey “get away from me”, and “got out of there as quickly as possible”.

The court heard Jones had sent the complainant gifts including weekly flowers for years and a dinner set. The complainant agreed he also sent Jones flowers at least once.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Maccas meals and Macbooks: How Australians are getting whacked by inflation
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesInflation Maccas meals and Macbooks: How Australians are getting whacked by inflation Jessica Yun September 15, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s inflation woes are spreading out from the fuel sector to everything from discount fast food meals to premium computers, keeping inflation higher as merchants begin to price in costs that they had once tried to absorb. Over the past year, food and beverage prices rose 3.2 per cent, alcohol prices gained 4.5 per cent, and clothing and footwear increased 4.8 per cent on average according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Everyday essentials, discount fast food, and Macbooks have all increased in price. MATT WILLIS “There are a bunch of businesses who haven’t shifted their prices or haven’t shifted them much because they keep hoping price shocks will be temporary,” said independent economist Chris Richardson. “But as this looks more and more like a forever war, businesses will build that into their pricing.” Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz largely closed amid its ongoing conflict with the US under President Donald Trump, while the Houthi militia movement in Yemen has curbed shipping through the Red Sea. Both steps have sharply curbed oil coming out of the key region.



“People know they used to be better off,” Richardson said. “Those fuel prices are starting to wreak havoc upstream and that will hit downstream everywhere from supermarkets and your Amazon purchases.” McSmart meals In mid-2025, McDonald’s froze the price of its McSmart Meal (two burgers, fries, and a drink; or three nuggets or a sundae instead of a second burger) at $7 for 12 months, but that freeze is now over. It will now cost you $7.95 to get a McSmart Meal, which now offers the option of a hash brown, apple pie or cookies – all smaller items – instead of a second burger. The more affordable offer, the $6.95 ‘McSmart Saver’, will get you a hamburger, small fries and a drink, and three nuggets – but is only available on the MyMacca’s app.



Macbooks, phones, and tech Billed as Apple’s “most affordable laptop ever”, the Macbook Neo launched in Australia earlier this year at a starting price of $899 – but in late June, Apple lifted their prices around the world, pointing to the data centre boom that has resulted in a shortage of storage and memory parts (nicknamed “RAMageddon”). The Reserve Bank’s assistant governor Sarah Hunter called out the AI boom as a contributor to global economic and inflation risks. “Anyone who’s bought a new iPhone recently might have noticed that the price went up quite a bit. That’s actually true for consumer electronics more generally,” she said on Monday.



“It certainly doesn’t move an aggregate needle, but it’s just to give you an example of that global environment potentially being more inflationary.” Grocery staples Supermarkets are one of the first to see how our purchasing patterns change, and Coles, Woolworths and Aldi have all announced lower shelf prices in recent months to keep shoppers on side. Swathes of pantry items now cost more than they did just months ago. A bottle of Bertolli extra virgin olive oil dressing, which was $10 three months ago, will now cost you $16 at full price at Coles. A four-pack of Mother energy drink that would have cost $9.30 in June, is now $14.50, according to figures provided by grocery price comparison site WiseList.



German discount supermarket Aldi isn’t immune from price hikes either. A box of White Mill banana bread mix that was $1.99 six months ago is now $2.49. Economists are flagging more pain to come. With harvest season now kicking in, higher diesel and fertiliser costs are yet to be passed on. “It’s not over yet,” said Richardson. Cafe and restaurants Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership ‘Don’t insult me’: Labor luminary unleashes over falling house prices, real wages Hospitality operators have been struggling with higher electricity, wage, and ingredient costs for years. Consultant and Catering HQ managing director Steve Sidd said his business has overhauled its menus across over 30 venues. Food costs, which usually cover around 30 per cent, had to be reduced to 25 and 26 per cent



“There have been so many costs we’ve had to absorb this year alone,” Sidd said. “We can only sustain so much, absorb so much cost before passing onto the consumer. We’ve had no choice but to put prices up.” “The scary part is, there’s only so much our customers are willing to pay as well.” Sidd has introduced more weekly specials to tempt diners in during the week, but has removed specials during the busy weekend period to maximise margins. In one instance, a popular lamb dish that had been sold for more than a decade had to be removed from the menu as lamb prices hit record highs, and replaced with a seafood dish. “I know my customers are not willing to pay for it,” said Sidd. “But if I didn’t do it, I’d have to close my doors. We’d go belly up.” He predicts that other operators, which aren’t adjusting menu prices and even discounting meals, will not survive. “More and more businesses are closing their doors every day. It’s scary.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Trump set to explode if his man does his job
World.content:
BusinessThe economyInterest rates Opinion Trump set to explode if his man does his job Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 15, 2026 — 11:59am

September 15, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Fed Week” has started with a bang, with the world’s benchmark interest rate breaking through a key threshold and oil prices surging solidly above $US100 ($140) a barrel again. When the members of the Federal Reserve Board’s Open Market Committee, which begins its two-day meeting on Monday afternoon (Washington time), sit down to decide whether to lift their policy rate, they’ll also have to factor in the hotter-than-expected inflation data from late last week. US Fed chair Kevin Warsh and President Donald Trump in May. Warsh is now in an awkward position, partly of Trump’s making, but compounded by his own decisions. Bloomberg Financial markets have no doubt what they’ll decide: they’ve priced in a 25-basis point cut at this meeting and at least two more, and perhaps three, similar moves between now and June next year. The probability of a rate rise at this meeting is priced at about 90 per cent. If the Fed does as the markets expect and raises the federal funds rate for the first time since July 2023, when the central bank was still dealing with the inflation shock generated by the post-pandemic disruptions to global supply chains, it will be on a collision course with the Trump White House.





The war in the Middle East has raged for nearly seven months, with no end in sight. Oil prices have rocketed from about $US60 a barrel before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February to about $US106 a barrel this week, having been above $US107 a barrel on Monday. US gasoline prices have risen about 45 per cent and diesel prices 60 per cent as a result of the war, with the average price of diesel – the key transport fuel – moving above $US6 a gallon for the first time last Friday. It’s now at $US6.23, compared with $US3.76 a gallon just ahead of the onset of the war. Trump’s trade wars and his war in the Middle East have bled into the inflation rate and the cost of living in the US. AP The longer the war drags on – the longer diesel and gasoline prices remain elevated – the greater the likelihood that the fuel costs that businesses appear to have largely absorbed to date will bleed into the wider economy and more materially into the inflation rate. The impact of Trump’s trade war seemed to have passed through the economy and the data earlier this year, having a one-off effect on goods inflation, but then Trump announced a new suite of global tariffs – and a punitive new tariff regime for Canada – that will prolong the tariffs’ impacts on prices.



Warsh hasn’t helped himself. Having decided that he doesn’t like the Fed providing guidance to the markets because wants the markets to provide signals to the Fed rather than respond to the Fed’s view of the outlook for the economy, he’s now getting what he asked for. Related Article Energy Fuel price blowout piles pressure on Albanese for second excise cut The yield on the US 10-year bond – the world’s most important and influential interest rate – topped 5 per cent on Monday. It momentarily hit 5 per cent in 2023, in response to the burst of inflation generated by malfunctioning global supply chains, but hasn’t held above 5 per cent since 2007, before the global financial crisis. The market is saying that the US has an inflation problem, and perhaps even a growing credit risk problem. If Warsh ignores the market’s message, the likelihood is that yields will rise even more. That rise in the 10-year bond yield has come despite (or perhaps because of) US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s arrogant and clumsy attempt to manipulate the market and lower the government’s interest costs by launching a buy-back of longer dates bonds this month. Bessent took on a $US32 trillion market, dared it to take on the US government and, not surprisingly, lost.



Bond investors have become increasingly focused on the government’s debts of more than $US40 trillion and a budget deficit that was $US1.97 trillion in the first 11 months of the US financial year (which runs from October 1 to September 30). The annual interest cost on that debt is running at about $US1.25 trillion and is rising every time a bond issued in a lower interest rate environment matures and has to be refinanced. Warsh also created reference points for himself at the Jackson Hole conference of central banks and economists last month, when, to make up for a poorly received press conference after he chaired his first Open Market Committee meeting, he presented himself as a firm inflation hawk. With the midterm elections now less than two months away, the Republicans are under pressure and Trump is becoming more desperate because he knows the personal consequences of the Democrats seizing control of Congress. “There should be no misunderstanding,” Warsh said at the time. “The Fed’s price-stability objective of 2 per cent ... is a firm, fixed target. Price stability is not self-executing, nor is inflation necessarily mean-reverting. It’s the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices.



“Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do. That’s our job, our mandate and our charge to keep.” It is indubitable that the inflation rate is, and has been for years, well above the Fed’s target so, if Warsh is to be true to the commitment gave at Jackson Hole, he has to raise the policy rate. Financial markets have priced in a 25-basis point cut at the Fed’s next meeting, and at least two more by June next year. Bloomberg If Warsh doesn’t, the rest of the committee – much as they might dislike the idea of defying their chair – might well do it anyway. Recent Fed meetings have shown a rise in the number of officials arguing for an increase in the rate. A failure to meet the market’s expectations and the expectations he himself also raised would undermine Warsh’s credibility and perceptions of his and the Fed’s independence from the Trump White House. It would also raise the prospect of investors adding a political risk premium to the yields.





So far, Trump has said nothing but nice things about Warsh, blaming other “very political” Fed members for Warsh’s failure to deliver the lower rates Trump keeps demanding. His opinion might change, dramatically and aggressively, if Warsh delivers and defends a rate rise – or even two – before the November elections. Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell – who the administration pursued with trumped-up (pun intended) criminal charges – could tell him what the personal consequences of a falling out with Trump look like. World.title: ‘I fear he’ll die in jail’: Cricket legends plead for action on Imran Khan detention
World.content:
PoliticsFederalForeign relations ‘I fear he’ll die in jail’: Cricket legends plead for action on Imran Khan detention Matthew Knott September 15, 2026 — 11:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Seven former Australian cricket captains have urged Foreign Minister Penny Wong to raise concerns with the Pakistani government about the treatment former prime minister and cricketing legend Imran Khan, fearing he will die in detention. Greg Chappell, who played 87 Test matches for Australia, said he was urgently seeking a meeting with Wong to discuss Khan’s situation. Khan, who served as prime minister from 2018 to 2022, has been jailed since 2023 and was last year sentenced to 14 years in prison after a corruption conviction. Former Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan has been jailed since 2023. AP Khan, 73, has faced more than 100 legal cases since losing power in a vote of no confidence, including charges of bribery, leaking state secrets and illegally selling state gifts.



Most of the convictions have been overturned or suspended, and Khan has denied all the accusations. His party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, has claimed they were politically motivated. “Mr Khan led Pakistan to its only World Cup title. He also led his country as prime minister,” Chappell and his fellow former captains, including three former Australians of the year, wrote in a letter sent to Wong on Tuesday. “Australians hold him in great regard — as a cricketer whose skill and leadership left a lasting mark on the game we share, and as someone who has helped improve the lives of Pakistanis by building cancer hospitals.” Allan Border, Ian Chappell, Belinda Clark, Kim Hughes, Mark Taylor and Steve Waugh also signed the letter to Wong. “We take no position on the legal or political case against him. That is Pakistan’s business. But the treatment of any person in detention is a matter of basic humanity, whatever their politics,” they wrote.



“We would be grateful if the Australian Government could raise this directly with the relevant Pakistani authorities.” Wong’s office was approached for comment. Wong met Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar in July. “I thanked him for Pakistan’s ongoing diplomatic efforts to promote dialogue and regional stability,” Wong said in a social media post. Fourteen former international cricket captains from five Test teams appealed to the Pakistan government earlier this year for better prison treatment for Imran Khan.



Greg Chappell said Khan’s health had deteriorated significantly since his long period in solitary confinement, and that he had lost most of his sight in one eye. Related Article Imran Khan ‘Terrible what they are doing to him’: Chappell, Gavaskar, Border, Waugh make humanitarian appeal for Imran Khan “My biggest fear is that he will die in jail,” he said. “I am hoping Australia can raise this at a government-to-government level to try to improve his condition. “This is a humanitarian issue, not a legal or political one.”



Australian Test skipper Pat Cummins last month joined calls for Khan to receive urgent medical care. “I hope Imran Khan is treated with the dignity anyone deserves,” Cummins said in social media post. Greens foreign affairs spokesman David Shoebridge said: “Many in the Pakistan Australian community are rightly concerned about the treatment of Imran Khan and asking why Australia is doing so little in response. “Many Australians have real affection for Imran Khan, we saw him as a graceful leader in the cricket world and those who have followed his career since have seen him fighting for democratic values. “For months I have been asking the Australian Government to make representations to the Pakistan Government and direct the Australian High Commission to seek a welfare check on Khan. This is the minimum we should expect in the situation.”



Pakistan’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has rejected allegations that Khan has been subjected “to punitive solitary confinement, cruelty or deprivation”. “His imprisonment follows convictions by courts of competent jurisdiction after judicial proceedings, and he remains entitled to pursue all remedies available to him under Pakistani laws,” the statement said. The ministry also said “the convicted prisoner is also permitted home-cooked food, exercise equipment and is provided appropriate dietary facilities”.

World.title: Posing as a 17-year-old girl online, I expected body image content. I got gender division
World.content:
NationalSocial media Opinion Posing as a 17-year-old girl online, I expected body image content. I got gender division Amber Schultz Reporter September 15, 2026 — 11:55am

September 15, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When I set up my fake profile of 17-year-old Olivia James, I expected my social media feeds to be flooded with body image content, “thinspiration” influencers, and beauty posts. Instead, it took just half an hour to be shown content that stoked gender division – though this time, the content didn’t attempt to control the behaviour of the “other side”. Unlike the teen boy’s feed, none of the content on the girl’s feed taught that one gender was superior, and the other subservient. Matt Willis Last week, I posed as a 17-year-old boy on social media. Within 13 minutes of scrolling, my fake profile of Jaden Michael was shown content that led him down the manosphere pipeline, culminating in one post at the hour mark telling women to be as subservient to their husbands as they are “to their bosses”. The federal government announced a crackdown on toxic content last week, requiring social media giants to allow Australian users to opt out of their algorithms. The reform is part of its digital duty of care bill that will force tech platforms to take reasonable steps to protect under-18s from misogynistic content, alongside posts that glorify crime or encourage terrorism, bullying or eating disorders.





The TikTok timeline 34 minutes : I was introduced to Adam Cam, who criticised a video of a manosphere influencer boasting that his wife carried both their luggage at the airport while he carried “the responsibility”. “[This] isn’t the flex you think,” Cam says. “The goal of a healthy relationship … is to make your partner’s life easier.”

: I was introduced to Adam Cam, who criticised a video of a manosphere influencer boasting that his wife carried both their luggage at the airport while he carried “the responsibility”. “[This] isn’t the flex you think,” Cam says. “The goal of a healthy relationship … is to make your partner’s life easier.” 60 minutes: Feminist content asking how many “Einsteins have spent their lives washing dishes”, followed by pro-choice arguments on abortion following rape.

Feminist content asking how many “Einsteins have spent their lives washing dishes”, followed by pro-choice arguments on abortion following rape. 75 minutes: An influencer told women to stop falling in love, and instead to focus on capitalism and money “like men”, arguing that “instead of delusions, we’d have a matriarch”. Importantly, unlike Jaden’s feed, none of the content attempted to control the behaviour of the other gender, nor did it teach that one side was superior and the other subservient. There were several posts criticising men’s behaviour. However, most content urged women to fight for their rights, identity and equality.



My experiment culminated in a reel featuring a speech by Ashley St Claire, a former right-wing influencer who was in a relationship with Elon Musk. St Claire said she was offered $40 million by Musk not to appear in a documentary about him. She said Musk deliberately stoked division on his platform X. While some content denigrated men, most encouraged women to fight for equality. TikTok “He is stoking flames that don’t exist in the real world,” she said. “He is causing deliberate division that may be catastrophic if it’s not regulated or tamed, or if we don’t do our part in putting it down.” A recent University of Melbourne study found roughly one third of teenage boys expressed misogynistic attitudes, mistrust of women, and a belief in “traditional” gender roles. Gen Z girls were also more likely to agree with all forms of violent extremist attitudes than their Millennial counterparts, driven by social media feeds. Teach Us Consent chief executive Chanel Contos said in her National Press Club speech earlier this month that platforms were not “rewarded for the quality of their content” but for how long we stare at our screens.



“What we see on our screens is intentionally designed to prioritise content that provokes the strongest emotional reaction, [creating] an environment where hateful content doesn’t merely exist, but it succeeds and dominates,” she said. The algorithm’s currency is outrage. Instead of connecting our youth, social media profits from division.
