World.title: Macklemore dumped from Ed Sheeran’s tour over pro-Palestine comments
World.content:
CultureCelebrityIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Macklemore dumped from Ed Sheeran’s tour over pro-Palestine comments Kayla Olaya Updated September 15, 2026 — 12:32pm ,first published September 15, 2026 — 9:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US rapper Macklemore says he was dropped as the support act for Ed Sheeran’s American tour after making pro-Palestine comments on stage this month. The Thrift Shop rapper stood by his “Free Palestine” comments, made during a performance at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium this month, in a detailed Instagram post that attracted criticism from a US-based pro-Israel activist group and the singer Pink. Macklemore has been dropped from Ed Sheeran’s tour after onstage support for Palestine. Getty In the post, Macklemore said Sheeran had told him that New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft called him to say Macklemore was banned from performing in a stadium owned by his business group. “Ed also told me that Kraft had rallied some of the other stadium owners, and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues,” he said in the post.



Sheeran, who is a famously apolitical artist, was forced to pick a side. While Macklemore says the pair remain friends, how did this controversy arise? Who is Macklemore? The Grammy Award-winning artist, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, broke records with his 2013 hit Thrift Shop with Ryan Lewis and featuring Wanz, becoming the second independently distributed song to reach number one on Billboard’s Hot 100. It came off the back of 2012 hit Same Love – also with Lewis – supporting same-sex relationships and marriage equality, three years before the US legalised it.



Known for independently producing and distributing his music, Macklemore has never been coy about his advocacy. When he sang at the NRL Grand Final in 2017, he called for marriage equality during an emotional performance one month before it was legalised in Australia. On Tuesday morning (AEST), the artist said via Instagram, after he was barred from Sheeran’s Loop tour of North America, that he had expressed support on stage for Palestine for the past three years. Macklemore, performing in Dublin last year, has proclaimed “Free Palestine” on stage. Redferns “What I said at MetLife, I have been saying on stages around the world for almost three years. So why is it an issue now?” Macklemore said, adding that he believed his comments during concerts had become a “resistance” and thus it “became so important to silence me”. “I’m sharing a stage with one of the biggest artists in the world, in some of the biggest stadiums in America. At a certain level of exposure, ‘Free Palestine’ becomes too much of a risk. If I kept doing the shows, saying Free Palestine, with Ed implicitly supporting it, the crowd getting loud and showing undeniable support for Palestinian liberation, what artist might speak out next?”



Sheeran has not commented, and a replacement opening act for his tour is yet to be confirmed. How did we get here? The controversy began at MetLife Stadium on September 4, during his support spot for Sheeran, when Macklemore exclaimed “Free Palestine” while introducing his protest song Hind’s Hall, and showed footage of the devastation in Gaza on a screen. Macklemore and Sheeran, pictured in 2014, have been longtime friends. Getty Written after the 2024 campus protests supporting Palestinians, the song is named for Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed after Israeli forces opened fire on her family’s car in Gaza City. (Macklemore also performed the song during his 2024 tour of Australia.)



Related Article Gaza Strip She was five years old and under fire. In this film, we hear her last words “A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine,” Macklemore said during the performance in New Jersey. The following night, he returned to the stage and said: “To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it in no way is criticism of you. “This message is for peace, love, for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.” In his Instagram post, Macklemore said he held no ill will toward Sheeran, who he considered a friend of 13 years. “As I told Ed multiple times on the phone, our friendship can’t change my responsibility to tell the truth about what happened,” Macklemore wrote.



Despite this, the controversy has wedged Sheeran into a position where he must make a political choice – as an apolitical singer. “Ed was in a f----ed-up position. He knew it. His typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before,” Macklemore said on Instagram. UK singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran performing at Melbourne’s Marvel Stadium in February during his Loop tour. Richard Clifford “He told me that the words ‘Free Palestine’ and the image of the Palestinian flag were hurtful to a lot of people he spoke with. “I told him that if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood. But he couldn’t get past his public-facing ‘don’t take sides’.”



A growing chorus of organisations and experts say Israel’s wartime actions in Gaza amount to genocide – an accusation Israel vehemently rejects. Pink and other critics lash out Macklemore’s tour comments drew criticism from fellow singer Pink, who is Jewish. She then attracted backlash herself. Singer Pink criticised Macklemore’s performance in New Jersey. AP “Last weekend [Macklemore] stood in front of a stadium full of music-loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens, dedicated a song to the movement of his choice, and then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn’t about them.



Related Article ★★★★

Sydney live reviews Macklemore brings Gaza protest song to Sydney “You don’t get to decide that for us,” she said. Pink also pointed out that in 2014, Macklemore apologised for a costume he wore which included a black wig, beard and a fake hooked nose, which critics labelled antisemitic. Macklemore addressed Pink’s comments in his Instagram post, saying the real victims were Palestinian people “who have been killed, starved, displaced and forced to live through unimaginable violence”. His post on Tuesday attracted support from activist Greta Thunberg, Irish band Kneecap, British singer Bob Vylan – who have each expressed support publicly for the Palestinian cause – and the Australian singer-songwriter Tones and I, who is friends with Macklemore and has collaborated with him previously.



US-based campaign group StopAntisemitism criticised Macklemore after his recent performances, saying “Jewish fans bought tickets to see Ed Sheeran sing ... [and] not to be ambushed by Macklemore’s anti-Israel propaganda”. According to its website, StopAntisemitism reaches nearly “one billion” people and transforms “awareness into action and advocacy into measurable change, including hundreds of firings, suspensions, expulsions, and arrests”. Who is Robert Kraft? Among the venues to bar Macklemore is Gillette Stadium – home to the NFL’s New England Patriots – in Foxborough, Massachusetts, south of Boston. Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the NFL team and stadium, said the decision to cancel Macklemore was a result of his recent comments “and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.



Owner of the New England Patriots, Robert Kraft. Getty Images “This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf. Their pain and loss are real,” Kraft said in a statement Monday. Macklemore’s advocacy “should not come at the expense of the Jewish community or obscure the responsibility of Hamas”, Kraft said. The tour’s promoter, Messina Touring Group, said in a statement to Rolling Stone that venues had notified it that “they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the line-up, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans”. Macklemore had been scheduled to perform at several stadiums owned by NFL-affiliated groups as part of Sheeran’s tour.



Related Article War Are we in World War III, and just don’t know it? While Macklemore did not name other stadiums that decided to bar him from performing, earlier this year, Ye – best known by his former name, Kanye West – performed in Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium (home to the Los Angeles Rams and the Los Angeles Chargers) and Florida’s Raymond James Stadium (home to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers). This was despite Ye’s long history of antisemitic remarks, praise of Adolf Hitler and the selling of merchandise depicting swastikas. with AP Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Complainant ‘M’ evidence to resume after court hears former 2GB broadcaster bought flowers weekly for former athlete
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent relating to six male complainants over a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the alleged physical acts occurred.

Jones, pictured on Monday, is standing trial on 22 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. Steven Siewert

Yesterday, the third of the six complainants, a former athlete dubbed “M”, started giving evidence.

“M” returns to the witness box today. Yesterday, he told the court:

Jones kissed him on the corner of his mouth at an event in Sydney about a decade ago. “I think I froze at that time,” “M” said.

The court heard Jones texted him that night: “Great to see you. Sorry I didn’t catch up after, had to go back to work. You looked great. I love you, I hope you can feel my kisses darling xxxx.”

“M” replied: “Nice to see you too. I had a very long day today and I am pleased to be in bed now; thanks mate xoxo.” The conversation ended in “M” saying “let me know when we can catch up. Lots of love” and Jones replying: “I will darling. Big kisses forever.”

The court heard that Jones texted “M” on another occasion, after receiving a photo: “I love the photo. I love you. I want to kiss you for hours. That is beautiful. We must catch up darling [name] xxx”. “M” said he did not respond immediately. Hours later, Jones wrote: “I hope my message did not upset you. I love you.” The man said he responded the next day, writing: “Not at all mate. It’s nice to be loved.”

The complainant said he had used the word “mate” for many reasons. “I know I’d made it very clear that ... it wasn’t moving into a relationship, so ‘mate’ was my way of pushing back, I guess.”

Reflecting on the messages, “M” told the court that he believed “it’s a person that is in love with me”, adding that he did not return those feelings.

“M” said that on the last occasion he visited Jones at his harbourside apartment, the broadcaster kissed him repeatedly on the cheek towards his lips and said words to the effect of, “I love you so much, you don’t know how much I love you.” The complainant said he could feel Jones’ genitals on his leg .

The complainant said he pushed the broadcaster away and said, “OK, mate”, in a tone intended to convey “get away from me”, and “got out of there as quickly as possible”.

The court heard Jones had sent the complainant gifts including weekly flowers for years and a dinner set. The complainant agreed he also sent Jones flowers at least once.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Maccas meals and Macbooks: How Australians are getting whacked by inflation
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesInflation Maccas meals and Macbooks: How Australians are getting whacked by inflation Jessica Yun September 15, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s inflation woes are spreading out from the fuel sector to everything from discount fast food meals to premium computers, keeping inflation higher as merchants begin to price in costs that they had once tried to absorb. Over the past year, food and beverage prices rose 3.2 per cent, alcohol prices gained 4.5 per cent, and clothing and footwear increased 4.8 per cent on average according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Everyday essentials, discount fast food, and Macbooks have all increased in price. MATT WILLIS “There are a bunch of businesses who haven’t shifted their prices or haven’t shifted them much because they keep hoping price shocks will be temporary,” said independent economist Chris Richardson. “But as this looks more and more like a forever war, businesses will build that into their pricing.” Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz largely closed amid its ongoing conflict with the US under President Donald Trump, while the Houthi militia movement in Yemen has curbed shipping through the Red Sea. Both steps have sharply curbed oil coming out of the key region.



“People know they used to be better off,” Richardson said. “Those fuel prices are starting to wreak havoc upstream and that will hit downstream everywhere from supermarkets and your Amazon purchases.” McSmart meals In mid-2025, McDonald’s froze the price of its McSmart Meal (two burgers, fries, and a drink; or three nuggets or a sundae instead of a second burger) at $7 for 12 months, but that freeze is now over. It will now cost you $7.95 to get a McSmart Meal, which now offers the option of a hash brown, apple pie or cookies – all smaller items – instead of a second burger. The more affordable offer, the $6.95 ‘McSmart Saver’, will get you a hamburger, small fries and a drink, and three nuggets – but is only available on the MyMacca’s app.



Macbooks, phones, and tech Billed as Apple’s “most affordable laptop ever”, the Macbook Neo launched in Australia earlier this year at a starting price of $899 – but in late June, Apple lifted their prices around the world, pointing to the data centre boom that has resulted in a shortage of storage and memory parts (nicknamed “RAMageddon”). The Reserve Bank’s assistant governor Sarah Hunter called out the AI boom as a contributor to global economic and inflation risks. “Anyone who’s bought a new iPhone recently might have noticed that the price went up quite a bit. That’s actually true for consumer electronics more generally,” she said on Monday.



“It certainly doesn’t move an aggregate needle, but it’s just to give you an example of that global environment potentially being more inflationary.” Grocery staples Supermarkets are one of the first to see how our purchasing patterns change, and Coles, Woolworths and Aldi have all announced lower shelf prices in recent months to keep shoppers on side. Swathes of pantry items now cost more than they did just months ago. A bottle of Bertolli extra virgin olive oil dressing, which was $10 three months ago, will now cost you $16 at full price at Coles. A four-pack of Mother energy drink that would have cost $9.30 in June, is now $14.50, according to figures provided by grocery price comparison site WiseList.



German discount supermarket Aldi isn’t immune from price hikes either. A box of White Mill banana bread mix that was $1.99 six months ago is now $2.49. Economists are flagging more pain to come. With harvest season now kicking in, higher diesel and fertiliser costs are yet to be passed on. “It’s not over yet,” said Richardson. Cafe and restaurants Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership ‘Don’t insult me’: Labor luminary unleashes over falling house prices, real wages Hospitality operators have been struggling with higher electricity, wage, and ingredient costs for years. Consultant and Catering HQ managing director Steve Sidd said his business has overhauled its menus across over 30 venues. Food costs, which usually cover around 30 per cent, had to be reduced to 25 and 26 per cent



“There have been so many costs we’ve had to absorb this year alone,” Sidd said. “We can only sustain so much, absorb so much cost before passing onto the consumer. We’ve had no choice but to put prices up.” “The scary part is, there’s only so much our customers are willing to pay as well.” Sidd has introduced more weekly specials to tempt diners in during the week, but has removed specials during the busy weekend period to maximise margins. In one instance, a popular lamb dish that had been sold for more than a decade had to be removed from the menu as lamb prices hit record highs, and replaced with a seafood dish. “I know my customers are not willing to pay for it,” said Sidd. “But if I didn’t do it, I’d have to close my doors. We’d go belly up.” He predicts that other operators, which aren’t adjusting menu prices and even discounting meals, will not survive. “More and more businesses are closing their doors every day. It’s scary.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Trump set to explode if his man does his job
World.content:
BusinessThe economyInterest rates Opinion Trump set to explode if his man does his job Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 15, 2026 — 11:59am

September 15, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Fed Week” has started with a bang, with the world’s benchmark interest rate breaking through a key threshold and oil prices surging solidly above $US100 ($140) a barrel again. When the members of the Federal Reserve Board’s Open Market Committee, which begins its two-day meeting on Monday afternoon (Washington time), sit down to decide whether to lift their policy rate, they’ll also have to factor in the hotter-than-expected inflation data from late last week. US Fed chair Kevin Warsh and President Donald Trump in May. Warsh is now in an awkward position, partly of Trump’s making, but compounded by his own decisions. Bloomberg Financial markets have no doubt what they’ll decide: they’ve priced in a 25-basis point cut at this meeting and at least two more, and perhaps three, similar moves between now and June next year. The probability of a rate rise at this meeting is priced at about 90 per cent. If the Fed does as the markets expect and raises the federal funds rate for the first time since July 2023, when the central bank was still dealing with the inflation shock generated by the post-pandemic disruptions to global supply chains, it will be on a collision course with the Trump White House.





The war in the Middle East has raged for nearly seven months, with no end in sight. Oil prices have rocketed from about $US60 a barrel before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February to about $US106 a barrel this week, having been above $US107 a barrel on Monday. US gasoline prices have risen about 45 per cent and diesel prices 60 per cent as a result of the war, with the average price of diesel – the key transport fuel – moving above $US6 a gallon for the first time last Friday. It’s now at $US6.23, compared with $US3.76 a gallon just ahead of the onset of the war. Trump’s trade wars and his war in the Middle East have bled into the inflation rate and the cost of living in the US. AP The longer the war drags on – the longer diesel and gasoline prices remain elevated – the greater the likelihood that the fuel costs that businesses appear to have largely absorbed to date will bleed into the wider economy and more materially into the inflation rate. The impact of Trump’s trade war seemed to have passed through the economy and the data earlier this year, having a one-off effect on goods inflation, but then Trump announced a new suite of global tariffs – and a punitive new tariff regime for Canada – that will prolong the tariffs’ impacts on prices.



Warsh hasn’t helped himself. Having decided that he doesn’t like the Fed providing guidance to the markets because wants the markets to provide signals to the Fed rather than respond to the Fed’s view of the outlook for the economy, he’s now getting what he asked for. Related Article Energy Fuel price blowout piles pressure on Albanese for second excise cut The yield on the US 10-year bond – the world’s most important and influential interest rate – topped 5 per cent on Monday. It momentarily hit 5 per cent in 2023, in response to the burst of inflation generated by malfunctioning global supply chains, but hasn’t held above 5 per cent since 2007, before the global financial crisis. The market is saying that the US has an inflation problem, and perhaps even a growing credit risk problem. If Warsh ignores the market’s message, the likelihood is that yields will rise even more. That rise in the 10-year bond yield has come despite (or perhaps because of) US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s arrogant and clumsy attempt to manipulate the market and lower the government’s interest costs by launching a buy-back of longer dates bonds this month. Bessent took on a $US32 trillion market, dared it to take on the US government and, not surprisingly, lost.



Bond investors have become increasingly focused on the government’s debts of more than $US40 trillion and a budget deficit that was $US1.97 trillion in the first 11 months of the US financial year (which runs from October 1 to September 30). The annual interest cost on that debt is running at about $US1.25 trillion and is rising every time a bond issued in a lower interest rate environment matures and has to be refinanced. Warsh also created reference points for himself at the Jackson Hole conference of central banks and economists last month, when, to make up for a poorly received press conference after he chaired his first Open Market Committee meeting, he presented himself as a firm inflation hawk. With the midterm elections now less than two months away, the Republicans are under pressure and Trump is becoming more desperate because he knows the personal consequences of the Democrats seizing control of Congress. “There should be no misunderstanding,” Warsh said at the time. “The Fed’s price-stability objective of 2 per cent ... is a firm, fixed target. Price stability is not self-executing, nor is inflation necessarily mean-reverting. It’s the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices.



“Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do. That’s our job, our mandate and our charge to keep.” It is indubitable that the inflation rate is, and has been for years, well above the Fed’s target so, if Warsh is to be true to the commitment gave at Jackson Hole, he has to raise the policy rate. Financial markets have priced in a 25-basis point cut at the Fed’s next meeting, and at least two more by June next year. Bloomberg If Warsh doesn’t, the rest of the committee – much as they might dislike the idea of defying their chair – might well do it anyway. Recent Fed meetings have shown a rise in the number of officials arguing for an increase in the rate. A failure to meet the market’s expectations and the expectations he himself also raised would undermine Warsh’s credibility and perceptions of his and the Fed’s independence from the Trump White House. It would also raise the prospect of investors adding a political risk premium to the yields.





So far, Trump has said nothing but nice things about Warsh, blaming other “very political” Fed members for Warsh’s failure to deliver the lower rates Trump keeps demanding. His opinion might change, dramatically and aggressively, if Warsh delivers and defends a rate rise – or even two – before the November elections. Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell – who the administration pursued with trumped-up (pun intended) criminal charges – could tell him what the personal consequences of a falling out with Trump look like. World.title: ‘I fear he’ll die in jail’: Cricket legends plead for action on Imran Khan detention
World.content:
PoliticsFederalForeign relations ‘I fear he’ll die in jail’: Cricket legends plead for action on Imran Khan detention Matthew Knott September 15, 2026 — 11:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Seven former Australian cricket captains have urged Foreign Minister Penny Wong to raise concerns with the Pakistani government about the treatment former prime minister and cricketing legend Imran Khan, fearing he will die in detention. Greg Chappell, who played 87 Test matches for Australia, said he was urgently seeking a meeting with Wong to discuss Khan’s situation. Khan, who served as prime minister from 2018 to 2022, has been jailed since 2023 and was last year sentenced to 14 years in prison after a corruption conviction. Former Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan has been jailed since 2023. AP Khan, 73, has faced more than 100 legal cases since losing power in a vote of no confidence, including charges of bribery, leaking state secrets and illegally selling state gifts.



Most of the convictions have been overturned or suspended, and Khan has denied all the accusations. His party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, has claimed they were politically motivated. “Mr Khan led Pakistan to its only World Cup title. He also led his country as prime minister,” Chappell and his fellow former captains, including three former Australians of the year, wrote in a letter sent to Wong on Tuesday. “Australians hold him in great regard — as a cricketer whose skill and leadership left a lasting mark on the game we share, and as someone who has helped improve the lives of Pakistanis by building cancer hospitals.” Allan Border, Ian Chappell, Belinda Clark, Kim Hughes, Mark Taylor and Steve Waugh also signed the letter to Wong. “We take no position on the legal or political case against him. That is Pakistan’s business. But the treatment of any person in detention is a matter of basic humanity, whatever their politics,” they wrote.



“We would be grateful if the Australian Government could raise this directly with the relevant Pakistani authorities.” Wong’s office was approached for comment. Wong met Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar in July. “I thanked him for Pakistan’s ongoing diplomatic efforts to promote dialogue and regional stability,” Wong said in a social media post. Fourteen former international cricket captains from five Test teams appealed to the Pakistan government earlier this year for better prison treatment for Imran Khan.



Greg Chappell said Khan’s health had deteriorated significantly since his long period in solitary confinement, and that he had lost most of his sight in one eye. Related Article Imran Khan ‘Terrible what they are doing to him’: Chappell, Gavaskar, Border, Waugh make humanitarian appeal for Imran Khan “My biggest fear is that he will die in jail,” he said. “I am hoping Australia can raise this at a government-to-government level to try to improve his condition. “This is a humanitarian issue, not a legal or political one.”



Australian Test skipper Pat Cummins last month joined calls for Khan to receive urgent medical care. “I hope Imran Khan is treated with the dignity anyone deserves,” Cummins said in social media post. Greens foreign affairs spokesman David Shoebridge said: “Many in the Pakistan Australian community are rightly concerned about the treatment of Imran Khan and asking why Australia is doing so little in response. “Many Australians have real affection for Imran Khan, we saw him as a graceful leader in the cricket world and those who have followed his career since have seen him fighting for democratic values. “For months I have been asking the Australian Government to make representations to the Pakistan Government and direct the Australian High Commission to seek a welfare check on Khan. This is the minimum we should expect in the situation.”



Pakistan’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has rejected allegations that Khan has been subjected “to punitive solitary confinement, cruelty or deprivation”. “His imprisonment follows convictions by courts of competent jurisdiction after judicial proceedings, and he remains entitled to pursue all remedies available to him under Pakistani laws,” the statement said. The ministry also said “the convicted prisoner is also permitted home-cooked food, exercise equipment and is provided appropriate dietary facilities”.

World.title: Posing as a 17-year-old girl online, I expected body image content. I got gender division
World.content:
NationalSocial media Opinion Posing as a 17-year-old girl online, I expected body image content. I got gender division Amber Schultz Reporter September 15, 2026 — 11:55am

September 15, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When I set up my fake profile of 17-year-old Olivia James, I expected my social media feeds to be flooded with body image content, “thinspiration” influencers, and beauty posts. Instead, it took just half an hour to be shown content that stoked gender division – though this time, the content didn’t attempt to control the behaviour of the “other side”. Unlike the teen boy’s feed, none of the content on the girl’s feed taught that one gender was superior, and the other subservient. Matt Willis Last week, I posed as a 17-year-old boy on social media. Within 13 minutes of scrolling, my fake profile of Jaden Michael was shown content that led him down the manosphere pipeline, culminating in one post at the hour mark telling women to be as subservient to their husbands as they are “to their bosses”. The federal government announced a crackdown on toxic content last week, requiring social media giants to allow Australian users to opt out of their algorithms. The reform is part of its digital duty of care bill that will force tech platforms to take reasonable steps to protect under-18s from misogynistic content, alongside posts that glorify crime or encourage terrorism, bullying or eating disorders.





The TikTok timeline 34 minutes : I was introduced to Adam Cam, who criticised a video of a manosphere influencer boasting that his wife carried both their luggage at the airport while he carried “the responsibility”. “[This] isn’t the flex you think,” Cam says. “The goal of a healthy relationship … is to make your partner’s life easier.”

: I was introduced to Adam Cam, who criticised a video of a manosphere influencer boasting that his wife carried both their luggage at the airport while he carried “the responsibility”. “[This] isn’t the flex you think,” Cam says. “The goal of a healthy relationship … is to make your partner’s life easier.” 60 minutes: Feminist content asking how many “Einsteins have spent their lives washing dishes”, followed by pro-choice arguments on abortion following rape.

Feminist content asking how many “Einsteins have spent their lives washing dishes”, followed by pro-choice arguments on abortion following rape. 75 minutes: An influencer told women to stop falling in love, and instead to focus on capitalism and money “like men”, arguing that “instead of delusions, we’d have a matriarch”. Importantly, unlike Jaden’s feed, none of the content attempted to control the behaviour of the other gender, nor did it teach that one side was superior and the other subservient. There were several posts criticising men’s behaviour. However, most content urged women to fight for their rights, identity and equality.



My experiment culminated in a reel featuring a speech by Ashley St Claire, a former right-wing influencer who was in a relationship with Elon Musk. St Claire said she was offered $40 million by Musk not to appear in a documentary about him. She said Musk deliberately stoked division on his platform X. While some content denigrated men, most encouraged women to fight for equality. TikTok “He is stoking flames that don’t exist in the real world,” she said. “He is causing deliberate division that may be catastrophic if it’s not regulated or tamed, or if we don’t do our part in putting it down.” A recent University of Melbourne study found roughly one third of teenage boys expressed misogynistic attitudes, mistrust of women, and a belief in “traditional” gender roles. Gen Z girls were also more likely to agree with all forms of violent extremist attitudes than their Millennial counterparts, driven by social media feeds. Teach Us Consent chief executive Chanel Contos said in her National Press Club speech earlier this month that platforms were not “rewarded for the quality of their content” but for how long we stare at our screens.



“What we see on our screens is intentionally designed to prioritise content that provokes the strongest emotional reaction, [creating] an environment where hateful content doesn’t merely exist, but it succeeds and dominates,” she said. The algorithm’s currency is outrage. Instead of connecting our youth, social media profits from division. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Business split on capital gains tax idea, survey shows
World.content:
New Zealand businesses are almost evenly split on the idea of a capital gains tax to address the country's long-term fiscal challenges.

According to the Deloitte and Chapman Tripp Election survey conducted by Business New Zealand, 46 percent of businesses surveyed support the idea of a capital gains tax.

Forty-five-point-seven percent don't support the idea of a capital gains tax, while just over 8 percent are unsure.

The survey canvassed the views of hundreds of businesses, both large and small across the country.

Although Business New Zealand noted this year's survey skewed towards larger firms, and the number of respondents was down on previous years.

It said the depth and breadth of questions, however, mean it remains one of the most useful barometers of business sentiment available.

When it comes to tax more broadly, just under 62 percent wanted no change to personal income tax, while just over 57 percent wanted no cuts to corporate tax. Around 65 percent oppose a wealth tax.

Over 66 percent support raising the age of superannuation entitlement - most commonly to 67 - and 89 percent support making KiwiSaver contributions compulsory for employers.

Business NZ chief executive Katherine Rich said the survey showed businesses are looking for stability and growth.

"This year's survey tells us that, above all, business wants confidence that the economy will keep growing, certainty that tax settings won't be pulled out from under them, and follow-through on the infrastructure plans that have been talked about for years."

Business NZ chief executive Katherine Rich. Supplied

Businesses remain worried about energy, with 80 percent saying future energy prices are an issue they are worried about.

Just over 61 percent think the government is not doing enough to reduce regulatory barriers to electricity supply.

Deloitte New Zealand chief executive Mike Horne said the results show firms were interested in long-term solutions.

"The survey also highlights the importance of energy, infrastructure and international competitiveness. These are not separate conversations.

"New Zealand's prosperity depends on our ability to produce more, connect more and compete more, and businesses are looking for the certainty and investment settings that help unlock those opportunities."

Business New Zealand said when asked to name the single most important issue for achieving sustained economic growth, just over 57 percent of respondents pointed to the economic environment itself.

Fifty-eight percent of respondents said they believe the government has a coordinated plan of action to raise economic performance.

However, just over 47 percent said regulatory changes over the past three years have increased the cost of doing business, against nearly 42 percent who disagreed.

Just 25 percent said that the government's accelerated depreciation deductions Investment Boost scheme positively influenced decisions to invest in new, productivity-enhancing assets; 47 percent said it had not.

World.title: Government should make AI training mandatory for all ministers and CEO's, expert says
World.content:
AI Educator drafts AI policy for New Zealand Midday Report Download MP3 7m

The next government should adopt 20 hours of mandatory AI training for all its ministers and chief executives, an AI expert says.

Consultant and educator Mark Laurence drafted his own AI policy costed at $300 million over three years, which he hoped will be adopted by the next government.

He said effective government leadership was the most important pillar.

"AI is moreso a leadership and cultural change challenge than it is a technical challenge," Laurence told Midday Report.

"The tools are here, the tools are powerful, the tools are reasonably intuitive and easy to coach people to use. What it rests on is: do we have the leadership to guide people into this technology and the holistic changes that it's bringing to organisations and by extension to society?"

He said it was vital government leaders had hands-on experience with AI.

"To put it really simply, you can't lead a transformation of this magnitude when you've only been briefed on the technology," he said.

"When the leaders have done the work to actually train themselves and really experience what this technology can do, and I'm not talking like: 'change the tone of voice of my email to make me sound more professional.' Really when they can feel the power of the tools, that's when the full realisation of what it means for our country will sink in."

Laurence was also calling for a $37 to 61 million fund for public education.

"That's budgeting for a million New Zealand adults being able to do a free course to understand the fundamentals of AI. It works out at about $60 per person," he explained.

"Finland have done a very similar version of this, and what I've done is try to replicate what we have done over five years with our digital boost programme, which cost around $60 million as well. That worked, that was independently judged to have worked in New Zealand, so why would we not do that again for the most consequential technology we have facing us?"

The highest priority, Laurence said, was for teachers.

"I've got a lot of empathy, we've got about 69,000 teachers out there at the moment, they're being squeezed from both sides. They're being asked to understand AI themselves, independently, because they're not getting the guidance," he said.

"We're also relying on them to guide our children, and if children are exposed too early or incorrectly to this technology we run the risk of growing up a nation of kids who are handing over their cognition to AI."

"If you cost all of that out, 69,000 teachers, $400 to 600 a year, comes to around $83 to 125 million over three years."

Laurence said his draft policy had been sent to every political party polling above one percent.

World.title: 'Horrendously high' number of HIV infections in Fiji babies - researcher
World.content:
A "horrendously high" number of babies in Fiji are dying due to HIV related complications, says a health researcher, as the prevalence of the disease grows there.

The New Zealand government website SafeTravel says people travelling to Fiji should avoid activities that could increase their risk of infection.

In March this year, it was estimated 9000 Fijians were living with HIV and officials said high risk drug use was adding to the rapid rise.

SafeTravel warns Kiwi travellers amid Fiji HIV outbreak Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Victoria University senior health researcher Sharon Mclennan told Checkpoint the situation in Fiji was "pretty bad" and had been driven partly by increased drug use.

"You see a lot of needle sharing going on, and that has been the fuse that lit this incredible increase in HIV.

Years of underfunding of the health service had also contributed to the problem, she said.

Mclennan said there had been a rise in mothers testing positive and babies being born with HIV.

"About one baby per week is being born and around about one baby per month is dying of HIV related complications... it's horrendously high, it's very high."

Mclennan said there had been a push to get more people tested for HIV, but there remained issues with the availability of tests and social stigma.

"People don't want to talk about it, because then they'll be found out for behaviours that are not socially acceptable and they may get shunned or questioned."

Fiji did not have a needle exchange programme, Mclennan said, but it was being discussed and planned for.

New Zealand had a role to play in helping Fiji deal with the problem, Mclennan said.

"Last year New Zealand gave $4 million towards Fiji's Ministry of Health for support for HIV, we can certainly step that up. We can step up technical assistance."

That included supporting Fijian people and their families living in New Zealand, she said.

"There's a lot of movement between here and the islands... and so making sure that our pacific populations know and are aware of HIV testing and treatment services here."

Most New Zealanders travelling to Fiji were unlikely to be at risk, she said.

"I think the risk if you're travelling for a family holiday over the school holidays is pretty low. But it's still good to see that the government is taking notice and providing New Zealanders with some advice."

World.title: Woman told police she had Tom Phillips in her car in May 2023 - but officers were diverted
World.content:
A credible sighting of Tom Phillips in May 2023 was not investigated properly by police as they were diverted to another incident, and police inaction led to avoidable delays, a report has found.

A woman was approached by who she thought was Phillips on 28 May 2023 for help jump starting his car near Te Anga Road. She drove him there, took a photo of him, and sighted his children.

A damning inquiry has found authorities could have prevented Phillips from disappearing with his children - or brought them home sooner.

The report released on Tuesday afternoon said agencies missed crucial chances to protect the children and repeatedly downplayed the harm they faced.

The woman called the police after the sighting and described him as Caucasian, in his late 30s to early 40s. She said he was wearing a black hat, black/grey shirt, black jeans, and work boots.

A Tom Phillips sighting. NZ Police

She said that he smelled strongly and like someone who had not had a shower in a very long time.

She also expressed her concern about the man and the children because they seemed to be stuck in the middle of nowhere on a forestry road. Her and her mother-in-law suspected it was Phillips.

Following the report, police dispatched a unit about half an hour after receiving the call, but that unit was diverted to a family harm incident shortly after at a different address on Te Anga Road. The report noted family harm incidents were usually given priority.

Not long after that, the unit advised no further action was required from police.

There was a brief follow up after this, by an "astute senior constable" but what followed was a "series of unfortunate mis-steps and circumstances" that together "conspired to compound the delay in police properly appreciating and investigating the significance" of the sighting.

There is no evidence that the first unit tasked with the report visited the woman's home or attempted to visit the location of the sighting. Police have not been able to explain to the inquiry why it was designated as no further action required, without any follow up.

Regarding the 28 May 2023 sighting, the inquiry found police inaction on the day led to avoidable delays.

World.title: US think tank proposes military shift to Guam, CNMI and Pacific Islands
World.content:
A US foreign policy think tank is proposing a major shift in America's military strategy in Asia that would put Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, and other Pacific islands at the centre of Washington's regional military posture.

Defense Priorities, a Washington-based think tank, said the US should move much of its military presence away from the "first island chain", including Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, and the Philippines, and concentrate more forces along the more distant "second island chain".

The proposal identifies Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, and the Marshall Islands as locations where US forces could be positioned farther from China's coastline.

Under the proposed strategy, Tinian in the CNMI could become one of several smaller air bases used to disperse US personnel and military assets across the Pacific.

In an explainer titled A second island chain strategy for Asia, Defense Priorities researcher Jennifer Kavanagh said the US already has at least 8000 military personnel along the second island chain, most of them on Guam.

Rather than significantly increasing that number, the think tank proposes spreading personnel across Guam, Palau, the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia and smaller airfields such as Tinian.

It said these locations could host intelligence and combat-support units, air defenses, drones and small groups of Marines equipped with mobile anti-ship missiles.

The strategy also calls for fighter aircraft and other specialised planes to operate from the second island chain, while submarines would remain based on Guam and naval vessels would rotate through the region.

Defense Priorities argues that shifting forces farther from China's coastline would make US bases more survivable while reducing the risk of Washington becoming involved in a major conflict with Beijing.

Guam would remain an important logistics hub and base for long-range military assets, but spreading forces across the wider Pacific could make the US military less dependent on the island.

The proposal comes as the US military is already investing in infrastructure in the Northern Marianas, including facilities on Tinian to support increased military operations.

The forward-deployed amphibious assault ship USS America (LHA 6), flag ship of the America Strike Group, steams alongside US Navy ships from the America Strike Group, Royal Australian Navy, Republic of Korea Navy, Royal New Zealand Navy, French Navy and Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force while in formation during a formation exercise as part of Talisman Sabre, 20 July 2025. US Navy / Petty Officer 2nd Class Cole Pursley

But the Defense Priorities proposal goes much further than expanding military infrastructure in the Pacific.

It calls for the United States to eventually end its mutual defense alliances with South Korea, Australia, the Philippines, and Japan and replace them with narrower security partnerships.

It also recommends Washington adopt an explicit policy of non-intervention over Taiwan.

The think tank proposes removing most US Army and Marine Corps deployments from Asia and significantly reducing American air and naval forces in the region.

Defense Priorities said the changes could be phased in over three to eight years, with most completed by 2030 and the transition finalised by 2035.

It argues that concentrating a smaller US military presence farther east would continue to protect American access to Asian markets and trade routes without maintaining large forces close to China.

World.title: 'We are deeply sorry': Government apologises to Tom Phillips' children after damning inquiry
World.content:
You can read the full report at the bottom of this page.

A public inquiry into the handling of the Tom Phillips case says the harm he caused in isolating the children as well as concerns from the maternal whānau were "minimised or overlooked by agencies for significant periods".

It also says that while agencies worked well together at times a more consistent and collaborative interagency approach "could have prevented the children's disappearance and brought them back sooner".

The Government has apologised to the Phillips children for failing to protect them.

"For that we are deeply sorry".

The Government, Police and Oranga Tamariki (OT) have accepted the findings and recommendations, with OT's chief executive calling the report "difficult and at times harrowing reading".

"It identifies opportunities that were missed to keep these children safe."

Phillips died following a shootout with police after they were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of 8 September 2025.

He had spent 1358 days in the bush with his children by that point and shot a police officer several times during the confrontation.

In November, former Attorney-General Judith Collins announced an inquiry into the handling of the Phillips case by authorities and whether all "practicable steps" were taken to ensure the safety and welfare of the Phillips children as well as whether they responded appropriately and in a timely way to locate the children once they had disappeared.

The Honourable Justice Simon Moore KC was appointed as the sole member of the inquiry.

The final report was released on Tuesday.

Justice Simon Moore KC RNZ / Dan Cook

Phillips disappeared with his three children in September 2021 and did not return for 18 days, despite extensive searches. Upon reappearing, Phillips was charged with wasting police resources.

Police also made a report of concern to Oranga Tamariki (OT), which the report says was "detailed and made promptly".

"Yet, it lacked key and critical explanations for the concerns it raised. police, at that time, appeared to consider that Tom Phillips had staged his and his children's death by how he had left the ute on the beach. They were also seriously concerned that he might take the children away again. These concerns were not sufficiently conveyed to Oranga Tamariki."

Moore KC said OT acted promptly on the report of concern and conducted a home visit within a matter of days.

"However, in assessing the question of risk posed to the children by Tom Phillips, Oranga Tamariki appeared to be largely dismissive of multiple concerns raised by the maternal family."

On October 6, 2021 OT reported to the Family Court that the children were "completely fine" and that, in the circumstances there may not be need for further OT involvement.

"Oranga Tamariki did not inform the Court of the concerns of the maternal family, or the ongoing police investigation and concerns. It should have.

"Had police and Oranga Tamariki worked more closely and collaboratively during this early stage, the taking of the children by Tom Phillips a second time could have been prevented or, at least, made more difficult."

Moore KC also said that during this time the Ministry of Education and Education Review Office could have also made inquiries of Phillips and his "ongoing suitability to home educate the children."

On or about 10 December 2021, Phillips again disappeared with the children.

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The report said police did not initially launch a search and rescue response or a Criminal Investigation Branch (CIB) investigation as occurred following the first disappearance.

"Intentionally they adopted a low-key approach by engaging with the local community. This strategy appears to have been predicated on the misconceived view that there were no concerns for the children's welfare, despite their isolation in dense bush segregated from family and friends.

"This view also overlooked information police held suggesting that Tom Phillips was highly motivated to keep the children hidden to avoid the Family Court proceedings."

Moore KC said the approach led police to miss "key opportunities early in the disappearance" to identify or discover evidence that may have led to the children's earlier recovery.

"Instead, police should have developed a proactive investigation strategy, including more Criminal Investigation Branch staff, and a police-led multi-agency response from the outset."

He said that extensive resources and investigative skills were applied to the task of trying to locate the children during the second disappearance.

"Police deployed a wide range of investigative methods, techniques and technologies, including area canvassing, public appeals, the offer of a reward, searching and clearing locations of interest, aerial searches, and electronic surveillance.

"And police took prompt and targeted steps, together with NZDF, in response to, and following, the October 2024 and April 2025 sightings."

Moore KC said some steps could have been taken earlier, including obtaining surveillance device warrants before August 2023, earlier use of covert intersection and road cameras and offering a reward prior to June 2024.

The report also referred to "avoidable delays" in identifying information including a member of the public calling police in May 2023 with a "credible sighting" of Phillips and the children.

"But police delays meant this sighting was not properly followed up in a timely way."

Police also "could and should have" linked the May 2023 Te Kūiti bank robbery to Phillips "much more promptly than they did". It took the police about three months.

Te Anga Road, where Tom Phillips was shot. Dean Purcell/New Zealand Herald via Getty Images

Moore KC said OT could also have done more, and should not have closed the report of concern in February 2022.

"It did so in the face of compelling concerns raised by the children's older sisters as to the risk and harm to the children of being isolated from family and society."

The agency should also have maintained communication with police, particularly in relation to the risks posed to the children, Moore KC says.

"This would have better informed the police response, and the urgency required in recovering the children. Oranga Tamariki should also have informed the Family Court of the risks to the children."

The inquiry also looked at how Phillips obtained and maintained a gun licence, weapons, and ammunition.

Moore KC said police did not take all practicable steps to respond to allegations by Phillips' former partner about firearm safety in early 2021.

"Police did not, but should have, identified and seized firearms after his licence was suspended and considered Tom Phillips' access to other firearms in the home where he was required to reside. Those additional steps could have contributed to recovering the children sooner."

Moore KC made nine recommendations including that police review their existing policies and practices regarding making reports of concern to OT and that Oranga Tamariki ensured that police concerns and evaluations are "understood rather than listed".

It is also recommended that Oranga Tamariki review the role and operation of s 132 (Care of Children Act) reports, in terms of scope, guidance, and facilitation of its interaction with the Family Court.

He also recommended that the Ministry of Education requires additional information when considering applications for, or reviewing, exemptions from enrolment and that the Ministry requires consent from all parents and guardians for exemption.

Oranga Tamariki have also been urged to use "the insights arising from this Inquiry to strengthen its practice guidance and training".

Minister for Social Development & Employment and Minister for Child Poverty Reduction Louise Upston. RNZ/Nick Monro

'We are deeply sorry'

Senior Minister Louise Upston, who is leading the Government's response to the inquiry, said agencies underplayed or overlooked the harm caused by Phillips isolating the children and missed "significant opportunities" to intervene.

The concerns of their maternal whānau were also repeatedly minimised as part of a parenting dispute.

"To the Phillips children directly, this report has found that our agencies did not take all practical steps to protect you," she said.

"For that we are deeply sorry."

The Government has accepted all nine recommendations from the inquiry, with police and other agencies already changing policies in response.

OT chief executive Amanda Malu said the agency accepted the findings and recommendations with changes underway.

"This report makes for difficult and at times harrowing reading," she said.

"It identifies opportunities that were missed to keep these children safe."

"I would particularly like to acknowledge the courage shown by the children's mother and older siblings, we did not listen in the way we should have, and this family deserved better from us."

Malu said OT was taking "immediate action" to address the issues identified and "strengthen practice across the organisation".

"I am heartened to read that from 2023 the actions of our staff in relation to this case were commended, especially on the day the children were found."

"However, some of our actions before that time fell short of my expectations."

Changes made including better information sharing and collaboration with police.

"The Police Commissioner and I are united in our resolve to ensure our agencies are working closely together when it comes to the safety and wellbeing of children."

Tom Phillips' campsite. Supplied/NZ Police

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers said in a statement police also accepted the findings and recommendations.

"As the Inquiry noted, this was a complex and unique situation and the investigation was undertaken in a very physically challenging environment over nearly four years.

"While the report acknowledges this specific situation is unlikely to be repeated, the findings will be valuable in assessing whether relevant processes and policies are fit for purpose."

Chambers said he would work with Malu to "ensure the recommendations are actioned, especially as they relate to information-sharing and inter-agency cooperation".

"Police acted commendably by making a report of concern to Oranga Tamariki.

"However it is clear there were gaps in information-sharing and follow-up discussions. That is a joint responsibility, and it is important we get that right."

Chambers said the inquiry also made it clear that in the initial stages the police investigation was "not given the focus and resource it required".

"As the Inquiry outlines, police did put significantly more resource into the investigation once it became apparent how determined Tom Phillips was to remain hidden. It is now clear that should have happened earlier.

"The issues identified in this report should not detract from the commitment of police staff who put everything they had into trying to find and safely return the children over nearly four years."

Chambers said the inquiry also recognised that "overall we tried every operational tactic available to us".

"We appreciate the acknowledgement of the risks staff faced and the courage shown by police staff involved in the search and on the night Tom Phillips was shot and the children were safely recovered."

World.title: Tauranga Hospital Emergency Department staff declare 'state of emergency'
World.content:
*Correction: This story has been updated to clarify the NZNO's stance

Emergency Department staff at Tauranga Hospital have declared "a state of emergency", warning of the risks of an ED which they say is often running at 150-200 percent of its capacity, without the staffing needed.

More than 100 Nurses Organisation (NZNO) members and ED staff at the hospital have written a letter to Health New Zealand's (HNZ) CEO Dale Bramley last Tuesday about their concerns.

The letter said the ED hasn't received the extra nursing staff required, as identified in "Care Capacity Demand Management" (CCDM) assessments over the past two years.

It said a patient collapsing in the ED wait room toilet was a stark reminder of the risks when overcrowding becomes normalised, and the ED is required to operate beyond their capacity everyday.

HNZ's regional director for Midland, Cath Cronin, said in a statement that the incident happened on 25 August, and that the patient had a medical event about two hours after they came to ED.

NZNO delegate John Wylie said staff being asked to assess and treat some patients in corridors had become routine practice due to the ongoing patient flow pressures.

"We are often working at more than 150-200% capacity, and I cannot recall any recent day when the ED was not running at over 100% capacity," he said.

The letter urged HNZ to approve the hiring of more nurses, based on calculations from the previous CCDMs.

Modelling for 2025/2026 found that 13.66 more roles were needed for Tauranga's ED, across nurses and health care assistants, and 16.78 more roles were needed for 2026/2027, in order to meet safe staffing.

NZNO president Anne Daniels said the need for extra staffing was likely to be even more, because of the big increase in presentations to ED this winter.

A response from Dale Bramley, dated a day after he received the letter from the workers, said he'd recently visited the Tauranga Hospital ED.

He said he'd had conversations with staff about the challenges on the frontline.

"I acknowledge the sustained pressures experienced by the department and the impact these can have on both staff wellbeing and the delivery of patient care,

"Ensuring Tauranga ED has the workforce and resources it needs to provide safe, high-quality care is a priority," he said in the letter.

Bramley said decisions on staffing sit with the regional director for Midland - Cath Cronin - and the interim group director of operations for Bay of Plenty, Jo Gibbs.

He said he'd asked Cronin and Gibbs to meet with staff, and agree on the way forward on uplifting staff numbers.

"I have asked that this meeting occurs within a fortnight," said Bramley in the letter.

Cronin said in a statement that Tauranga Hospital's ED continues to experience significant demand, reflecting rapid population growth and increasing complexity of patient presentations.

"Winter illnesses have added further pressure to an already busy service.

"We recognise some patients have experienced longer waits than anyone would want," she said.

Cronin said they had offered to meet with staff at Tauranga Hospital, and were working out a time for the meeting.

Workforce capacity must evolve alongside demand as the community continues to grow, she said.

Cronin said Tauranga Hospital is part of the government's Budget 2026 hospital redevelopment programme, which includes a new acute services block with a "significantly expanded" ED.

In August, NZNO president Anne Daniels posted on social media that there needed to be a change of government for student nurses to see a real future in New Zealand.

But NZNO said that was not an official policy and the post was being removed.

World.title: 'Ongoing matter' relating to Labour’s top cop candidate Rakesh Naidoo - Police Minister
World.content:
The Police Minister says there's an "ongoing matter" in relation to Labour's top cop candidate, Rakesh Naidoo, but won't say what it is.

Naidoo's candidacy - announced in June - prompted public criticism from Police Commissioner Richard Chambers and Minister Mark Mitchell, both claiming the superintendent should have declared his intentions earlier.

An internal review later concluded that Naidoo had complied with police policy, though noted it would have been "prudent" for him to have given his superiors more advance warning.

Mitchell was asked about Naidoo by media on Tuesday, saying there were "two or three different facets to this situation".

"And they have dealt with one of them."

Police Minister Mark Mitchell. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

After the review's findings were announced, Mitchell confirmed to RNZ he had two phone calls with Chambers on 8 and 9 June.

"[The calls] were to discuss the situation, including the response to media queries, concerns the minister held in relation to the disclosure timeline, including pre-existing concerns regarding a sensitive briefing Mr Naidoo had attended with the minister prior to Mr Naidoo advising anyone at police of his political intentions."

Mitchell declined to release information in relation to the sensitive briefing under section 6 (c) of the Official Information Act.

Section 6 (c) relates to prejudicing the maintenance of the law, including the prevention, investigation, and detection of offences, and the right to a fair trial.

Mitchell's office confirmed to RNZ earlier this month the grounds for withholding under Section 6c of the OIA still applied.

Mitchell referred to the OIA again on Tuesday and said "the OIA is very clear it says there's matters that can't be disclosed because there's an ongoing matter".

He said he was unable to comment further.

Chris Hipkins, August 2026. Zach Cornelisen / RNZ

RNZ has approached Labour and police for comment on Mitchell's remarks.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said Mitchell had "crossed a line here".

"He is the Minister of Police, and he is using that office to spread claims about a Labour candidate who doesn't even know what the specific accusation against him is. You cannot use the power of the police portfolio to invent allegations against political opponents.

"Mark Mitchell should be ashamed of himself. Mark Mitchell should not be commenting, directing or be privy to police employment matters."

Police declined to comment on Tuesday.

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers. VNP / Phil Smith

RNZ earlier asked police for comment on whether there was an investigation into Naidoo.

A spokesperson said "we have no further comment on the matter".

A Labour spokesperson told RNZ last week they had not been informed of an investigation.

Speaking to RNZ last week for the first time since being recruited by Labour, Naidoo said he would not do anything differently with hindsight, pointing to a police review which cleared him of any wrongdoing.

In a sit-down interview marking his entry into the election campaign, Naidoo remained diplomatic about the criticism levelled at him by his superiors.

"In my view, they were expressing themselves based on the information that they had," he said.

World.title: Young Brisbane Lions star Logan Morris re-signs with reigning premiers
World.content:
Young Brisbane Lions star Logan Morris has signed a two-year contract extension, tying him to the club until the end of 2029.

The 21-year-old, who earned his first All-Australian blazer this year, was set to be one of the biggest names on the market at the end of next season.

The signing comes as the Lions prepare to take on the Hawks in a preliminary final on Saturday at the MCG.

"There’s no point dragging [contract negotiations] out if I know what I want to do, and I wanted to stay at Brisbane," Morris said.

"I wanted to just get it done and now I can focus on this week, and hopefully the next few years will be exciting."

Morris kicked 67 goals in the 2026 home-and-away season, finishing second in the Coleman Medal behind Sydney's Charlie Curnow.

It marks the third huge signing coup for the Lions in a week, after Zac Bailey and Dayne Zorko also extended their careers with the club.

When asked about interest from other clubs that may have made higher offers, Morris said he had not given much thought to the money.

"I just thought … more about what I'm happy with and the team that I'm at; I don't want to leave a team where I'm happy where I am mentally and I've got a good group of mates," he said.

"I think playing within a good team that’s got good values and playing with all my mates is more valuable to me than a bit more money, so that's what it ultimately came down to."

World.title: Ella Heads cops big ban for bump that broke star Demon's jaw
World.content:
Port Adelaide defender Ella Heads has been handed a three-match AFLW ban for her bump that fractured the jaw of Melbourne's Eliza McNamara.

McNamara had just fired off a handball in Sunday's 51-point win when Heads ran in and collected the midfielder front-on with her shoulder.

A dazed McNamara had blood coming out from her face as she was assisted from the ground.

The 24-year-old was taken to hospital, with the Demons confirming on Monday she had undergone surgery, with no timeline set for her return.

The incident was classified as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact, drawing a three-match ban.

"That was a really poor challenge," former AFLW star Kate McCarthy said.

"It was probably one of the worst bumps I’ve seen on the AFLW field in regards to being late, being high and just being really careless and not eliciting that duty of care that we now know is placed on you as an AFLW player when you elect to bump."

That equates to a quarter of the 12-round home-and-away season, and Heads will miss games against Sydney, the Western Bulldogs and Adelaide unless Port can downgrade the charge.

In other tribunal news, West Coast's Abbygail Bushby was handed a one-match ban for her clumsy collision with the Brisbane Lions' Sophie Peters.

Peters had her head over the ball when Bushby ran in and tumbled over her opponent.

Richmond's Montana McKinnon was handed a one-match rough conduct ban for her run-in with St Kilda's Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: India refuses to accept Asia Cup cricket trophy from Pakistani minister
World.content:
Political tensions between India and Pakistan have spilled onto the cricket field again, with India's women refusing to accept the Asia Cup trophy from Asian Cricket Council (ACC) chairman Mohsin Naqvi.

India dominated from the start to win the tournament for a record eighth time, beating Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final in Dubai.

After winning the toss, India scored 5-183 before dismissing Sri Lanka for 111 in 20 overs.

The presentation ceremony was delayed nearly an hour, during which the Indian team conducted its own medal presentation, with Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia presenting the best fielder medal to Nandani Sharma.

Naqvi — chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board and the ACC, as well as Pakistan's interior minister — stood on the dais with several ACC officials, but the Indian team did not appear to receive medals or the trophy, with social media footage showing them leaving the field as the officials waited on stage.

The ceremony ended abruptly after medals were presented to the Sri Lankan team and match officials, and Naqvi presented the runners-up cheque to Sri Lanka captain Chamari Athapaththu.

"This is BCCI's stand [to not take trophy from Naqvi]. We can't say anything on this," India coach Amol Muzumdar said.

"India are officially the champions. Trophy or no trophy doesn't matter to us.

"For us, this tournament is over, we are the champions. That's good enough. It was on the big board that India are the champions of Asia Cup 2026."

Cross-border tensions between India and Pakistan brought the two countries to the brink of war last year, with the acrimony also spilling onto the cricket field. Indian cricketers have avoided handshakes with Pakistan players and refused to accept the trophy and medals from a Pakistani official at several tournaments.

The Indian men's team beat Pakistan three times in the Asia Cup, including the final, but Suryakumar Yadav's team refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi and did not shake hands with Pakistan players in any of the three games.

The Indian women's team did not shake hands with the Pakistan team in its match earlier in the tournament, after which Muzumdar also said: "That stand has been taken by BCCI and we stand by it."
